Members of the same people who settled Easter Island also discovered Hawaii, a new study finds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Native Hawaiians and Easter Islanders genetically descend from the same "ultravoyager" Polynesian group that crossed vast distances of ocean to reach these remote islands, a new study finds.

Easter Island (also known as Rapa Nui) and Hawaii are part of Polynesia, a group of more than 1,000 islands spread over an area of the Pacific Ocean roughly equal to the areas of North and South America combined. Hawaii and Easter Island are the farthest of these isles from each other, at about 4,500 miles (7,200 kilometers) apart — around the distance from San Francisco to Lima, Peru.

The researchers discovered the connection by analyzing the genomes of 1,050 modern individuals across Polynesia, including 317 Native Hawaiians and 12 Easter Islanders. "Each person's genome contains genetic code from both parents, and from all four grandparents, and their parents, and so on," study co-author Alexander Ioannidis, a computational geneticist at Stanford University, told Live Science. "Each genome encodes an enormous number of ancestors. So with even a few individuals, we can get information about an enormous number of people from each island."

Specifically, the scientists compared the length of chromosomal segments shared among people from different islands. The longer these shared segments are between two people, the more recently they shared a common ancestor.

Even though Hawaii and Easter Island are far-flung, the researchers discovered that the Indigenous people of Hawaii and Rapa Nui are the most genetically related to one another. The team reported its findings Oct. 8 in the journal Science.

"This was really shocking at first — these islands are so distant from one another," Ioannidis said.

The scientists found that Hawaii and Easter Island were likely both settled by members of a single "ultravoyager" culture from the Mangareva islands, about 3,440 miles (5,530 km) southeast of Hawaii and 1,600 miles (2,600 km) west of Easter Island. (In 2020, the researchers found that members of this ultravoyaging group had mixed with Indigenous people in what is now Colombia, although it's unclear if this partnering occurred on an island or on the continent.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Once you know there was this extremely capable long-distance ultravoyaging culture capable of reaching one of these islands, having it reach the other makes more sense," Ioannidis said.

The area near Mangareva, including the Austral Islands, the Society Islands, the Marquesas Islands, and the Tuamotu Archipelago, "spans an area the size of Europe," Ioannidis said. "Sailing in-between these islands would have required skilled navigation. So it makes sense that developing such long-distance navigation skills would have ultimately helped people settle far-off Easter Island and Hawaii."

All in all, these genetic findings suggest the ancestors of Native Hawaiians and Easter Islanders shared some time together as a common group after splitting away from the population of ancient Mangareva. Some members of this group then went on to settle Hawaii, and others from this Mangareva group voyaged to Easter Island.

This new genetic data linking Hawaii, Easter Island and Mangareva "agrees very well with what we see archaeologically," Patrick Kirch, an archaeologist at the University of Hawai'i at Manoa who did not take part in this research, told Live Science. "It gives scientists a lot of confidence when independent lines of evidence from different disciplines give similar results."

The researchers also investigated the effects of genetic bottlenecks that resulted when these islands were settled by small numbers of people — phenomena known as "founder effects."

"If you have a rare genetic trait that happens to occur in this small number of individuals, if this small population grows rapidly, this trait can go on to show up in a high percentage of the resulting population," Ioannidis said. "So if a rare genetic variant once only affected a few people, it can start affecting a decent number of individuals."

The scientists found that Native Polynesian populations examined in the study often experienced a compounding set of founder effects over time. This is because islands settled by a few people then went on to send out small groups to settle other islands, and so on.

Previous research has looked at the founder effects in groups of European descent, such as the Amish, Finns and Ashkenazi Jews, resulting in standard screenings for certain genetic conditions in these groups.

The new study revealed that an even stronger founder effect has been overlooked among Native Hawaiians, with founder effects more than 10 times larger than in those European groups.

"The founder effect doesn't just reflect genetic diversity, but also cultural and linguistic diversity," Kirch said. "It probably helps explain why the cultures of eastern Polynesia all share a lot in common — they all trace to one central group."

These findings not only shed light on Polynesians' past, but also their current health. The researchers found that three genetic variants that are exceedingly rare among the global population — linked with dislocated lenses in the eyes, progressive vision loss, and kidney failure — are carried by 2 to 3% of the eastern Polynesians they studied.

"There should be a lot more resources going into learning more about gene variants of potential clinical significance among this population of Native Hawaiians, which is twice as large as the U.S. Amish population," Ioannidis said. "There are really opportunities for precision health here."

Shanks, C., Huang, E. C., Thomassin, C., Emde, A., Rodière, V., Moraga, M., Sandoval, K., Merriman, T., Pascart, T., Moreno-Estrada, A., Castel, S. E., Fox, K., & Ioannidis, A. G. (2026). Message in a bottleneck: Nested founder effects from French Polynesia to Rapa Nui and Hawaiʻi. Science, 394(6820), 216–221. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aec7662

#6486. Japan Just Powered Up a Quantum Computer Built From Single Atoms—and It May Not Need a Giant Freezer to Run

Just how big could the quantum leap really be?

One of Japan’s leading scientists in quantum computing says that his lab has switched on the power to “Japan’s first full-stack, neutral atom quantum computer,” according to a recent press release.

This announcement is not linked with peer reviewed research, but the lab leader, photo-molecular physicist Kenji Ohmori, has decades of research, publication, and leadership in the field. The computer, named Shunkai, is part of a nationwide Japanese consortium of universities and corporate interests that seeks to realize “a fault-tolerant universal quantum computer that will revolutionize economy, industry, and security by 2050.”

There are many flavors of experimental quantum computers on our busy planet today. That’s because, to date, there’s definitely never been a “fault-tolerant universal quantum computer” by a very long stretch. When traditional digital computers were developed, they had guardrails because of the way our electrical and logic industries had developed before them. Quantum computing is a deeply different paradigm where the next step is more ambiguous: all the options have drawbacks and limitations that are more confusing and pervasive than what we have now. It’s like VHS versus Betamax, but on steroids.

Neutral atom quantum computing is one of the suggested paradigms for a robust and usable quantum computer. These setups use special atoms whose electrons circle in a further orbit from the nucleus than expected, after being stimulated to sort of “puff up” so the electrons piggyback to an outer ring. This means a single atom can function as a qubit, or quantum bit—the smallest unit of information equivalent to a bit in a traditional computer—compared with two atoms in most other quantum computers.

Japan’s Institute for Molecular Science said in their statement that these single-atom qubits, which can function without being cooled to near absolute zero, can even work at room temperature “without the need for a refrigerator.” That’s interesting, because “room temperature” in quantum computing means above freezing, and you do need a refrigerator to reach the lower part of that temperature range. You just don’t need a deep freezer powered by liquid nitrogen. Time will tell precisely how “room temperature” Shunkai actually is.

The term “full stack” refers to the levels or layers of abstraction in a computer system. When you open your laptop or use your smartphone, you interact with it and experience computing results in realtime, without any additional technology or devices. That’s because the computer presents you with seamless results, but underneath, your input passes through multiple layers as it’s turned into computable code and run through software and eventually hardware. Many quantum computer prototypes work as just the processor, but Shunkai’s team says their machine will work as a complete computing experience and even be available for outside users to work on.

In the statement, Shunkai is described as “operational,” but that doesn’t seem to include work or results—just a completed assembly that can be turned on. The team’s goals are still listed in the future tense, and Ohmori’s consortium goals also include a cold atom quantum computer, meaning one that’s supercooled. The consortium’s other goals include “a society in which human beings can be free from limitations of body, brain, space, and time by 2050.” It’s just not clear how achievable any of these goals are yet.

Caroline Delbert is a writer, avid reader, and contributing editor at Pop Mech. She's also an enthusiast of just about everything. Her favorite topics include nuclear energy, cosmology, math of everyday things, and the philosophy of it all.

A proposed shift in recommendations for hepatitis B vaccination in the U.S. could leave millions of young adults unprotected, a new modeling study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A proposed change to decades-old guidance on hepatitis B vaccination would lead to a dramatic increase in chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infections among young people, a new modeling study predicts.

Previously, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommended that all newborns be vaccinated against HBV within hours of birth ‪—‬ a strategy known as "universal birth-dose vaccination." But in December 2025, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) advised ending this recommendation, and the CDC accepted that advice.

The new guidance would recommend birth doses only to babies whose mothers tested positive for HBV or whose HBV status was unknown. The guidance suggests that mothers who test negative should instead ask their doctors about whether their child needs a birth dose — an approach the CDC calls "shared clinical decision-making." The new recommendation states that babies who forgo the birth dose should be at least 2 months old before starting the HBV vaccine series.

Health experts widely criticized the proposed change when it was announced, and for the moment, its implementation has been put on pause by legal action. The modeling study, published Oct. 19 in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, predicts what would happen if it came to pass.

"Overall, this modeling study has many strengths and I think presents an accurate projection of how the vaccine recommendations may impact future chronic HBV in the U.S.," Dr. Norah Terrault, a transplant hepatologist at the University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine who wasn't involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

When caught in infancy or early childhood, over 90% of HBV infections become chronic. About 15% to 25% of people with chronic HBV go on to develop liver scarring (cirrhosis), a form of liver cancer called hepatocellular carcinoma, or another chronic liver disease. So, an uptick in chronic HBV infections would translate to an uptick in these harmful liver conditions.

"Not every pregnant person is tested for hepatitis B," said study co-author Dr. Amir Mohareb, an infectious-diseases physician-investigator at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School. For those who are tested, there's a chance their results are inaccurate or that they're not provided the right care after testing positive. "Something can be missed at any step in the care process, so the vaccine dose at birth provides protection," he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Mohareb and his colleagues built a simulation model using published data, including the current prevalence of HBV and the screening rate among pregnant people. The team also factored in the HBV test's sensitivity, the share of children who are fully vaccinated by age 2, and the risk of developing chronic HBV infection in different age groups. They made estimates of how often children are exposed to the virus through contact with infected household or community members.

HBV is "very, very transmissible," Mohareb said. It can spread from mother to child at birth or through exposure to tiny amounts of bodily fluids, like blood from a scratch, after birth. So, even if a baby does not get HBV from their mother, if they are unvaccinated, they can still get from another family member or from other children.

Infants and young children have a greater risk of their HBV infections becoming chronic than people infected in adulthood.

With this data, the researchers tested what would happen if vaccination were postponed to 2 months of age for babies whose mothers tested negative. Among babies born in 2026, 19% more would have chronic HBV infections by age 20, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination, they found.

In this scenario, the babies would still start the HBV vaccine series, albeit two months later than usual. However, the CDC's proposed recommendation offers more wiggle room; it says that parents should consult with their children's doctors to "decide when or if their child will begin the hepatitis B vaccine series" at all.

The researchers ran a stimulation to compare these two scenarios: one where kids get their first shot two months late and one intended to capture this looser "shared clinical decision-making" scenario.

"Other vaccines whose recommendations employ similar language had uptake as low as 25%," Mohareb noted. This aspect of their modeling has some uncertainty, he emphasized, since it's unknown exactly how the public will respond to such loosening of the guidance.

The researchers assumed that about 87% of kids would complete the vaccine series by age 2 under the deferred strategy, while only 50% would under the shared decision-making strategy. That 50% coverage, in turn, would increase chronic HBV infections acquired by age 20 by 83%, and about 50% and 70% of those born under that guidance would be susceptible to HBV infection at age 20.

That's about 1.8 million people in this age group per year, compared with fewer than 250,000 under universal birth-dose vaccination. "This represents a population that is at risk for acquiring HBV via sex, drug use etc — behaviors more prevalent among young adults," Terrault said.

To test the robustness of the findings, Mohareb's team varied the most uncertain inputs across wide ranges and ran the model 1,000 times. In every simulation, the birth-dose strategy led to fewer chronic infections than either alternative.

These conclusions seem "robust" because "they are the same conclusions no matter how we change the numbers of the model," Mohereb noted. Though of course "the specific magnitude of change depends on how many people defer vaccination," he said.

The new study does not specifically show how many additional cases of liver disease or cancer would result from the uptick in HBV infections. But Terrault said that the risks of liver failure, cirrhosis and liver cancer "would be anticipated to increase due to the missed opportunity to protect against infection."

Mohareb stressed that he is in no way opposed to the principle of shared decision-making between doctors and patients. "They should always make the decision together," he said. "But we rely on our public health agencies not to tell us that we should be making decisions with the patient, but rather to tell us what policy would make us healthier as a country."

Childhood HBV infections in the U.S. dropped from more than 25,000 cases a year in 1985 to fewer than 100 reported cases in 2024. This steep decline is credited to HBV screening during pregnancy, antibody treatment for babies born to HBV-positive mothers and universal birth-dose vaccination.

"Certainly without following a universal dose vaccination recommendation there would be a lot more hep B infections early in life," Dr. Brian McMahon, a hepatologist and the director of the Liver Disease and Hepatitis Program at the Alaska Native Medical Center, told Live Science in an email.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Mohareb, A. M., Ganapathi, L., Dugdale, C. M., Rajbhandari, R., Ciaranello, A., Neilan, A. M., Jhaveri, R., Kim, A. Y., & Hyle, E. P. (2026). Projected effect of 2026 federal changes to the childhood immunization schedule on chronic hepatitis B virus infections in the United States. Annals of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.7326/annals-26-02135

#6481. Hasan Minhaj Thinks America’s Greatest Accomplishment Is Cereal

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series dives deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

Comedian and actor Hasan Minhaj is known for quippy questions, biting comebacks, and colorful commentary, but his most delightful soundbites are about food. During a recent  hour-long chat, he named a wide range of favorites, including bananas and oranges (“they come prepackaged and are great for traveling”); macaroni and cheese (“I love every category and version of it, from the box of Kraft to anyone’s Thanksgiving mac ’n’ cheese”); and dal chawal (specifically his mom’s version of the lentils and rice dish, “pure comfort food and my love language”).

These are the best-of-the-best bites for Minhaj, which is coincidentally the name of his new movie—Best of the Best, streaming now on Netflix—that he cowrote and produced with Prashanth Venkataramanujam and stars in as a professor and former dancer. The film pays homage to real-life Bollywood competitions, following collegiate dancers Maya and Anjali (played by Maitreyi Ramakrishnan and Priyanka Kedia, respectively), whose characters were inspired by “deeply passionate college kids in the biggest world that a lot of people have never heard of.”

Fiery passion is at the center of Minhaj’s life, especially when it comes to actual spice. “Some people want to drive at 85, some like a nice even 65, and some take it five miles below the limit,” he explains in a speedy analogy. “My spice level? I want to feel things in all caps. Life is to be lived. So I’m like, ‘Give it to me!’ Give me the full robustness of flavor that’s possible. I am a maximalist and love it all!”

His other spice of life is chai, “a form of commiseration, community, and love in Indian households—and an entry point to gossiping.” He loves that everyone does chai differently (he and his wife, Beena, prefer a more ginger-forward profile, while his parents like it sweeter). That’s why he became an investor and partner in the New York City-based Kolkata Chai in 2024, working with brothers Ani and Ayan Sanyal to expand the reach of a drink so engrained in their lives and culture. “It’s a welcome change to a lot of people’s only chai experience being at Starbucks in Middle America. It’s really amazing how you can change the complete perspective of an entire culture because of a drink that people can explore and make their own.”

Read on for Minhaj’s answers to our Amused Bouche questionnaire—it’s no surprise they’re chock-full of equally heartwarming and appetizing soundbites.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

America is celebrating its 250th-year anniversary, and I think as a country, America’s greatest accomplishment is what we brought to cereal. I have been caught many a time red-handed with my full paw inside of some Golden Grahams, going to town. I will kill half a box, straight up, no milk. It is a snacking cereal. I’ll be watching a prestige drama and stress-eating Golden Grahams. Sometimes I’ll even drizzle honey over a bowl. I’ll also do the same with Honey Bunches of Oats. There’s a Montagues-and-Capulets debate here of blue box or orange box. I’m a blue box guy, because I love the almonds, extra crunch, and sweetness. It was my granola mix before I started eating granola, and it’s like trail mix without dastardly raisins coming in and f—ing shit up!

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

A strawberry Toaster Strudel, one of my all-time favorites. I popped it in the toaster as a kid, and it was an eye-opening experience. When I came home from elementary school, it felt like I was a master chef making myself this crisp little strudel cake and frosting it. I felt like a confectionery master. It was incredible. I toasted it on a level three and would sometimes pop it up and flip it midway through.

I actually didn’t hit my growth spurt until much later in high school, so I was quite undersized and malnourished-looking when I was younger. I was bullied a lot. My mother would make me eat three hard-boiled eggs on the way to school. And I hated hard-boiled eggs. Now that I’m a parent of small children, I understand the efficacy of hard-boiled eggs. But now I will pan-fry hard-boiled eggs, because really my hatred of them came from texture and temperature issues. But if you cut them in half and fry them yolk side down, there’s a crispness that makes it turn into a crunchy, almost taco-like topping that you can put on top of bread and butter.

It’s a really delicious, warm-and-gooey snack that I started making when I tried to give my daughter a hard-boiled egg and she immediately spit it out. I’m like, “Yeah, the cycle of torture continues! There needs to be a better way! Let me figure out a way to make this delicious.” The secret was making a quesadilla as the on-ramp she needs to get eggs in her. It was an experiment I worked backward from, kind of like writing a joke, telling a story, or working on a screenplay. My daughter loves quesadillas but hates eggs, so by making it into crunchiness that would blend right in, it wouldn’t feel like a squishy thing that I’m force-feeding her.

Growing up, we were never allowed to order dessert from restaurants. It is my greatest joy to order dessert from restaurants. I’ll tell the missus to order whatever she wants. Sometimes she’ll be indecisive. She always wants the chocolate lava cake, but she’ll be eyeing a berry tart. It’s a distant second, but I’ll take the bullet and order both for us to share. Sometimes when I do it, I’ll look over my shoulder to be like, “Are mom and dad going to find out?” But now I’m dad. We’re mom and dad!

I do not cook from cookbooks, but I will cook from YouTube Shorts. There’s just something about the looping nature of it breaking down the recipe. It’s tickling something in my mind and letting me know, “Hey, it’s not that hard. You can totally do it! You’ll get to completion, and it’s going to look pretty good.” And then as soon as doubt kicks in, the video starts playing again and snaps me out of it. It’s like the feeling of playing a song that you love over and over again, like “This Is How We Do It” by Montell Jordan. Play it again! “Men in Black”—play it again! I want to listen to it again, and that’s the feeling I get when I search “chicken tinga recipe” on YouTube Shorts.

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

My wife does most of the cooking, but I want to put on the record that I try. I do cook, but a lot of the reaction is like, “Oh, you tried. I appreciate the effort. And that’s great for you. Why don’t you enjoy the omelet that you’ve made?” But I think I make a great soft-scramble, and what I bring to the breakfast table is pretty solid. I used to burn all of my food because I got impatient and cranked up the heat too fast. I learned you can’t bring microwave energy to a stove. Once I understood that foundational element in not burning your eggs, it was a huge unlock. Then I got to experience the full variety of eggs that aren’t charred.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

Dal chalwal: just lentils and rice. It has always been the first thing my mom makes for me when I get home to Sacramento, from college until now. It’s this beautiful gesture of love that I’m eating dal chawal with my mother, and her grandchildren are eating it with her at the same time. It’s pure comfort food and my love language.

When you’re playing dinner-party DJ, what’s spinning?

It’s a seasonal thing. Beena is really the entertainer and has been an incredible host since we met. For a holiday party, she’ll queue up a Pentatonix holiday playlist. Thematic, but a little left of center and unexpected.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

Beena loves a theme. We host Halloween on our block every year and call it Boo Bash. We go all out with a Halloween-themed live band, fog machines on the dance floor—aka the driveway—children’s face painting, bounce house, fake blood as drinks in IV bags. Her level of joy and imagination is unparalleled. She’s incredible. I add pizzazz, but I’m like, “Go off, queen!” She is the show. She’s the show creator, and I’m the showrunner.

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

My grandparents on both sides of my family have passed away, but I’m lucky enough that I was raised by my grandmother on my mother’s side from third to fifth grade. There’s a specific memory of when my grandmother made biryani. When the lid came off the pot and the steam and aroma of all the flavors escaped for the first time, she would put a ladle in and scoop it out for me, with meat that is so tender because it’s been cooking for so long. That’s the feeling that I would chase and book a flight immediately for, but it’s just a feeling. A feeling of love from it taking all day to make biriyani and that she loved me enough to put in that time and energy. Goat biriyani especially was a special-occasion dish, like when a cousin was getting married, and I associate it with being with family and something happy happening. In Hindi you call it ghar kha khana, the food from home. Biryani is the crème de la crème and the chef’s kiss of Indian cuisine for me. Especially my grandmother’s.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

The comedian goes as hard for Golden Grahams and Honey Bunches of Oats as for his mom’s dal chawal and his grandmother’s biryani.

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series dives deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

Comedian and actor Hasan Minhaj is known for quippy questions, biting comebacks, and colorful commentary, but his most delightful soundbites are about food. During a recent  hour-long chat, he named a wide range of favorites, including bananas and oranges (“they come prepackaged and are great for traveling”); macaroni and cheese (“I love every category and version of it, from the box of Kraft to anyone’s Thanksgiving mac ’n’ cheese”); and dal chawal (specifically his mom’s version of the lentils and rice dish, “pure comfort food and my love language”).

These are the best-of-the-best bites for Minhaj, which is coincidentally the name of his new movie—Best of the Best, streaming now on Netflix—that he cowrote and produced with Prashanth Venkataramanujam and stars in as a professor and former dancer. The film pays homage to real-life Bollywood competitions, following collegiate dancers Maya and Anjali (played by Maitreyi Ramakrishnan and Priyanka Kedia, respectively), whose characters were inspired by “deeply passionate college kids in the biggest world that a lot of people have never heard of.”

Fiery passion is at the center of Minhaj’s life, especially when it comes to actual spice. “Some people want to drive at 85, some like a nice even 65, and some take it five miles below the limit,” he explains in a speedy analogy. “My spice level? I want to feel things in all caps. Life is to be lived. So I’m like, ‘Give it to me!’ Give me the full robustness of flavor that’s possible. I am a maximalist and love it all!”

His other spice of life is chai, “a form of commiseration, community, and love in Indian households—and an entry point to gossiping.” He loves that everyone does chai differently (he and his wife, Beena, prefer a more ginger-forward profile, while his parents like it sweeter). That’s why he became an investor and partner in the New York City-based Kolkata Chai in 2024, working with brothers Ani and Ayan Sanyal to expand the reach of a drink so engrained in their lives and culture. “It’s a welcome change to a lot of people’s only chai experience being at Starbucks in Middle America. It’s really amazing how you can change the complete perspective of an entire culture because of a drink that people can explore and make their own.”

Read on for Minhaj’s answers to our Amused Bouche questionnaire—it’s no surprise they’re chock-full of equally heartwarming and appetizing soundbites.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

America is celebrating its 250th-year anniversary, and I think as a country, America’s greatest accomplishment is what we brought to cereal. I have been caught many a time red-handed with my full paw inside of some Golden Grahams, going to town. I will kill half a box, straight up, no milk. It is a snacking cereal. I’ll be watching a prestige drama and stress-eating Golden Grahams. Sometimes I’ll even drizzle honey over a bowl. I’ll also do the same with Honey Bunches of Oats. There’s a Montagues-and-Capulets debate here of blue box or orange box. I’m a blue box guy, because I love the almonds, extra crunch, and sweetness. It was my granola mix before I started eating granola, and it’s like trail mix without dastardly raisins coming in and f—ing shit up!

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

A strawberry Toaster Strudel, one of my all-time favorites. I popped it in the toaster as a kid, and it was an eye-opening experience. When I came home from elementary school, it felt like I was a master chef making myself this crisp little strudel cake and frosting it. I felt like a confectionery master. It was incredible. I toasted it on a level three and would sometimes pop it up and flip it midway through.

I actually didn’t hit my growth spurt until much later in high school, so I was quite undersized and malnourished-looking when I was younger. I was bullied a lot. My mother would make me eat three hard-boiled eggs on the way to school. And I hated hard-boiled eggs. Now that I’m a parent of small children, I understand the efficacy of hard-boiled eggs. But now I will pan-fry hard-boiled eggs, because really my hatred of them came from texture and temperature issues. But if you cut them in half and fry them yolk side down, there’s a crispness that makes it turn into a crunchy, almost taco-like topping that you can put on top of bread and butter.

It’s a really delicious, warm-and-gooey snack that I started making when I tried to give my daughter a hard-boiled egg and she immediately spit it out. I’m like, “Yeah, the cycle of torture continues! There needs to be a better way! Let me figure out a way to make this delicious.” The secret was making a quesadilla as the on-ramp she needs to get eggs in her. It was an experiment I worked backward from, kind of like writing a joke, telling a story, or working on a screenplay. My daughter loves quesadillas but hates eggs, so by making it into crunchiness that would blend right in, it wouldn’t feel like a squishy thing that I’m force-feeding her.

Growing up, we were never allowed to order dessert from restaurants. It is my greatest joy to order dessert from restaurants. I’ll tell the missus to order whatever she wants. Sometimes she’ll be indecisive. She always wants the chocolate lava cake, but she’ll be eyeing a berry tart. It’s a distant second, but I’ll take the bullet and order both for us to share. Sometimes when I do it, I’ll look over my shoulder to be like, “Are mom and dad going to find out?” But now I’m dad. We’re mom and dad!

I do not cook from cookbooks, but I will cook from YouTube Shorts. There’s just something about the looping nature of it breaking down the recipe. It’s tickling something in my mind and letting me know, “Hey, it’s not that hard. You can totally do it! You’ll get to completion, and it’s going to look pretty good.” And then as soon as doubt kicks in, the video starts playing again and snaps me out of it. It’s like the feeling of playing a song that you love over and over again, like “This Is How We Do It” by Montell Jordan. Play it again! “Men in Black”—play it again! I want to listen to it again, and that’s the feeling I get when I search “chicken tinga recipe” on YouTube Shorts.

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

My wife does most of the cooking, but I want to put on the record that I try. I do cook, but a lot of the reaction is like, “Oh, you tried. I appreciate the effort. And that’s great for you. Why don’t you enjoy the omelet that you’ve made?” But I think I make a great soft-scramble, and what I bring to the breakfast table is pretty solid. I used to burn all of my food because I got impatient and cranked up the heat too fast. I learned you can’t bring microwave energy to a stove. Once I understood that foundational element in not burning your eggs, it was a huge unlock. Then I got to experience the full variety of eggs that aren’t charred.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

Dal chalwal: just lentils and rice. It has always been the first thing my mom makes for me when I get home to Sacramento, from college until now. It’s this beautiful gesture of love that I’m eating dal chawal with my mother, and her grandchildren are eating it with her at the same time. It’s pure comfort food and my love language.

When you’re playing dinner-party DJ, what’s spinning?

It’s a seasonal thing. Beena is really the entertainer and has been an incredible host since we met. For a holiday party, she’ll queue up a Pentatonix holiday playlist. Thematic, but a little left of center and unexpected.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

Beena loves a theme. We host Halloween on our block every year and call it Boo Bash. We go all out with a Halloween-themed live band, fog machines on the dance floor—aka the driveway—children’s face painting, bounce house, fake blood as drinks in IV bags. Her level of joy and imagination is unparalleled. She’s incredible. I add pizzazz, but I’m like, “Go off, queen!” She is the show. She’s the show creator, and I’m the showrunner.

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

My grandparents on both sides of my family have passed away, but I’m lucky enough that I was raised by my grandmother on my mother’s side from third to fifth grade. There’s a specific memory of when my grandmother made biryani. When the lid came off the pot and the steam and aroma of all the flavors escaped for the first time, she would put a ladle in and scoop it out for me, with meat that is so tender because it’s been cooking for so long. That’s the feeling that I would chase and book a flight immediately for, but it’s just a feeling. A feeling of love from it taking all day to make biriyani and that she loved me enough to put in that time and energy. Goat biriyani especially was a special-occasion dish, like when a cousin was getting married, and I associate it with being with family and something happy happening. In Hindi you call it ghar kha khana, the food from home. Biryani is the crème de la crème and the chef’s kiss of Indian cuisine for me. Especially my grandmother’s.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Scientists sequenced the genome of a woman who lived 30,000 years ago and discovered that she had mixed Eastern and Western European ancestry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have sequenced the genomes of three Late Stone Age people who lived in Europe 30,000 years ago and discovered that they had closer biological ties than researchers previously thought. The new finding suggests that places like southwestern France may have been critical cultural hubs during the last ice age.

Shortly after Neanderthals disappeared from Europe, a Stone Age culture known as the Gravettian spread across the continent. Artifacts found during archaeological excavations ‪—‬ including portable art, such as "Venus figurines" ‪—‬ have shown that the Gravettian culture lasted from about 34,000 to 25,000 years ago. But ancient DNA has been recovered from only two dozen human skeletons from the Gravettian period, so questions about these people's ancestry remain unanswered.

Based on the small number of genomes from Gravettian people that were previously sequenced, experts believed that groups in Western Europe were largely separate from groups in Eastern Europe. But in a study published Oct. 23 in the journal Science Advances, researchers sequenced the genomes of three people who lived in what are now Spain, France and Italy during the Gravettian period. They discovered that one person had mixed genetic ancestry that revealed East-West exchange at least 30,000 years ago.

"Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed," study first author Pere Gelabert, an evolutionary anthropologist at the University of Vienna, said in a statement.

The new information about mixed ancestry comes from a woman who died around 30,000 years ago and whose bones were found in Isturitz Cave in southwestern France. Originally used by Neanderthals, Isturitz Cave was occupied off and on from about 80,000 to 10,000 years ago. Cups made out of human skulls dated to roughly 15,000 to 12,000 years ago have also been found in Isturitz Cave.

Researchers found that the DNA from the Gravettian woman in Isturitz Cave was most similar to the previously known Western European genomes, but with an intriguing connection to Eastern and Central European groups.

This discovery of gene flow from the East is uncommon for the Late Stone Age, also known as the Upper Paleolithic, the researchers wrote in the study. It "could be explained by movements of people from Eastern Europe during the Gravettian period, which eventually contributed to this ancestry in Isturitz." Specifically, the researchers dated this "pulse" of gene flow to about 31,500 to 32,500 years ago.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The DNA evidence supports the archaeological theory that Isturitz Cave was an important cultural and biological hub for tens of thousands of years during the Late Stone Age, as the cave was located at a critical passage between continental Europe and the Iberian Peninsula, the researchers wrote.

All three newly sequenced Gravettian genomes revealed close biological connections to Western European groups, as well as genetic traits suggesting they had dark skin, dark hair and dark eyes. What's more, all of them had parents who weren't closely related to each other, suggesting that those populations may have actively avoided inbreeding.

"Overall, our results suggest that population structure and gene flow in western Europe during the Gravettian were more complex and dynamic than previously assumed," the researchers wrote.

Gelabert, P., Sawyer, S., Villalba-Mouco, V., Cheronet, O., Oberreiter, V., Gárate, D., Normand, C., Straus, L. G., González Morales, M. R., Gutiérrez-Zugasti, I., Cuenca-Solana, D., Darricau, J., de Lumley, H., Tejero, J.-M., Stahlschmidt, M., Higham, T., Giannì, M., van der Sluis, L. G., Gómez-Montes, C., … Pinhasi, R. (2026). Early Gravettian genomic data from Western Europe reveal population movements before the LGM. Science Advances, 12(43). https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh6128

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6476. The 8 Best Ergonomic Keyboards Reduce Wrist Pain and Strain

It may look strange, but an ergonomic keyboard can be a game changer if you’re worried about repetitive strain injuries such as carpal tunnel syndrome.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

As an editor, I type for a living, so I’ve seen and felt firsthand how quickly long hours at a keyboard can take a toll on your wrists, hands, and shoulders. Ergonomic keyboards feature wider, angled typing beds that allow you to type without tightening your shoulder blades or twisting your forearms quite as much as you normally would. That minimizes the strain caused by the subtle ways we twist and tilt our bodies when we sit at our computers all day.

Strain-related and musculoskeletal injuries (damage to your body's bones, muscles, ligaments, tendons, or joints) are a major portion of lost-workday injuries in the U.S.: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) identifies repetitive tasks and awkward postures as potential risk factors for musculoskeletal disorders such as carpal tunnel syndrome, which contribute to the reported 335,570 days-away-from-work cases involving sprains, strains, and tears recorded by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) in 2023 and 2024. Ergonomic office gear, including split keyboards and vertical mice, is not a silver bullet for these issues, but can reduce the long-term strain you put on your body while using a mouse and keyboard working nine to five, five days a week.

It’s also worth noting that the distinctive shape of an ergonomic keyboard often comes with an adjustment period. Depending on the design, it can take days or even weeks to get used to using one. The short-term inconvenience will be worth it, though, especially if you are starting to feel pain in your wrists, arms, shoulders, or back while working at a computer.

To help you make the switch, I’ve broken down the basics of what you need to know about using ergonomic keyboards and recommended the best models I’ve found based on hands-on testing at my home and office. After making the change myself, I noticed I could work longer without the same tension in my hands and shoulders.

Ergonomic keyboards are designed to encourage a more natural typing position by reducing how much you bend your wrists inward, rotate your forearms, or hunch your shoulders while typing. Many use split layouts, angled keys, or “tented” centers to help maintain a neutral posture.

These keyboards aren’t a magic fix for pain or repetitive strain injuries. A smattering of studies commissioned by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) and other government agencies over the past 20 to 25 years have shown that using this gear minimizes pain and strain in folks with musculoskeletal disorders, but have not established that using them long term will prevent them. That said, there is enough anecdotal evidence to suggest that they do reduce muscle strain, which should theoretically slow the onset of meaningful muscle pain.

At the very least, they can make extended computer use more comfortable in the long term, especially when combined with a well-adjusted workspace and better typing habits.

I’ve recommended these ergonomic keyboards based on a mix of hands-on testing and in-depth research into some of the most popular models available today.

I have personally tested four keyboards in real-world daily scenarios over five months, spending about three to four weeks with each keyboard, using them for four to six hours a day for at least three days per week.

Using each keyboard over a relatively long period of time is crucial. It often takes days (or even weeks) to get fully comfortable typing on a new model, especially if you’re switching from a standard keyboard for the first time. I’ve taken enough time to not only judge each keyboard on basic performance, but also how much time and effort you may need to put in before you resume typing with your usual speed and accuracy.

Of course, I also evaluated based on overall usability, including how the keyboards felt for both productivity and extended typing sessions. Typing feel and comfort were paramount, as well as quality-of-life features that make a keyboard more functional or helpful.

I vetted the four models I haven’t tested yet in person using the same criteria, but relied on reviews from my technology reporters at other publications, as well as user reviews published by brands and retailers. Over time, I will amend or replace these reviews with firsthand testing notes and recommendations.

The Logitech Ergo K860 provides the balance of ergonomic support and accessibility for new ergo users trying this kind of gear for the first time. Its soft, unibody form factor splits between the two sides of the keyboard, reducing shoulder blade stretch, with angled keys to match. While it isn’t a perfect ergonomic solution, I found that it provided enough support to ease my fatigue at the end of a long workday.

And unlike conventional keyboards that lift the back of the keyboard to tilt it toward you, this model tilts at the front. As it turns out, “reverse tilting” is actually easier on the wrists because you aren’t flexing to reach the keys. It makes a bigger difference than you think: My wrists and fingers were a lot more relaxed when they draped naturally over the keyboard.

The keys are super smooth to type on, and the very large wrist rest makes typing more comfortable. The downside is that the Ergo K860 takes up a reasonable amount of space on your desk. That’s the price you pay for a better typing experience, but it may be an issue for folks with a compact setup.

Full Logitech Ergo K860 Ergonomic Keyboard Review

The Periboard 512 is a very budget-friendly soft-split keyboard with a decent number of quality-of-life features and a very office-friendly vibe. It sits flat and is more compact than it looks, making it at least a bit more convenient than the Logitech Ergo K860. It still takes up its fair share of desk space, though.

It features an integrated palm rest, though it isn’t cushioned, along with a classic curved key layout to help keep your hands in a more neutral position. The keycaps themselves are contoured to better match the shape of your fingertips.

The Periboard 512 also includes multimedia shortcuts at the top of the keyboard for quick access to functions such as browser navigation, email, volume controls, mute, sleep mode, and search.

The Logitech Wave Keys was my first ergonomic keyboard, and I would recommend it as a starter model for anyone who’s hesitant to try one. It’s a small investment at only $60, and it doesn’t take long to get the hang of typing on its more compact but ergonomically angled keys.

Though that tighter key formation doesn’t provide relief for your shoulders, it can be helpful if you find yourself hyperextending your fingers to reach certain keys. That was the biggest benefit in my case: With the keys closer together, I didn’t have to strain my fingers as much as I usually do, even with a laptop keyboard. Still, the best and worst part of the Wave Keys is that its ergonomic impact is limited: It helps a little, and it’s very easy to use right away, but if you have a documented repetitive strain injury, it may not go far enough to relieve pain.

The keyboard connects via Bluetooth or Logitech’s USB receiver. I just popped the little gadget into the back of my monitor, turned the power switch, and I was up and running. It’s a pretty no-frills design overall, but it’s a very easy adjustment if you’re making the initial change to an ergonomic keyboard.

The Kinesis Freestyle2 represents the deep end of the ergonomic keyboard pool: It’s a full-blown split keyboard, which breaks up the keys into two separate pieces so you can position the sides to type without squeezing in your shoulder blades. It also features interior risers, which enable both tenting and reverse tilting to one of three heights. This is a full suite of ergonomic features, and should allow you to find the most comfortable option possible.

Having three fairly intensive ways to customize how the keyboard feels is, as you might expect, pretty daunting. It takes time and experimentation to find the settings that both feel comfortable and usable. But once I figured things out, I found that having all that control was really helpful. The more you’re willing to commit, the more you’ll get out of it.

And teaching yourself to type on any split keyboard takes some effort. You have to adjust to operating both sides of the keyboard independently. It isn’t that much different from how you normally type, but it feels like a whole new world. For me specifically, it took some time for my fingers to not instinctively reach over to the other side, and to remember that the “B” and “N” keys were on either half.

That said, the Freestyle2 comes with a detachable joint so you can push the sides into a standard keyboard layout. It’s helpful while you’re learning, but don’t get too comfortable: The Freestyle2 is a good keyboard, but there’s no reason to invest in this design if you aren’t committed to mastering the split configuration and optimizing for ergonomic support.

Once I got the hang of using it, the Freestyle Edge RGB Plus has become my favorite ergonomic keyboard because it’s so full-featured. I played around with configuration for a few weeks, and found that shoulder-width and rotated inward was the most comfortable. I also prefer the padding on this model over the Freestyle2 because it's thicker and feels more supportive.

The lift kit, which enables tenting, comes pre-installed. That alone may be worth the extra $50, as it is much easier to set up than other true split keyboards, including the Kinesis Freestyle2. That said, you also get improved typing feel of mechanical keys, which makes for more comfortable typing across the board.

As the name suggests, the Freestyle Edge RGB Plus adds RGB backlighting to the mix. That, in conjunction with its mechanical keys, is meant to give it a gaming keyboard vibe. It features nine programmable lighting profiles, all accessible without a configuration app. (Personally, I liked the third option the best—it’s a color spectrum that is always changing.)

And just like most gaming keyboards, it offers a lot of customization options, including a set of Mac-specific keycaps so you can have an Apple key. It is a tenkeyless model (TKL), so it doesn’t have a number pad, and doesn’t come with the connector piece that you get with the Freestyle2. So this may serve better as an upgrade for experienced split keyboard users, rather than a starter model. The mechanical keys are a good enough reason for keyboard enthusiasts and gamers to invest right away.

Full Kinesis Freestyle Edge RGB Plus Review

If you want a fully featured ergonomic split keyboard, the Advantage360 stands in a league of its own. Unlike most fully split keyboards, it combines fully wireless connectivity, mechanical switches, and contoured keywells into a premium design. The concave layout reduces finger travel and strain, while the completely separate halves let you position each side naturally for your shoulders and wrists, without a tether cable locking them together.

The Advantage360 also places commonly used keys like delete, backspace, space, and enter into dedicated thumb clusters, shifting the workload from your pinkies. Beyond the hardware, Kinesis also offers SmartSet programming support, allowing you to remap keys, create your own macros, and customize layouts through a companion app, which is a feature that’s still relatively uncommon among ergonomic keyboards.

With multiple tenting options and wireless flexibility, the Advantage360 is made for people who truly want a customizable ergonomic setup rather than just a more comfortable keyboard. The advanced configuration is an adjustment, so be prepared for a steeper learning curve than other, more beginner-friendly split models we recommend.

Similar to the Logi Ergo K860, Razer’s Pro Type Ergo is a low-profile soft split with a wide, domed shape and a large wrist rest, with several height and angle adjustments. Its concave keycaps give your fingers a target to sink into for increased typing accuracy, helping new users find their footing.

In that vein, I also like that it has a three-part spacebar, one for each hand as well as a little extra key in the middle in case you accidentally cross one hand over. There are two “B” keys on either side of the split, which may take some getting used to since a majority of keyboards only have one of each key.

Though it’s from Razer, which is primarily known for gaming, this model is part of the brand’s Pro Type productivity line, which is theoretically made for the office. Of course, you might not realize that, given the prominent RGB lighting. It also features media keys and two customizable rollers in the top corners, which you can customize (along with the lighting) through Razer’s Synapse configuration app.

Fans of gaming keyboards will likely feel more at home on the Pro Type Ergo than other keyboards and, again, I think it has a lot of nice features that help ease you into using a split design.

The Q11 Ultra also does a good job helping typists who are new to split keyboards find their way around. The unique design allows you to push the two pieces so that they’re basically flush so you can use it as a standard keyboard. And unlike some of my other recommendations, it doesn’t have a domed shape or tenting, so it sits flat and feels more like a standard board.

Keychron is one of Popular Mechanics’ longtime favorite keyboard brands, and the Q11 reflects many of the reasons why: It features great mechanical typing feel, Bluetooth and 2.4-gigahertz wireless support, and a web-based configuration app to customize its RGB lighting, remap keys, and create macros.

Its Achilles’ heel as an ergonomic keyboard is its lack of tenting. You won’t get quite as much relief from this model as you would from the Kinesis keyboards, especially in the back and shoulders.

Ergonomic keyboards change the design of the keyboard in a few different ways so you can use it without holding a position that twists or pulls your muscles for an extended period of time. Unfortunately, these changes can make the keyboard a little more tricky to use (at least until you get used to it), so every model strikes a balance between offering ergonomic support and making the experience approachable for new users. Here are some of the changes you’re most likely to use.

Fixed or “Soft” Split: The more approachable ergonomic keyboards create a small, static split between the two sides of the keyboard and tilt the keys out so your hands can approach from the sides, rather than the front. This doesn’t allow for as much customization as a true, two-part split keyboard, but it takes less time to get the hang of things.

Split: Split keyboards have two distinct halves, one for each hand. This offers support similar to the soft-split: By positioning the two sides so they tilt away from each other, meeting your arms where they naturally hover over your desk, you reduce strain on your back and shoulders.

Split keyboards have two sections to keep your hands, wrists, and forearms at a comfortable distance to reduce strain. Fixed split keyboards are one-piece designs where the key sections are separated and angled, but still connected. Fully split versions have two separate keyboard halves that can be positioned as needed.

Tenting: Some split keyboards have risers on the inner sides, which tilt the center of the keyboard up, creating a tent-like triangular formation. Like a vertical mouse, this allows you to type without twisting your wrists down to type on a flat surface.

Some fixed split keyboards feature a contoured dome-like design, which provides a small amount of tenting. But, similar to the unibody split, it does not provide as much customization or support as the two-part solution.

Reverse Tilt: Lastly, while most keyboards feature feet in the back that tilt the keys toward you (so you can see them better), an ergo keyboard may have feet in the front to tilt the keyboard away from you. Reverse tilt minimizes the need to keep your wrists flexed throughout the day.

Like most things wireless, the beauty of a wireless keyboard is that it eliminates the tangled mess of wires that cramp up your workspace. Likewise, anything wireless requires a battery and a reliable wireless connection, which can sometimes be a chore to set up. Go for a wired ergonomic keyboard if you prefer a plug-and-play setup, and opt for a wireless version if you’d prefer more flexibility.

All of these keyboards will work on any PC, but most have the Windows key layout with “Control,” “Start,” and “Alt” in the lower left corner instead of “Command” a.k.a. the “Apple” key. Some of our recommendations do offer a Mac-specific design if you use a Mac and, understandably, want the keys to match your OS.

If you regularly alternate operating systems, look for models with built-in OS toggles such as the Logitech Wave Keys, or a design with replacement keycaps, such as the Kinesis Freestyle Edge RGB+. For the best result, it’s worth checking the manufacturer’s specifications to confirm compatibility.

Once you determine the style and shape of the keyboard you want, compare each model’s specs to narrow down any extra features you desire in your keyboard. Some ergonomic keyboards have one-touch internet access or multimedia keys that allow you to do things like quickly change the volume or create your own shortcuts, as well as backlighting options.

There’s no way to avoid the fact that typing on an ergonomic keyboard feels weird if you’re used to a regular layout. The first time I laid my hands on an ergo keyboard, everything felt just a bit out of place—all the keys were not quite where I remembered them and were tilted at a different angle. It can take a little while for your muscle memory to adjust to typing on an ergonomic keyboard, but once you get over that hump, the payoff can be hours of more comfortable typing.

Sure! Many ergonomic keyboards are even more customizable than standard gaming keyboards, especially with a tented split design. You can get a gaming-friendly option with a configuration app that allows you to remap keys and make macros, as well. Again, it all comes down to getting over that initial acclimation period. In the end, you will be more comfortable playing with a keyboard that doesn’t strain your muscles over time.

This is the magic question. First and foremost, ergonomic peripherals are a must for folks who experience pain while using their computers because of repetitive strain injuries (RSIs). By giving you a way to avoid flexing the muscles that have been injured, you can continue working or otherwise using your PC without pain.

For everyone else, it really comes down to personal preference. I think everyone should use them, though. I’ve found that I’m more comfortable at the end of a long workday when I haven’t been pinching my shoulder blades and twisting my forearms. If you want to increase your comfort at your office (or home office), I think an ergo keyboard’s worth a try.

The PBS Nature film "Tiger Island" captures rare glimpses of tiger behavior, including a mother, father and cubs spending time together ‪—‬ a first for these usually solitary cats.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A male tiger approaches his cubs and greets them with a head-bobbing motion while their mother rests nearby. The surprising interaction, captured in the PBS Nature documentary "Tiger Island," a two-part series that follows two big-cat families across Nepal.

The footage marks the first time a tiger "family" has been documented spending time together, and it could challenge conventional assumptions about how the seemingly solitary cats behave around their young, said Dan O'Neill, a wildlife biologist and filmmaker who contributed to "Tiger Island." Previously, it was thought that tiger moms raise their cubs for up to two years without any help from the male tiger.

"It just shows that we really know nothing about them," O'Neill told Live Science. "And they're so much more complex than people realize."

That's just one of the scenes in Tiger Island that challenges our understanding of the tigers' solitary nature. In another scene, a female tiger cares for another tigress's cubs.

"We have these very rigid ideas of how these animals live," O'Neill told Live Science. But the natural world is "diverse and ever-changing," and tigers are no exception, he said.

The footage of the female caring for another tiger's cubs could offer clues about how mother tigers protect their young. Male tigers, like male lions, sometimes kill cubs ‪—‬ a behavior known as infanticide ‪—‬ particularly when a new male takes over a territory. Allowing another female tiger to care for cubs might help more cubs survive to adulthood, O'Neill suggested. Previous observations of female tigers have shown females helping to co-parent each other's cubs, but it's a rare event.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To capture these scenes, the crew used drones with powerful optical-zoom lenses and quiet propellers to observe the tigers in places that were difficult to access without disturbing the big cats. Traditional camera traps often capture animals along trails, leaving much of their private lives unseen. O'Neill noted that the drone propellers were quieter than the local bees where the filming took place, thus giving the crew candid views of the tigers as they went about their lives.

Though tigers (Panthera tigris) are solitary animals, they often live close to or share habitat with human communities. That means tigers sometimes attack people and kill livestock, O'Neill said. "It would be absolutely naive and wrong to suggest that they [attacks on people] don't happen," O'Neill said. As a result, conservation efforts must account for the circumstances in which people and big cats encounter one another, rather than treating human communities as separate from wildlife, he said.

The same issue affects other big cats. O'Neill, a researcher with the wild-cat conservation organization Panthera, has spent years studying jaguars, pumas and snow leopards. He said the popular image of these animals living in remote wilderness can obscure how closely they overlap with human lives.

For O'Neill, conservation requires more than studying the animals' behaviors or protecting their habitats. It also means helping people who bear the cost of living alongside these apex predators.

"Helping those people is how you help tiger conservation," he said.

In the U.S. "Tiger Island" Part Two airs on Wednesday, Oct. 28 at 12:30 am on the PBS channel.

A new study revealed that people who rely on AI for basic tasks like math problems became less motivated over time. In response, Live Science polled its readers to see if they agree with these findings.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Artificial intelligence (AI) tools like chatbots are becoming part of everyday life, helping people write messages, answer questions and learn new skills. While some of these processes may save people time, a new study reveals a possible new downside of consistently relying on AI assistance.

The research, presented at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco earlier this month, found that people who relied on AI assistance for tasks like math problems and reading comprehension were more likely to give up or struggle when the assistance was taken away. The findings suggest that leaning too heavily on AI could weaken people's motivation to push through challenges.

The research raises the question of what happens when people stop exercising their brains. So do you think AI is making you less motivated, or even "dumber," or is it simply making you more efficient? Vote in our poll, and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

The promise of AI automation to fix the administrative problems facing universities is a fallacy. These systems will only increase the burdens of already-struggling institutions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Universities are at a critical point as students and faculty embrace the use of AI. Already, universities like Harvard are introducing courses that feature an AI avatar as an "instructor."

The promises AI offers higher education are familiar: an increase in efficiency as a consequence of less administration, more teaching coverage, better feedback and smarter assessment. But introducing artificial intelligence (AI) systems in an attempt to fix these problems is not the answer. If anything, AI systems will magnify and speed up the bureaucracy that is driving universities' decline.

In practice, the more likely outcome is darker: AI will not simply sweep away the bureaucratic machinery of universities; it will give that machinery a new regime of AI compliance — more policies, more forms, more trackers, more oversight roles and more work downloaded onto faculty who are already stretched thin.

The danger is not that AI will destroy universities but that universities will use AI to preserve the very processes that make them dysfunctional. If this happens, we might see faculty spending less time on research, less time on teaching, and more time on activities that do not directly contribute to the production of knowledge and education of students.

This is already evident in the existing assessment system in the U.K., but shades are creeping into systems elsewhere, providing a window into the future for U.S institutions. A single piece of student work may pass through a plagiarism-detection platform, a grading interface, a moderation spreadsheet for faculty to share feedback, a grade-transfer system, and an exam-board record. Each stage generates its own logins, deadlines, exception rules and audit trails. None of this is inherently malicious. Anonymous marking, moderation, appeals, accessibility and academic integrity are legitimate concerns. But when each concern is implemented as a separate system, the combined effect is administrative incoherence.

In essence, faculty become the human interface between incompatible platforms, spending their time reconciling grades and chasing missing evidence rather than teaching. While this example pertains to U.K. universities, the trend to expand the administrative staff extends to North America. AI simply introduces a new opportunity to increase administration.

AI could, in principle, solve this. It could integrate systems, automate routine reporting, draft feedback, identify inconsistencies and remove duplicate data entry. Yet the institutional incentive is rarely to remove work; it is to make work visible. A university that automates a broken workflow does not necessarily simplify it. It may simply produce faster reports about the broken workflow, more sophisticated dashboards and more elaborate evidence of compliance. The bureaucratic impulse survives by changing its vocabulary: risk management, assurance, transparency, governance, responsible innovation.

At least one possible outcome is that universities will create AI-use policies, require module-level AI statements, mandate disclosure forms, introduce approved-tool lists and establish review committees. Faculty will be asked to redesign assessments, monitor suspected misuse, document their decisions, complete training, and explain their approach to students. Much of this labor will be invisible. It will appear not as a new job title but as an additional expectation attached to teaching.

When something goes wrong, the academic is exposed; when the system works, the institution claims the credit. That asymmetry is corrosive.

That asymmetry is corrosive. It teaches committed staff that careful judgment is not valued as expertise but rather as a compliance risk to be managed, and the consequences will fall unevenly. Experienced faculty, after voicing their concern to no avail, may leave, retire early or disengage. Early-career academics, already precarious because they don't have tenure, will have the least power to resist. Students will receive less of the resource that matters most: sustained intellectual attention.

One possible outcome is that universities will encourage the development of faculty AI avatars and cut hours and employment. The institution will then justify hiring more ‪—‬ not fewer ‪—‬ compliance and "educational enhancement" staff to manage and maintain these AI avatars, negating the idea of efficiency and cost savings. In this scenario, bureaucracy will expand to manage the problems created by its own expansion while undercutting quality for the students who are paying high tuition fees. One might need to hire staff for oversight of these avatars, administrators and lawyers to manage licensing agreements, quality control staff in case things go wrong, and IT teams for integrating them into learning platforms and websites.

There is an alternative to the administrative tasks. AI should be governed by a simple institutional rule: no new compliance requirement without the removal of an equivalent existing burden. If a university requires assessment redesign to accommodate AI, or the introduction of new technology, it should provide protected time, technical support and a single integrated platform. If it expects faculty to manage AI use, it must give them clear institutional backing rather than leaving them to improvise. And critically, it should show how the technology makes work more efficient before rolling it out across the board.

But the deeper issue is not technology but institutional purpose. A university exists — or should exist — to cultivate understanding, judgment and intellectual independence. If its systems consume faculty time, fragment the student experience, and reward documentation over learning, then AI becomes another instrument of managerial self-preservation. The question is not whether universities can adopt AI. It is whether they can resist using AI to automate their own absurdities.

If they cannot, the outcome will be an educational system that looks progressively sophisticated while becoming increasingly hollow ‪—‬ full of monitoring, low on trust; rich in measuring, poor in teaching; obsessed with compliance, indifferent to the people who make education possible; overly procedural sans intellectual life. It will become an audited theater of learning not worth students' time.

A woman's unexplained abdominal pain led doctors to a diagnosis that has only been documented a few hundred times over the past 400 years.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 42-year-old woman in Somaliland, Africa

The symptoms: The woman went to the hospital after having three years of chronic, dull pain in her lower abdomen, as well as a growing sense of heaviness in her abdomen that had worsened in recent months.

When doctors reviewed her medical history, they learned that, three years earlier, she had experienced a number of symptoms that seemed to indicate a pregnancy. She recalled her abdomen growing over time and feeling "fetal movements," her doctors noted in a report of the case. Then, the movements stopped, the abdominal growth halted, and the enlargement gradually subsided. She had not sought medical care during or after this apparent pregnancy.

What happened next: When doctors physically examined the woman's abdomen, they found a hard, irregular mass that extended to her belly button and barely moved when they touched it. Blood tests showed mild anemia, meaning she had fewer healthy red blood cells than normal. Her white blood cell count and kidney and liver tests were normal, and a pregnancy test was negative.

An ultrasound revealed a calcified mass and an empty uterus. Calcification is a buildup of calcium that hardens tissue into a solid mass.

To get a better look at the mass, which occupied the woman's lower abdomen and pelvis, the doctors ordered an advanced CT scan to create a 3D model. The imaging revealed that the mass contained clearly identifiable fetal skeletal structures, including a skull, a spinal column, ribs, and arm and leg bones. The mass measured roughly 7 by 5 inches (18 by 13 centimeters).

The diagnosis: Doctors concluded that the woman had a lithopedion, or "stone baby." The term comes from the Greek words "lithos," meaning stone, and "paidion," meaning child.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a typical pregnancy, an egg is fertilized in a fallopian tube — the structure between the ovaries and the womb — and then travels into the uterus, where it implants in the uterine lining. By contrast, lithopedions most often start as abdominal pregnancies,‬ a type of ectopic pregnancy in which the embryo instead implants on the lining of the abdominal cavity.

There, the embryo shares the space with organs like the stomach, kidneys and appendix. These misplaced pregnancies are almost never viable and are highly life-threatening for the mother. Because the placenta attaches directly to delicate abdominal organs and blood vessels, these carry a severe risk of catastrophic internal bleeding.

If the fetus dies at a developmental stage when it is too large for the mother's body to naturally break down and absorb, her immune system can sometimes treat the retained tissue as a foreign object. To protect the mother from inflammatory complications and infection, the body progressively deposits calcium over the fetal remains, creating a protective casing. In this case, the calcified fetus likely accounted for the woman's chronic abdominal pain and increasing sense of heaviness, her doctors concluded.

The treatment: The doctors performed abdominal surgery to completely remove the calcified fetal mass from the woman's pelvis.

The day after surgery, she developed a mild fever and nausea, but both resolved with treatment. She remained stable and improved during her hospital stay before being discharged in good condition.

Follow-up visits over the next six months showed she had healed well, with a complete resolution of her abdominal pain.

What makes this case unique: Only about 340 cases of lithopedion have been documented in the medical literature over the past 400 years, with the earliest documented in 1582.

This woman's case stands out because she was 42 years old, while many recent cases have been diagnosed in postmenopausal women. (Women typically experience menopause around 51 to 52 years old.) In these cases, the initial ectopic pregnancy occurred during the woman's childbearing years, but she unknowingly carried the calcified remains for decades before developing symptoms. For example, a 74-year old woman from India carried her "stone baby" for more than three decades. By contrast, the woman's recent case was caught after only three years.

The case also highlights the challenges of maternal healthcare in resource-limited settings such as Somaliland, where a lack of access to routine prenatal care and early pregnancy scans can lead to delayed diagnoses. That said, the successful use of advanced 3D imaging and complete surgical recovery demonstrate that excellent outcomes are possible even in these constrained environments, the doctors noted.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Ali, A. M. H., Mohamed, A. O., & Ibrahim, K. J. (2026). Lithopedion Following Presumed Primary Abdominal Pregnancy in a 42-Year-Old Woman from Somaliland: A Case Report and Literature Review. International Medical Case Reports Journal, Volume 19, 1–8. https://doi.org/10.2147/imcrj.s634443
