Developing research suggests that ancient interbreeding wasn't random — it was socially patterned, directional and far more complicated than the headlines suggest.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Deep in a limestone cave on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, two very different sets of humans left behind nearly identical traces of their lives — similar stone tools, the remains of the same prey animals, the same types of seashells pierced and strung into ornaments. They may have been separated by thousands of years and may not have directly interacted. Yet the overlap between them was striking enough that researchers studying the site had to look twice.

The site, Üçağızlı II, offers one of the clearest examples of a conundrum that scientists have long wrestled with: Neanderthals and modern humans (Homo sapiens) didn't just collide and go their separate ways. They inhabited the same areas, and, as dozens of genetic studies have confirmed, had sex, across tens of thousands of years and on multiple continents. The DNA of nearly every person alive outside Africa today carries the proof: Roughly 2% of the non-African genome is Neanderthal.

And yet, there is not a single archaeological site that shows them living together. Knowing that modern humans and Neanderthals mated is not the same as understanding how it happened. Who approached whom? Were these interactions consensual? Were they the result of violence or trade alliances? Who raised these hybrid babies? And what does the genetic record tell us about the social lives of two different kinds of humans navigating each other's existence for the first time?

Some of the answers, it turns out, are written on the X chromosome — and they are stranger than expected.

The first high-coverage Neanderthal genome was sequenced in 2010, and for the next 15 years, researchers kept noticing something puzzling: Neanderthal DNA was less common from the X chromosomes in people alive today.

One of the two sex chromosomes in humans, the X chromosome represents about 5% of the DNA in cells. Most females carry a pair of X chromosomes in each cell, while most males have one X and one Y.

Everywhere else in our genome, traces of long-ago breeding between Neanderthals and modern humans showed up in roughly consistent proportions. But on the X chromosome, there was far less Neanderthal DNA.

In people today, the X chromosome (bottom right) has less Neanderthal DNA than the non-sex chromosomes do.

The leading explanation was negative selection — the idea that Neanderthal gene variants unique to the X chromosome were somehow incompatible with modern-human biology and had been gradually eliminated from the gene pool over thousands of generations. It was a reasonable hypothesis, given that incompatibilities elsewhere in the genome did lead to the weeding out of Neanderthal DNA on other chromosomes over time.

To understand why the negative selection explanation didn't explain the X chromosome data, however, it helps to know what different parts of the genome actually do. Some stretches of DNA are protein-coding regions; they contain the instructions for building proteins, the molecular machinery that does most of the work inside cells. Others are regulatory sequences that don't build proteins themselves but help control when and how much of a protein gets produced. And then there are still other stretches of DNA that don’t appear to code for proteins or directly regulate gene expression, though researchers suspect at least some have functions we don’t yet fully understand.

Alexander Platt, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, hypothesized that if the problem was that Neanderthal gene variants on the X chromosome were inherently harmful, modern-human X gene variants would have been advantageous in Neanderthals. As a result, X chromosomal DNA extracted from Neanderthal skeletons should show an excess of modern-human DNA in stretches of the genome where they'd provide measurable benefit. They reasoned that this excess would likely appear in protein-coding genes or the regulatory regions that control their expression, not noncoding DNA.

But that's not what they found. Instead, Neanderthal X chromosomes carried more modern-human DNA in the noncoding regions of the genome than in coding regions. This pattern didn't reflect selection for better gene variants. It was a signature of reproduction ‪—‬ a record of who was passing chromosomes to whom.

In a typical pregnancy, the mother contributes an X chromosome via the egg, and the father contributes either an X or a Y via the sperm cell. So, while an individual is guaranteed to inherit their mother's X, they don't necessarily carry their father's — males exclusively inherit their mother's X. That pattern differs from the other 22 pairs of chromosomes, which mothers and fathers contribute to equally. Across a population, then, two-thirds of X chromosomes are inherited from mothers and one-third from fathers.

This fact makes the X chromosome a particularly sensitive recorder of who was reproducing with whom.

Tracking the flow of X chromosomes can reveal trends in Neanderthal-human mating. If Neanderthal males paired with modern-human females more often than Neanderthal females paired with modern-human males, you'd see more modern-human X chromosomes flow into the Neanderthal gene pool.

X data suggests that when the two types of humans mated, the mother was usually a Homo sapiens.

When the team ran simulations to explore this idea, the data suggested what Platt described as a persistent, recurring mating preference: Males with more Neanderthal ancestry tended to reproduce with females with more modern-human ancestry. And this trend held across at least two distinct mating periods separated by around 200,000 years, said Platt.

This finding gave the researchers a new window into the timeline of mating between Neanderthals and modern humans. Platt's team identified at least two distinct pulses: one roughly 45,000 years ago, which produced the majority the Neanderthal DNA that lives on in non-African genomes today, and an earlier period over 200,000 years ago, whose genetic traces survived not in modern-human populations but in Neanderthals.

The pattern of Neanderthal males having offspring with H. sapiens females appears in both periods, separated by more than 150,000 years.

What the X chromosome data alone cannot say is why the pattern exists. It documents who reproduced with whom. It says nothing about who wanted whom.

That distinction matters, because the same genetic signature can emerge from very different causes, and some have nothing to do with sexual preference.

Rajiv McCoy, a geneticist at Johns Hopkins University, pointed out that biology alone could produce a genetic signal like this one. When closely related species interbreed, the success of a pregnancy can depend not just on whose genes are inherited but on which parent belongs to which group.

Even if Neanderthal genes work fine in a modern-human genetic background, hybrid pregnancies may simply have been more likely to succeed when the Neanderthal was the father rather than the mother. That's not because of either parent's sexual preferences, but because of how their respective biologies interacted in the womb, McCoy told Live Science.

Researchers have recently proposed a few mechanisms that fit neatly with this theory. One study suggests that Neanderthal red blood cells restricted fetuses' growth in the womb. Another proposed that Neanderthal mothers carrying hybrid offspring may have been more prone to preeclampsia, a life-threatening pregnancy complication. Nothing in the existing data definitively rules such causes, McCoy said.

Neanderthal males were more likely to produce hybrid offspring that contributed to our gene pool than were Neanderthal females.

In practice, the two explanations are hard to separate. "Our models have no way of distinguishing mating from mating that produces a viable and fertile offspring," McCoy said. If hybrid pregnancies failed more often when the mother was Neanderthal, the genetic record would look similar to a world where Neanderthal females mated less often with H. sapiens males. Sexual encounters that didn't result in offspring left no genetic trace.

For now, the question of what drove that bias — social preference, or biology — remains open. Whatever barriers existed between the groups, they clearly weren't absolute. Multiple distinct episodes of interbreeding over thousands of years, McCoy noted, is itself evidence that the fertility of hybrid individuals was "sufficiently intact to leave a lasting mark."

Bridget Alex, a researcher in human evolutionary biology at Harvard University who has spent her career reconstructing the timing and geography of Neanderthal-H. sapiens overlap, cautioned that all this is hampered by one fact: no direct archaeological evidence reveals how the two groups interacted.

"Despite a century and a half of Neanderthal research," she told Live Science, "no one's ever found a Neanderthal and Homo sapiens fossil in the same exact layer dated to the same exact period at the same exact site."

Instead, we have a regional and variable patchwork shaped by conditions that shifted over thousands of years and hundreds to thousands of miles.

Neanderthals inhabited a territory stretching from Siberia to Iberia to Southwest Asia between roughly 250,000 and 40,000 years ago. Modern humans were evolving in Africa during much of that span and came out repeatedly, in multiple waves, meeting Neanderthals in different times and places, with likely very different outcomes each time, Alex said.

"It's not like the Neanderthals living in what's now Spain could call up the ones in what's now Uzbekistan and be like, 'OK, what's our policy with modern humans? Do we kill them, have sex with them, ignore them?'" she said. "My assumption has always been that interactions would vary across time and space depending on the particular environmental conditions, social conditions, and just the whims of a particular group."

Grotte Mandrine contains artifacts from tens of thousands of years of Neanderthal occupation — and a single layer suggestive of Homo sapiens occupation.

At Grotte Mandrin, a cave in the Rhône Valley in southern France, archaeologists found one of the most illuminating records of what those encounters may have looked like. Ludovic Slimak, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Toulouse who has spent years excavating the site, described it as something genetics alone can't offer: "an extraordinarily precise archaeological sequence of Neanderthals and [Homo] sapiens occupying exactly the same place," he told Live Science in an email.

Neanderthal artifacts fill layer after layer of radiocarbon and luminescence dating up to about 57,000 years ago. And then, in one thin layer dated to between 56,800 and 51,700 years ago, there's a set of different stone tools and a single tooth that appear to belong to H. sapiens. Then, in layers immediately above, beginning around 51,700 years ago, Neanderthal artifacts appear again. That group of modern humans arrived, lived briefly in a continent otherwise inhabited entirely by Neanderthals, and then disappeared.

"What strikes me most is not mixture but proximity without fusion," Slimak told Live Science in an email. In other words, the two groups left no trace of cultural exchange or shared practice.There were "two human populations occupying the same landscape, probably encountering one another, while remaining culturally and biologically very different," Slimak said.

Genetics also paints a portrait of two very different social architectures. Two sites exemplify the trends: At Sunghir, a burial site in Russia dating to around 34,000 years ago, two H. sapiens adolescents were interred head to head beneath thousands of ivory beads and mammoth-bone spears. Ancient DNA analysis showed they were not immediate family members, yet they were buried together in an elaborate ceremony that implies a social world much wider than their immediate group.

Graves from more than 30,000 years ago in Sunghir in Russia show that two adolescents buried together were not closely related, suggesting Homo sapiens had wider and more flexible social networks than Neanderthals.

In contrast, at Chagyrskaya, a cave site in Siberia, Neanderthals buried in what appears to be a single community layer included a father and his teenage daughter, and a second pair of individuals who shared roughly a quarter of their DNA.

While these are just two sites, they reflect a broader trend that shows up repeatedly in genetic data: Human groups tended to operate through what Alex described as a nested structure: Tens of thousands of years ago, small groups of perhaps 20 or 30 individuals maintained broader ties through ceremonies, intermarriage between human groups and exchange with other groups.

In contrast, data from Neanderthal sites reveal that they tended to cluster in small, tightly knit groups that remained relatively separate from other Neanderthal populations.

Homozygosity, or DNA regions where a person inherited two copies of the same gene variant, is an inverse measure of genetic diversity. Adapted from Skov et al, 2022.

Unlike modern humans, Neanderthals didn't regularly mate with individuals in other communities, Alex said. The result, written in their genomes, is that individuals within a single Neanderthal group were often closely related. Their genomes show low genetic diversity across the board, — "kind of suggesting they're always a population on the verge," Alex said, "like an endangered species."

Still, there had to be some out-group mating. At sites where researchers have extracted genomes from several Neanderthal individuals, the pattern is consistent: Male Neanderthals were more closely related to each other than female Neanderthals were to each other. Females, by contrast, seemed more likely to have come from elsewhere. This is the signature of a "patrilocal" social structure in which males stay in their birth groups and females move between them.

Neanderthals' insularity sharpens a key question: If Neanderthal groups weren't regularly folding in Neanderthal females from distant communities, they would probably be even less likely to incorporate female H. sapiens. So how did modern-human women end up producing offspring with Neanderthal men at all?

Fernando Villanea, a population geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder, thinks the question may be framed backward. The image of Neanderthal males raising hybrid children with modern-human females within Neanderthal communities, he argues, probably inverts what actually happened.

Something the genomes of late Neanderthals — those living toward the end of their long history in Eurasia — make clear is that they were roughly 10 times more inbred than the modern human ancestors who were then expanding out of Africa in large numbers, he noted. That level of inbreeding isn't usually a choice; it reflects how small and fragmented Neanderthal populations likely were.

We need to imagine scenarios where a majority of modern human groups traveling into Eurasia are encountering a vanishing minority of Neanderthals.

Archaeological and paleoclimatic data fill in the context: The ecosystems Neanderthals were best adapted to were shrinking as the planet entered a warmer, more humid period. Modern humans, who had evolved in hotter, wetter African environments, were simply better suited to Europe's new conditions, experts think.

The resulting numerical imbalance changes how scientists think about mating between Neanderthals and modern humans.

"We need to imagine scenarios where a majority of modern human groups traveling into Eurasia are encountering a vanishing minority of Neanderthals," Villanea told Live Science.

In the crucial period between roughly 50,000 and 44,000 years ago, when much of the interbreeding that left a trace in our DNA took place, Neanderthal DNA made up 5% of the modern human genome. Given how heavily humans outnumbered Neanderthals at the time, "that's a lot of matings occurring between the two." The most likely story, Villanea proposes, is "human groups absorbing surviving Neanderthal individuals and raising their children in a mostly human group."

His 2018 study in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution established that this happened across multiple distinct episodes — and the later ones are particularly telling. Some ancient H. sapiens genomes from Europe around 40,000 years ago, according to the study, carry Neanderthal ancestry from individuals who lived just a few generations after archaeologists can no longer find any physical trace of Neanderthals in the region at all.

Even the very last Neanderthal survivors were still contributing to the H. sapiens gene pool. A 2024 study by Leonardo Iasi and colleagues similarly determined that almost 90% of total Neanderthal ancestry in humans today came from a main pulse roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago, likely in the Middle East, with the rest trickling in from more sporadic encounters scattered across Eurasia.

That paints a picture of meetings becoming rarer and rarer as Neanderthals disappeared, with hybridization continuing whenever they did meet up. "This, to me, says deliberate integration of Neanderthal individuals into human groups," Villanea said.

We know that some hybrid Neanderthal-H. sapiens survived because "we still carry the legacy of their existence," Alex said. However, we know they didn't thrive, because the Neanderthal ancestry of our ancestral populations eroded quickly.

While some hybrids survived, they likely suffered from health problems.

Most genes work in concert with other genes across the genome. When Neanderthal-specific variants entered the modern-human genome, it was like trying to put gears from one machine into a slightly different one; the parts didn't quite fit together. As a result, natural selection removed the Neanderthal variants rapidly. Villanea's calculations, based on the rate at which chromosomes recombine during cell division, suggest the drop from the original approximately 5% Neanderthal DNA roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago to the roughly 2% carried today happened in around 10 human generations.

"That's very fast," he said. "In real-life terms, that means a lot of hybrids did not survive to reproduce, and the ones that did probably had to deal with life-long health problems."

Platt's team looked at genetic evidence from multiple sites across Eurasia and found that the genetic purge ran in the opposite direction, too. Modern-human DNA was also being selected out of Neanderthal genomes.

Neither had inherently superior genes, Platt concluded. The gene variants were simply optimized for the separate evolutionary histories of their respective lineages, hundreds of thousands of years of independent adaptation that made certain combinations disadvantageous, if not fatal.

If Neanderthal males and modern-human females really were producing more surviving offspring than the reverse pairing, where did those children end up?

Villanea was cautious about reading too much into the X chromosome pattern on its own to answer that question. The imbalance Platt found is real, he said — not a statistical quirk. But "there is nothing in the X chromosome data that says it's based on human or Neanderthal mating preference," as Platt proposes.

The same pattern could, in theory, emerge from Neanderthal males leaving their birth groups to find mates, but as archaeological evidence suggests, this was not typical behavior. More likely, he argues, is something biological.

Hybrid children were likely raised in Homo sapiens groups.

In Peromyscus maniculatus and Peromyscus polionotus — two closely related species of North American deer mouse — a phenomenon called genomic imprinting causes hybrid offspring to develop differently in the womb depending on which species was the father and which was the mother. This pattern has nothing to do with behavior or preference. A similar process in early humans could have made Neanderthal father-H. sapiens mother pairings more likely to produce surviving offspring than the reverse, without either group consciously choosing anything.

"We simply don't know enough yet," Villanea said.

Distinguishing between these explanations — social behavior versus biological incompatibility — will require more Neanderthal genomes from the critical period of contact, ideally spanning multiple geographic regions, experts said.

There's another clue in genetic evidence from a 2026 study of 27 late Neanderthals who lived between 50,000 and 40,000 years ago in what is now Belgium and France. None of those individuals showed any sign of recent ancestry from modern humans, even as H. sapiens from the same era demonstrably carried Neanderthal DNA.

If hybrid children had been raised in Neanderthal groups and went on to reproduce there, those groups' genomes should retain traces of those events ‪—‬ but they don't.

As for whether modern-human groups were patrilocal — with males staying, females moving — the answer is considerably more variable than in Neanderthals. Modern-human communities across cultures show a range of patterns, with both sexes leaving their birth groups depending on circumstance, Alex said. That flexibility may have been part of what made human groups better able to absorb outside individuals.

Neither genetics nor archaeology has yet been able to answer the question at the center of this story: whether these encounters were by choice, by circumstance, or by force. Platt's team set it aside deliberately, and Alex is careful about it, too.

"We still wouldn't know if it was consensual or coerced," she said.

It's worth being specific about what different scenarios would look like archaeologically. If Neanderthal and modern-human individuals mingled through peaceful alliances, we might expect to find toolmaking techniques or symbolic objects crossing between groups at contact sites — precisely the kind of evidence that is absent at Grotte Mandrin, where, as Slimak noted, the two groups' technical traditions remained entirely distinct.

Slimak, writing from Grotte Mandrin in the middle of his excavation season, urged even more restraint. The genetic data, he said, are "consistent with an asymmetry" — gene flow moved more successfully through Neanderthal males and H. sapiens females than the reverse — but that is where the certainty ends.

The data says nothing about culture, desire, attraction or intent. "That entire social world has been added afterwards," he said.

The same signal, he pointed out, could emerge from a variety of histories — female mobility, demographic imbalance, alliance, exchange, capture, differential survival among hybrids. And these factors could contribute alone or in combination. Even the categories available for describing female movement may be too blunt. A single instance of migration, in traditional societies, can involve marriage, family strategy, alliance, obligation and violence all at once, in combinations that leave no trace for archaeology to disentangle.

"We may identify that a woman came from elsewhere," Slimak said. "We cannot recover her consent."

However, the convergence of genetics, demography and archaeology does reveal a structural picture, if not a sociological one.

The interbreeding was directional and repeated, patterned in ways that map onto the social organization of both groups — and driven in large part, Villanea's model suggests, by the sheer demographic weight of a growing human population folding in what remained of a disappearing one. Neanderthal males, in dwindling and insular communities, appear to have been the ones whose genes crossed into the larger H. sapiens world. Their children, in all likelihood, were raised as humans.

"Genes do not preserve past loves," Slimak said. "They preserve what was transmitted. And between transmission and lived experience lies almost the whole of human society."

See the new facial reconstruction of a man from Roman-era Scotland who was decapitated after his death and buried near a Roman fort.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers have virtually reconstructed the face of a man who was decapitated after his death almost 2,000 years ago and then buried near a Roman military fort in Scotland.

While it's unclear why the man was beheaded, other burials hundreds of miles away may offer a clue. A chemical analysis of the man's remains suggests that he grew up in southern Britain. Beheading bodies may have been an obscure burial rite for some southern Britons, as other decapitated bodies from about the same time have been found in that region, John H. Reid, an archaeologist at the Trimontium Trust who was not involved in the excavations, told Live Science.

Another mystery is why a southern Briton was on the Roman frontier, but it seems that he was working for the Roman army when he died, researchers at National Museums Scotland said in a statement. However, his skeleton shows the man's right arm had such limited movement that he could not have used a sword, so he was probably not a soldier, they added.

Despite this disability, however, it's possible that the man used weapons in his other hand, or had a job in the Roman army that did not require frontline fighting, such as a clerk.

"He could have been left-handed, or he could have had a 'desk job'," said Reid, who is the author of the book "The Eagle and the Bear: A New History of Roman Scotland" (Birlinn, 2023).

The man was probably about 50 years old when he died between A.D. 142 and 165. His remains were then buried near the Roman fort at Inveresk, on Scotland's east coast just southeast of what's now Edinburgh, according to the statement.

An analysis of the man's skeleton indicated that he had lived an active life. His nose had been broken and healed, and his right elbow showed extensive bone growth, perhaps from arthritis. Reid said the bone growth may have been his body's response to a physical injury.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Researchers at National Museums Scotland and the independent U.K.-based forensic anthropologist Christopher Rynn created the facial construction based on the man's skull.

The facial reconstruction is based on the shape of the man's skull. He is shown here without a beard, which was based on what was common at this time.

The Roman fort at Inveresk was built around A.D. 140 and acted as a command-and-supply center for Roman forts along the Antonine Wall, which ran along the shortest route between Scotland's west coast and east coast — roughly the line between Glasgow and Edinburgh, although neither city existed at the time.

The Romans had hoped to secure all of Scotland under their rule after their invasion of Britain under Emperor Claudius in A.D. 43. They tried to impose control after their victory against a coalition of native Caledonian tribes at the Battle of Mons Graupius (possibly near the Scottish city of Perth) in about 83. But by about 120, the Romans had retreated to the heavily fortified line of Hadrian's Wall, near the modern border of England and Scotland.

The fort at Inveresk was built for a second push that aimed to secure Roman control over southern Scotland by establishing the Antonine Wall. But this failed too, and after A.D. 162, the Romans withdrew again to Hadrian's Wall, until the final collapse of Roman rule in Britain in the early fifth century.

Jess Turner, an osteoarchaeologist at National Museums Scotland, with the skull of the man buried outside the Roman fort at Inveresk.

Reid told Live Science that Scotland's soil seldom preserved human skeletons, making the discovery of a Roman-era burial an uncommon find. Although the man had been decapitated after his death, other aspects of his grave indicated he was buried with dignity. In other words, his burial was unlike those of executed criminals, who were often decapitated in Roman-era Britain, he said.

The remains from six Roman-era burials have been found at Inveresk, and four of the dead had been similarly beheaded, the statement said.

There are several ways non-Romans could have served with the Roman army, Reid told Live Science. They might have been employed as servants or artisans attached to the Roman legions, or they might have been soldiers in Roman auxiliary units or even citizen-based legions, he said. By the time of the Antonine Wall, few members of the Roman army in Scotland would have been from the Italian peninsula, he added.

The chemical analysis looked at the ratios of isotopes, or variations of chemical elements, in the man's remains. This analysis suggested that the man had grown up in southern Britain. Alternatively, he may have been recruited from a nearby region, such as the coast of what's now the Netherlands, that gave the same isotopic profile, Reid said.

Reid and his colleagues have found extensive evidence of the Roman army at the Burnswark site in southern Scotland, including the deadly whistling sling bullets they used against their "barbarian" foes. Archaeological work there is ongoing.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

A biology student found a Native American stone spearpoint when searching for shark teeth along the coast of Virginia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On the last day of an ecology field trip to Virginia's Eastern Shore, a biology undergraduate student discovered more than she expected. While searching for shark teeth, Brooklyn Rolph, a student at Mary Baldwin University in Virginia, stumbled upon a stone spearpoint estimated to be around 4,500 years old.

"Wow, this is so crazy," Rolph said in a statement. Already primed to look for pointy objects underwater, Rolph found a stone spear and immediately alerted the professors running the trip. "They were ecstatic," she recalled.

The stone artifact is about 6 inches (15 centimeters) long and, according to local archaeologists, a type known as a Lehigh/Koens-Crispin point. This kind of stone tool was made by Indigenous people across the East Coast of the U.S. from around 4,500 to 3,000 years ago. Sometimes called a "broadspear," the stone point also may have been used as a knife by prehistoric hunter-gatherers in the Late Archaic period.

The stone point is likely 3,000 to 4,500 years old.

The field trip was part of an ecology course led by Mary Baldwin University faculty members who had secured a permit from the state to explore the barrier islands off the Eastern Shore, the southern part of the Delmarva Peninsula that includes most of Delaware and parts of Virginia and Maryland.

Just after a lunch break on Sept. 21, the last day of the excursion that aimed to let students study plants and animals in the coastal ecosystem, Rolph set out to quickly explore a mound of shells on the island and noticed the spearpoint at the edge of an inlet. Her professors were blown away by the lucky discovery.

"The set of circumstances that came together that made this possible is quite unbelievable," Paul Callo, a biology professor at Mary Baldwin University who was co-leading the trip, said in the statement. "The tide was coming in, so the spear point was soon to be buried."

When Rolph showed Callo the artifact, he was "truly at a loss for words," he said. "It is certainly awe-inspiring to see and touch something that was made by human hands thousands of years ago."

The barrier island where Rolph found the stone point is part of a natural area owned by the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation, which means the artifact is now the property of the Commonwealth of Virginia. Archaeologists collected it from the Mary Baldwin group and have taken it to the Virginia Department of Historic Resources for further study.

Rolph was fine with not keeping the spearpoint. "That's how you get cursed!" she said.

She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6440. Even for Desperate Restaurants, Fake Reviews Just Aren’t Worth It

A new report proves that planting fake Yelp reviews has dire long-term impacts on restaurants

When Yelp was first launched in 2004, it flopped. The company’s initial model of an email-based referral service failed to take off until its creators realized users were taking the platform into their own hands; in lieu of sending one another recommendations via email chain, they began using a “hidden” link at the bottom of the startup’s website to write unsolicited reviews of everything from doctors to restaurants. Yelp 2.0 launched in 2005, and gave those reviews a more visible place to live online — one that emboldened users to feel more authentic stewardship, by way of direct authorship, over hyping up the businesses they enjoyed (or didn’t). The startup bought a whopping 20-million-business database, and amplified a world of reviews outside of the restaurant- critic echo chamber. It was a fresh democratization of information, which was itself one of the more optimistic legacies of the Y2K internet.

It’s been over 20 years since Yelp was founded. At its best, the platform still feels like a place where the voices of hungry, curious diners can share their personal experiences and offer recommendations and tips; at its worst, it feels like a bloated repository for reviews filled with misdirected anger, unreasonable expectations, or else completely fake customer reviews. Initially, unsubstantiated and unreliable reviews were more often written by a person — either someone from the business itself, or paid by the business; now, a fake review can be penned by a paid influencer, a detailed generative AI prompt, or purchased from third-party agencies that will produce fake bot reviews in bulk.

Fake reviews were perhaps inevitable. Bot-driven comments became ubiquitous during an overripe moment in the untamed internet’s lifespan. But how does a restaurant shamed for gamifying its reviews — even if it was, presumably, out of desperation in a tough economic landscape — regain customers’ broken trust?

… The offending restaurant’s foot traffic went down by 8 percent, and dipped even lower around the holidays, a time when would-be diners rely even more on Yelp.

In 2026’s AI-addled digital ecosystem, researchers are starting to understand even more about how paid-for, planted reviews impact the restaurants behind them, and whether trying to gamify platforms to achieve high ratings is worth it at all for businesses. A recently published working paper on the consequences of restaurants flagged by Yelp for fake (planted, incentivized) reviews found that since 2023, more than 4,900 businesses have been flagged with Yelp’s “Consumer Alert” banner, which exists on the penalized business’ page for a 90-day period and lets Yelp users know that the business has been caught peddling fake reviews. In 2020, the fast-casual chain Burgerim was found guilty of planting fake reviews, and received over 200 digital warning banners across its various locations’ Yelp pages.

The impacts of that digital pillory extend far beyond its 90-day duration. Yi Cao is an assistant professor of accounting at George Mason University, and the co-author of the paper; almost immediately, Cao noticed the offending restaurant’s foot traffic went down by 8 percent, and dipped even lower around the holidays, a time when would-be diners rely even more on Yelp. Cao’s team cross-analyzed the business’ performance on Yelp with real-life foot traffic reports (from global location data firm SafeGraph) and credit card transaction data (courtesy of Consumer Edge), and discovered that most of the penalized restaurants struggled to recover to pre-alert traffic even after a year and a half. The stink of chicanery lingered.

While Cao says his team doesn’t know every signal that Yelp uses to identify fake reviews, they do know that it relies “substantially on reports from consumers and business owners,” and that “they also have an algorithm running in the background to screen reviews for AI-generated language — which is a sign of possible review inflation.” At this point, the cost of planting a good review is only getting steeper as the technology capable of detecting it improves. “This is a classical theory of a trade-off between the benefits of manipulating reputation and the risks of getting caught,” Cao explains, “When the risk is relatively low, the business owners decide the incremental benefits are worth the risk.”

Yelp’s real restaurant reviews don’t necessarily need to be etched in stone, but as AI-penned reviews become less detectable and more sophisticated, what diners want now, more than ever, is a human touch and a sense of authenticity.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what might be a new dwarf planet in our solar system, orbiting the sun on an inclined plane past Pluto.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what might be a tiny new world in the far reaches of our solar system, hidden beyond the orbit of Neptune — and it is among the largest and brightest objects ever discovered beyond Neptune.

If confirmed, the miniature world would increase the number of officially recognized solar system dwarf planets to six. Upper estimates of the object's size place it at more than half the diameter of Pluto, the largest known dwarf planet.

"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Matthew Holman, an astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory and member of the Rubin team who wrote the code that helped discover the prospective dwarf planet, said in a statement. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."

The potential dwarf planet, designated 2026 ED138, orbits the sun at roughly 46 times the distance between Earth and the sun. The potential new planetoid has been hiding behind galactic camouflage; with its orbit tilted at a 25-degree angle from the solar system plane, it's at just the right angle to get lost in the light from the inner Milky Way, the researchers said.

Many telescopes struggle to see past the millions of stars making up our galaxy's bulge. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, however, images the entire southern sky every few nights with the largest digital camera ever built, sending out millions of nightly alerts for every object that has changed brightness or position. This makes it exceptional at identifying anything that moves, from solar system objects to transient events like supernova explosions.

The observatory had only just begun its 10-year mission of scanning the sky in July, and ED138 stood out in the data.

Holman works on the software algorithms that process the extreme amounts of data the observatory collects. The code he developed with his colleague, Kevin Napier, compares billions of observations to determine which ones are detections of the same moving object. Running data from Rubin through the code revealed the unusually large object.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By looking at past data from Rubin and archival images from the Dark Energy Camera mounted on the Victor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (both in Chile), the team was able to map out ED138's orbit over the past 10 years.

The Kuiper Belt is a region of the solar system beyond Neptune that is a wild frontier of small, mostly icy bodies made from frozen methane, ammonia, water and rock. It ranges from roughly 30 to 50 times the distance between Earth and the sun, and is home to most of the known dwarf planets, including Pluto. Thousands of Kuiper Belt objects have already been discovered. These space rocks can be frozen time capsules that hold clues about the early solar system's formation.

A model of the solar system showing the five dwarf planets officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) and the orbit of the newly discovered dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138.

Dwarf planets are the largest Kuiper Belt objects that we know of. Bigger than asteroids but not quite planets, dwarf planets are big enough to be rounded under the force of their own gravity but too small to clear their orbits like planets do. While the International Astronomical Union (IAU) has officially confirmed five dwarf planets — Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake — astronomers studying dwarf planets often recognize at least nine, with several more candidates whose properties are still unknown.

Depending on which astronomer you ask, there could be anywhere from a handful to hundreds of dwarf planets in this part of the solar system. Identifying which Kuiper Belt objects are dwarf planets is tricky because they are often very dim and move very slowly from Earth's perspective, since their orbits are so large and distant. The likeliest candidates have high albedo (surface reflectivity) and diameters greater than roughly 370 to 500 miles (600 to 800 km).

What makes ED138 special is its size, inferred from its brightness, albedo and distance from the sun. It's estimated to have a diameter between 370 to 930 miles (600 to 1,500 km). For comparison, Pluto — the largest dwarf planet recognized by the IAU — is 1,477 miles (2,377 km) in diameter. Ceres, the smallest IAU-recognized dwarf planet, is 595 miles (958 km) in diameter. Future observations of ED138 will give researchers a more accurate idea of its diameter and density to determine if it's round enough to join the dwarf planet club.

"If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman said in the statement. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for ten years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach."

Damien Pine (he/him) is a freelance writer, artist, and former NASA engineer. He writes about science, physics, tech, art, and other topics with a focus on making complicated ideas accessible. He has a degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Connecticut, and he gets really excited every time he sees a cat.

#6438. Food-Themed Fashion Is Starting to Feel Gluttonous

﻿The millennial avocado obsession walked so the Loewe tomato clutch could run

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

There was a time, not too long ago, when a purse shaped like a baguette felt like a thrilling — even subversive — novelty. Now, we hardly bat an eye when we see that Moschino has made a trompe l’oeil celery purse, or that Big Bud Press is making a hot-dog-and-pretzel-print jumpsuit in collaboration with a Los Angeles bar. How did we get here? And has it all become a little too much?

Fashion has long found inspiration from the culinary world, but the influx of food-fueled prints, graphics, and trompe l’oeil accessories that picked up steam during the pandemic have now reached a cultural tipping point.

The then-emerging brand made food a central theme of its vision: Its cake-topped aviator caps, Ferrero Rocher heels, and beeswax-sculpted cheese hats — hyperrealistic, absurdist food designs capable of achieving instant social media virality. Prior to working in fashion, Puppets designer Carly Mark was working as an artist whose pieces revolved around candies and snacks. As she told Business of Fashion in 2023, the Puppets universe felt like the ideal pairing given what she considers food and fashion’s motivators: pleasure and money.

During the pandemic, the much-duped “strawberry dress” took over TikTok, and Tombolo Company found a hit on its hands with its vongole shirt, which debuted in 2019, but found peak popularity in 2021. The shirt appeared in Vogue in 2020, and InsideHook called it an “obvious bedfellow to day-drinks, rooftops and weekenders” — in other words, a status symbol. Katie Kimmel’s T-shirts made chicken-parm enthusiasm akin to being a devout sports fan, and in 2022, this very publication called “seafood kitsch” the look of the summer, as items like Rachel Antonoff’s super-popular seafood-tower dress flew off the digital shelves.

Why was food so primed to become a motif in clothing at this point in culture? One could make the argument that it has roots in the millennial optimism years: Earlier in the 2000s and 2010s, the concept of “foodies” was new. Brands printed tongue-in-cheek food- and coffee-related motifs and slogans (a fervent love of avocados comes to mind) on hipster apparel, as the idea that “you are what you eat” developed growing fervor. That period was a key stepping stone in the evolution toward the far more elaborate and pervasive marketability of food-as-identity we see today. Content creator Cole Poska, who is a partner and creative director at Beyond Studios, tells Eater that “food brands have something most brands would kill for: decades of nostalgia, iconic identities, and consumers who are borderline obsessed with them.” Poska’s own Instagram often reimagines restaurant merch just for fun; his designs for Cheesecake Factory apparel went viral, such as a hat that resembles the iconic brown bread. He points out that people will defend their favorite fast-food order like it’s a family member, and with the kind of loyalty that’s hard to manufacture. The same could be said about their martini order, or favorite taco spot; it’s all a way of telling others who we are through what we like.

But the fatigue is undoubtedly here. In 2024, Bon Appétit asked “Why Does Every Dress Have Pasta and Cocktail Shrimp on It?” And as the novelty factor of a shrimp-print dress has worn off, the next question might be: Will there be any true longevity for these food-as-fashion moments? Our feeds overflow with products that are hurriedly designed for flash-in-the-pan viral trends and quickly destined for a landfill; arguably more so if the object in question prioritizes shock value and gimmicks over function and brand identity.

This is undoubtedly all related to the accelerated speed of trend cycles and shortened consumer attention spans. However, as Leah Asmelash wrote last year for CNN, the rising costs of food also casts an increasingly sinister shadow over food-themed fashion. In 2026, a $425 cardigan emblazoned with oysters has waning originality compared to a few years ago; it falls into banality at best and the Hunger Games at worst; its wearer indicating that they’re financially comfortable and, more importantly, well-fed. In that light, beyond its role in identity, food has become more of a status symbol than ever. A sweater touting one’s love of caviar is shorthand for their access to and appreciation of luxury, culinary and otherwise. But sporting the mass-market Temu version? It’s more akin to wearing a faux Gucci belt.

“Food brands have something most brands would kill for: decades of nostalgia, iconic identities, and consumers who are borderline obsessed with them.”

If it’s possible to escape the sense of accelerated-trend-cycle disposability, it may have to be through a more subtle approach than, say, a bag that looks like a giant stick of butter. Sam Salad is the co-founder of Meals, a Los Angeles-based, workwear-inspired apparel company that, by its own description, “bakes ‘food culture’ into apparel, blurring the lines between the clothes we eat and the food we wear.” Utility is at the forefront of Meals, which offers a classic chef pant with a slightly fuller cut, in both basic colors and subdued aesthetic homages to blue cheese and watermelon. When Meals launched in 2019, Salad was selling premium denim along Venice’s Abbot Kinney Boulevard, a hotbed of Instagrammy food culture and trendy restaurants like Gjelina that helped inspire his own brand. “Design today has to translate across languages and platforms,” Salad tells Eater.

Food is hardly a new bedfellow for fashion designers, even if today’s hyper-fast trend cycle has kicked it into overdrive. “Food is totally universal,” Salad says. “Issey Miyake once merchandised their pleats collection as little omakase sets.” He cites that collection among other fashion-meets-food moments that he considers successful, such as the iconic Salvador Dalí- and Elsa Schiaparelli-designed lobster dress. At the time of its 1937 creation, the dress was a scandal: It assumed a conformity-defying sartorial stance and was fittingly worn by Wallace Simpson. Today, its highly devolved spawn are available on Shein for $13.

As it stands, one clear way out of corny, food motif purgatory is for brands — fashion or food — to focus less on quantity and more on storytelling and quality. “We do a few things really well, and that’s enough,” Salad says, “Like In-N-Out [Burger].”

Poska’s philosophy is similar. “I’d rather make one thing people talk about for a year than 20 things people forget about tomorrow,” he says. “The first person to make a candle look like a stick of butter is a genius. The hundredth person is just making a candle.”

Researchers hope recursive self-improvement could tackle the skyrocketing costs of developing advanced AI models. But is it viable?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists in China are exploring what it would take to develop "the last AI built by humans" — a powerful, self-improving artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of creating its own successors.

In a new paper, researchers examine how approaches to recursive self-improvement (RSI) could help tackle the rising financial and computational costs of developing ever-more advanced AI models.

RSI refers to the idea that future AI models could direct their own training and development, using what they learn from each round of improvements to guide subsequent rounds of development.

This recursive feedback loop could eventually enable AI systems to develop newer, more powerful generations of models with minimal human input.

The study, which was uploaded to the preprint database arXiv Sept. 10 but has not been peer-reviewed, proposes a framework for classifying AI systems based on their self-improvement capabilities, from Level 1 (lowest) to Level 5 (highest).

At the lower levels, development remains largely human-led. As AI systems move up the scale, they become increasingly capable of identifying their weaknesses and deciding how to address them, eventually gaining the ability to make their own “meta-improvements” — improving how they improve themselves.

Whether AI could ever achieve this level of sustained self-improvement remains an open question. Previous experiments have, however, demonstrated more limited forms of RSI.

In one study earlier this year, an AI system called A-Evolve-Training was tasked with improving the performance of a 30 billion-parameter large language model (LLM).

Over four rounds, A-Evolve-Training modestly improved the LLM's benchmark performance by testing different training techniques and using the results to change how it approached subsequent experiments.

Peter Bentley, a professor of digital biology at University College London, questioned whether such experiments offer a credible route to RSI.

"This idea that some AI is magically going to start generating better and better AIs by themselves [is] nonsense," Bentley told Live Science in an email.

Bentley pointed out that self-improving computer systems have been around for decades. Evolutionary computation and reinforcement learning, for instance, are both based on the principle of systems refining their performance over time in response to feedback.

Could AI really self-improve? Some experts are skeptical.

The much greater challenge, he said, is developing AI systems capable of autonomously conducting the research needed to create more powerful successors — not to mention overcoming their dependence on human expertise and physical computing infrastructure.

"You can't 'recursively self-improve' unless you can also enhance your own training, enhance your hardware, and test it exhaustively in real world settings," Bentley added.

The study's authors acknowledged some of these challenges. Developing RSI-capable systems could require enormous investments in computing power, as well as human supervision to ensure successive improvements delivered meaningful gains. All of this becomes effectively redundant if the resources needed to develop and test subsequent AI models outweigh any benefits they offer, the authors noted.

Scientists would also need a reliable way to determine whether an AI system was genuinely becoming more capable over iterations, rather than exploiting weaknesses in tests used to measure its capabilities. This is a known problem in AI development, where models can achieve higher benchmark scores by exploiting testing methods or cherry-picking results.

Kayla Blomquist, an AI researcher at the University of Oxford and co-founder of the Oxford China Policy Lab, said that, while the paper doesn't provide a practical road map to RSI, it could help developers and policymakers understand the technical challenges and safety risks associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems.

She also questioned whether there would ever be a clear point at which AI became completely independent of human development. "The paper describes a gradual handover of responsibility rather than a single moment, so there may never be an obvious 'last' model built by humans," Blomquist added.

#6436. We’re in the Era of the $200 Cup of Coffee

Can coffee join the ranks of wine when it comes to high-end tastings?

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Starting this week, it’s also home to a $200 cup of coffee.

Bushwick’s Sey Coffee recently announced that it would be touring a rare Panamanian geisha from Finca Sophia, a coffee farm in Panama’s Chiriquí highlands. Sey scooped up the geisha at auction for $44,275, which comes to $6,325 per kilogram, or roughly $200 per cup. The geisha is billed as extraordinarily aromatic, floral, and juicy; Doug Cohen, Sey’s director of brand strategy, advises enjoying it with a clean palate, completely black, and taking your time with it. “As the coffee cools, different aspects of its character become apparent, and that evolution is part of the experience,” he says.

Even among fourth-wave coffee shops where prices continue to climb higher, Sey’s $200 cup is an outlier. “Coffee as a premium product is relatively new,” says Cohen. “For so long, coffee has been treated as a commodity, and its value has been constrained by that perception.” He says that both before and right after COVID, folks were becoming more curious about coffee, and educating themselves on platforms like Youtube, Discord, and online forums about how to appreciate it and “understand just how high the ceiling of quality can be.” The arrival of the $200 cup of coffee from a cafe in a neighborhood at the epicenter of conversations about both culinary innovation and gentrification feels ripe for closer examination.

So, how did this coffee end up at this price? “We have been purchasing coffee from Finca Sophia for several years,” Cohen says. “This release really grew out of that existing relationship.” When Finca’s general manager told Cohen that the farm’s yields were down by approximately 95 percent, Cohen says a bigger question was raised: “What does it mean to be a good partner when the people you have built relationships with are facing a difficult year?” Buying up the geisha beans felt like a way to both support Sey’s producer, and further develop what Cohen calls “elevated coffee experiences.”

In the 2010s, the artisanal coffeehouse wave washed over the country, and especially Brooklyn, with hipster gusto. Sey Coffee was an integral part of that boom. Initially called Lofted Coffee, it operated out of its founders’ Bushwick loft until it rebranded to Sey in 2017, and expanded operations to its present Bushwick location on Grattan Street. That space has become something of a local icon since; Sprudge called its aesthetic “shoebox crossed with an airplane hangar”; the minimal-industrial, cream-hued interiors hit a very Axel Vervoordt-with-a-cyber-sigil-tattoo note (positive). The shop’s cachet has drawn coffee lovers, artists, yuppies, and artist-yuppies; customers have snacked on the gluten-free pastries from L’imprimerie (and now, post-L’imprimerie closure, pastries from Smør), and often post up with their dogs thanks to the semi-indoor-outdoor layout.

Sey is hoping to elevate the coffee shop model to something more premium, with a stated focus on ethics and sustainability. Thus far, it’s earned acclaim for those efforts. Food & Wine named it the best coffee shop in New York and received positive media attention for opting out of tipping, choosing instead to pay its staff up to more than 80 percent above the NYC hourly minimum wage; full-time baristas can make up to $31 per hour in addition to receiving benefits and a share of the cafe’s revenue.

Increasingly, coffee is getting the same treatment as high-end dining and tasting experiences. There’s the omakase-style menu at NYC’s Driftaway Coffee, or San Francisco’s Komakase coffee tasting room, both of which steer coffee away from quick consumption and toward a world of degustation that appears to have more in common with pricier wine and spirit tastings. The expansion of “espresso house” chain Watch House stateside is also an indicator: The London-based specialty roaster expanded to a fourth location in New York City this summer, raising eyebrows for its $32 cup of coffee while also reportedly scouting for more locations in Austin, Chicago, and Miami.

The emerging demand may be just much about luxury as it is about craft. I can’t help but wonder if the $200 cup of coffee is happening in Bushwick because the Girls-era Bushwickian has grown up and wants more exclusive experiences. Is this what happens when, as culture writer Raven Smith said on his new BBC podcast last week, the indie outgrows its sleaze? “For us, this is not about pushing prices higher for the sake of it,” Cohen says. “It is about challenging how we assign value to coffee in the first place. What is an extraordinary coffee actually worth?”

As much as we may lament climbing prices for specialty coffee and espresso, why wouldn’t this happen to the category when so many other aspects of food and beverage — from cocktails to sushi to bread — are following the same trajectory? Higher consumer costs notwithstanding, the marketing of specialty beans does steer U.S. coffee culture away from its productivity-focused consumption and the work-optimized “coffee break.”

“Why do we accept that certain wines can command thousands of dollars, yet question whether coffee can have comparable value?” Cohen asks. It’s a fair question, albeit one that I’d answer with another: Once we acknowledge that coffee should command a higher price, who still gets to drink it?

#6435. Steal My Food Itinerary: 3 Days on Prince Edward Island

Canada’s smallest province is big on fresh produce, pristine seafood, gorgeous views, and warm conviviality.

Recently I spent a few days exploring Prince Edward Island, a place that embraces its local foodways with gusto. There’s a complex history here, with roots in Indigenous Mi’kmaq, Acadian, Irish, Scottish, and other cultures. And if one thing unites these histories, it’s the island’s abundance of seafood and produce, which have helped earn it the nickname Canada’s Food Island. How can you not want to visit Canada’s Food Island?

On a stretch of land only about 140 miles long, you can eat oysters pulled out of nearby waters, potatoes grown on local farms, dig into a juicy burger made with PEI beef, and lick ice cream made with milk from the cows you pass along those famous red-dirt roads. That’s a lot of good eating packed into a place you can drive across in an afternoon.

I had to structure my visit, therefore, around where to dine, but also include a bucket-list visit to Green Gables Heritage Place. (I am a complete freak for L.M. Montgomery’s novel Anne of Green Gables, set on PEI around the turn of the last century.) I also had to schedule time at the PEI International Shellfish Festival, which promised endless trays of freshly shucked oysters and clams, hot buttered lobster rolls, steaming bowls of mussels, and plenty of entertainment, from shucking competitions and cooking demos to live music and dancing.

My husband and I rented a car and stationed ourselves in Charlottetown, the island’s main hub. Prince Edward Island is situated in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, just a hop away from Nova Scotia. You’re never far from the ocean here, and on a sunny day, the air seems to sparkle. The island is known for its red-sand cliffs and beaches, rolling landscapes, fishing harbors, and lighthouses. If you’ve read Anne of Green Gables, you’ll know just how pretty PEI is.

We landed late Thursday afternoon, ready to hit the ground running. With just shy of three days, I had carefully mapped out the places I wanted to visit, using Charlottetown as my base.

Charlottetown isn’t big, and most things here are walkable within 20 minutes or so. First stop in PEI: Slaymaker & Nichols, a gastropub and inn with the feel of an old-fashioned supper club. It takes its name from the 19th-century circus that once performed on the site. They take cocktail making seriously here. The summery feel of the day prompted me to try the watermelon mule, with hibiscus-infused vodka and chunks of pickled watermelon. I liked it, especially alongside the creamy lobster dip with tomatoes and harissa, and the buttery shrimp pil pil, with lots of tasty little spears of asparagus.

I was saving myself for my first lobster roll, which we grabbed up the street in an unremarkable spot. It was pretty mediocre, so I won’t go on about it. But after eating, we stopped into Reddins, a speakeasy that channels PEI’s Prohibition history in a dark, intimate third-floor bar with vintage furniture, good jazz, and whimsical cocktails. Our excellent bartender, AB, told us the space had once been a pharmacy where folks came during Prohibition to get their “medicine” — drugstores could legally dispense alcohol by prescription. We tried a few of the signature cocktails, and the one that stood out was the Pink Canary, with vodka, rose, lychee, citrus, and rosé bubbles, served in a small bathtub. Yup, you heard that right. It was sweet and awfully fun to sip.

Tip: You need a secret password to get in when you buzz from downstairs. You can get it online, or just do as we did and ask the hostess next door for help.

In the pouring rain, we made our way to nearby Victoria Row for breakfast at local roaster Receiver Coffee. Fuel for the day included strong coffee, a particularly good cup of Earl Grey cream tea, and the Ham Slam, a big fluffy cheddar biscuit layered with a runny fried egg, Black Forest ham, Swiss, and Dijon mayo.

We swung by the shellfish festival (more on that later) but the rain wasn’t welcoming, so we got back in the car and drove out to tiny and charming Victoria-by-the-Sea. When I say tiny, I mean it: The town is half a square mile, with a population under 200. Despite the town’s size, Landmark Oyster House, set there in an old general store with pretty green shingles and a steep gabled roof, thrives.

Our friendly waiter (everyone is abundantly friendly on PEI) suggested Raspberry Point oysters to start. They hit the spot: medium-sized, briny, and sweet, served with lemon wedges and freshly grated horseradish, which is now how I think every oyster should be eaten. We also tried the scallop dog, with buttery sweet scallops, bacon jam, red pepper aioli, and pickled shallots nestled in a toasted bun. It came alongside a very good, eggy potato salad.

After seeing the cheery lighthouse and visiting a couple of little gift shops, we popped into Island Chocolates, a family-run shop and café where bars and truffles are hand-crafted, often using local ingredients like haskap, a berry that tastes somewhere between a blueberry and raspberry. That fruity haskap truffle had a nice thick shell of milk chocolate.

Sun out? Check. We spent the afternoon at the festival and got a substantial fix of oysters and clams. The lobster rolls here were stuffed with unadorned lobster meat, then melted butter from a gigantic vat was ladled over the top.

For dinner, both our bartender and waiter at Slaymaker recommended North Shore Canteen in French River, a local haunt for sure. (A slew of chefs from the shellfish festival were two tables down from us.) The menu, which changes with the current haul, hit on the day’s best ingredients: halibut, striped bass, the aforementioned shellfish, beef, and potatoes. We opted for a very generous portion of local beef tartare, amazingly tasty with capers, roasted garlic, and freshly grated Parmesan, served with Covered Bridge potato chips. We wanted to try more PEI beef and opted for a juicy hanger steak with chimichurri and black garlic, which showcased it well. Dessert was a must: parsnip cake drizzled with caramel sauce for the win.

It was time for me to check Green Gables off my bucket list. This is an article about where to eat, so suffice it to say that if you’re a fan, this is 100 percent worth a visit to see the house, wander the Haunted Wood and Lover’s Lane, and taste some nonalcoholic raspberry cordial (IYKYK).

All that walking made me hungry, which was good because this was a much anticipated two-lunch day.

First stop: Blue Mussel Café, a bright and very welcoming, beloved PEI restaurant set just back from the water in Rustico Harbor. I think it’s obvious what to order, and for good reason: These are excellent mussels — plump, fresh, and brought to the table piled high in a large stainless steel bowl. You can have them prepared with rosemary and lemon or beer and wine. I’d rate them equally, but I did like the hit of rosemary. Melted butter comes in a small ramekin on the side; I used it to dip each mussel, and my husband poured it all over the top. I didn’t have it, but the other signature, seafood chowder, looked popular. It’s made with haddock, salmon, scallops, mussels, and PEI potatoes, and served with a giant biscuit. Noted for my next visit.

We hightailed it to our next meal because I had yet to have the perfect lobster roll. Richard’s Fresh Seafood in Covehead Wharf delivered. This is one of the island’s longest-running fish shacks, where you can savor fish and chips and beer on the deck overlooking the fishing boats, or camp out on the nearby beach under the lighthouse with a lobster roll. no mistake: This is the quintessential lobster roll. It was an exercise in abundance, packed with sweet lobster meat that managed to be chunky and fine, bound with lemon and chive mayo and tiny bits of onion, all stuffed in a buttery toasted bun. It came with crunchy coleslaw, crispy fries, and a paper cup of ketchup. There are other menu items, but this lobster roll alone is worth the trip to PEI.

For our final dinner, we drove back toward North Rustico Harbor to Rustico Cannery, which opened this past spring. The airy, modern space has giant windows and a big deck that takes in super sunset views.

I needed greens, and Rustico delivered. We had crisp romaine hearts with a creamy, spicy charred jalapeño dressing, lardons, Parmesan, and sourdough crunchies. My husband hit the jackpot with his dinner: panko crusted, pan-fried haddock with pickled beet remoulade, jalapeño relish, confit potatoes, and coleslaw.

A final note: Many places are seasonal, so check if they’re open if you’re visiting in cooler months.

In two new surveys, U.S. adults report lying to their doctors and their children's doctors about symptoms in hopes of being prescribed antibiotics.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nearly 30% of U.S. adults have lied to doctors in an effort to obtain antibiotics, either by exaggerating their actual symptoms or by fabricating symptoms, the results of a new national survey suggest. Additionally, in a second survey, about one-quarter of children's caregivers reported lying about their kids' symptoms to get antibiotics on their behalf.

"As clinicians, we know that patients lie to us sometimes," Dr. Jeffrey Linder, a general internist and primary care clinician-investigator at Northwestern Medicine, wrote in a commentary about the survey findings.

However, the results are still important because the inappropriate use of antibiotics can contribute to the mounting problem of antibiotic resistance, in which bacteria build up a tolerance to the drugs designed to kill them. Recent data released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) highlight the extent of the problem: In 2023, drug-resistant bacteria and fungi caused about 9.7 million infections in the U.S., up from 2.8 million in 2017. In turn, the estimated number of deaths caused by drug-resistant germs rose from 35,000 to 50,800 between the two years.

A major factor driving resistance among bacteria is the misuse of antibiotics — in other words, using antibiotics for ailments like viral infections, which the drugs do not treat. For individual patients, such prescriptions don't cure their illness and can result in an upset stomach or issues with the gut microbiome, the community of microbes in the intestines. Simultaneously, they place extra pressure on bacteria to evolve resistance, granting the germs opportunities to pick up new strategies for thwarting antibiotics.

Doctors play a big role in ensuring that the antibiotic prescriptions they write are necessary. Part of their decision-making process comes down to what patients say about their symptoms, some of which may be fabricated, the two new surveys suggest.

The new surveys were published Friday (Oct. 30) in the journal JAMA Network Open.

The first survey was completed by nearly 960 adults from across the U.S. in January and February 2026. It asked whether the respondents had ever told a healthcare provider that their symptoms were worse or more long-lasting than they were in order to get antibiotics, as well as whether they'd ever made up symptoms for the same reason. It then inquired about what motivated a given patient to lie — or avoid lying, if they were truthful — as well as posed contextual questions about their demographics, health behaviors and beliefs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Overall, about 28% of the respondents reported misrepresenting their symptoms, including 26% who exaggerated their existing symptoms and 17% who fabricated symptoms. They most frequently lied about cold-like symptoms, such as fever, cough and sore throat. About two-thirds of these patients were at least moderately confident that their lie would motivate a clinician to prescribe them antibiotics, and 77% said the strategy worked for them at least once.

Often, patients' motivations for lying centered around feeling very sick, holding strong beliefs that antibiotics would help them recover quickly and get back to their responsibilities, and wanting control over the treatments prescribed to them. Compared with people who didn't lie, those who lied were also more likely to feel that clinicians didn't take them seriously or more likely to endorse statements suggesting that antibiotic resistance is a hoax.

"Greater antibiotic knowledge and aversion to taking antibiotics were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation," meaning lying about symptoms, the study authors noted.

Less than 30% of these patients regretted their lies or taking the antibiotics prescribed to them. Those that did express regret noted experiencing side effects, noticing that the treatment didn't help or feeling that the lying itself was morally wrong.

The second survey was much smaller; it included 236 parents and other guardians of children and teens under 18 years old. It posed similar questions but asked whether the caregivers had lied about their children's symptoms and, if so, what motivated them to lie.

About 27% reported lying about a child's symptoms to get antibiotics, with 87% of these caregivers believing that their lying worked at least once. Their reasons for lying were very similar to those expressed by the respondents in the first survey.

"These findings suggest that symptom misrepresentation may contribute to antibiotic overuse in pediatric care," the study authors concluded.

Ideally, antibiotics should be used only when truly needed, to help relieve the pressure on bacteria to gain resistance.

The surveys reached a diverse group of people, including a range of ages, demographics and locations within the United States; however, the respondents were not necessarily representative of the whole U.S. population, the authors noted. The prevalence of lying should therefore be seen as a tentative measure to be checked in future studies, rather than an unbiased, population-level metric, they wrote. It's also possible that not all the respondents who lied disclosed that they did so or remembered that they had done so.

Especially in outpatient settings, which account for most antibiotic use among U.S. patients, it can be difficult for doctors to quickly determine whether a patient needs an antibiotic.

One factor is that there's a lack of fast, surefire diagnostic tests for many bacterial infections. Outpatient appointments are also extremely short, so doctors sometimes worry about overlooking an infection that could then get worse, Julia Szymczak, a medical sociologist at the University of Utah School of Medicine, previously told Live Science. Another major factor is that clinicians can face pressure to prescribe antibiotics from their adult patients or from children's caregivers, as the new surveys reflect.

But in the face of these pressures and patients' occasional lies, Linder argues that it's still up to the clinicians to do the right thing. "While clinicians might interpret patients' symptom maximization and questions as demands for antibiotics, symptoms do not determine the indication, a diagnosis does," he wrote in the commentary.

"It does not track that approximately 80% of respondents who reported misrepresenting their symptoms obtained a prescription," he added, "unless prescribers were being willfully deceived or, more likely, just getting worn down with what they perceive as patient demand, regardless of actual clinical appropriateness."

When it comes to making decisions about individual patients, Linder argued that doctors don't necessarily need to think about the big picture of antibiotic resistance and how their patient's case fits into that global trend. Rather, providers should simply ask whether a given prescription is more likely to help or hurt that patient, he said.

"Clinicians' obligation is to act in patients' best interest," he said, "even if patients are hoping we do something different, even if patients do not like it, or even if patients lie about their symptoms."
