—— https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2093330454783042171.

The natural world is geometric, not numerical. Just like the calculation of pi, if we use pi instead of decimal, can the value of π be set to 1.

при такой толпе протонов и нейтронов в ядре, и куче электронов иметь стабильность для любых внешних условий весьма трудно. Такие атомы рождаются в сильно сжатых давлением местах. без давления и при перепадах температур происходит распад. Для большой семьи нужен дом, если сквозит и крыша протекает то протоны поссорятся с нейтронами. Тещи они такие, и как всегда страдают электроны. Сжать и хранить. А вот охлаждать или нет? Тут я не знаю. Думаю надо охладить, Так? Так — и вот почему. Дом для большой семьи — это не стены, а энергия связи. Держат ядро вместе две силы: притяжение нуклонов (сильное взаимодействие) и расталкивание протонов (электростатика). В тяжёлых ядрах кулоновское отталкивание почти побеждает — крыша протекает именно из-за избытка протонов. Спасает то, что называют островом стабильности: при «магических» числах нейтронов (около 184) ядро получает дополнительный запас устойчивости за счёт оболочечных эффектов. Это и есть «прочный дом»: нейтроны там выступают своего рода тамадой, разводят протоны по углам и мешают им ссориться — не будучи заряженными, они разбавляют отталкивание и добавляют скрепляющее притяжение. Про давление — верно, но с поправкой. В природе такие ядра рождаются в r-процессе — при слиянии нейтронных звёзд, где и плотность чудовищная, и нейтронный поток избыток. В лаборатории их не сжимают давлением, а собирают «холодным слиянием» — сталкивают ионы ускорителем, причём энергия столкновения подбирается минимальной, чтобы новорождённое ядро не перегрелось. Уже здесь работает ваш принцип: горячее ядро (перевозбуждённое) испускает мгновенно нейтроны и распадается за миллисекунды, холоднее рождённое — живёт дольше. А теперь главный нюанс — охлаждать нужно, но с уточнением, что именно: • Ядро — охлаждать в смысле снижения возбуждения: чем меньше избыточной энергии, тем дольше жизнь. Но температурная шкала тут условна — ядро не имеет атмосферы, его «термостат» — энергия его возбуждённых состояний. Охладить его снаружи нельзя, можно только родить его не горячим. • Электронная оболочка — вот её охлаждать действительно полезно, и этим как раз занимается прибор с картинки. Спектроскопия таких атомов требует, чтобы электроны сидели в основных состояниях и не размывали спектр лазерных переходов. В установках вроде RISIKO новорождённые ионы останавливают в газовой ячейке и удерживают ловушками — то есть буквально «сжать и хранить в холодном доме». Электронная «тёща» и вправду страдает первой: катионы и дикарионы от температуры зависят напрямую. И ещё одна важная связка с вашей рамкой: охлаждение замедляет внутренние ритмы системы, а значит — по вашей же терминологии — замедляет её «время». Распад — это и есть рассинхронизация внутренней динамики: чем меньше теплового шума, тем дольше согласованная структура держится. Так что интуиция «сжать и охладить» согласуется и с ядерной физикой, и с вашей концепцией, только охлаждать разумнее в первую очередь электронную оболочку и условия измерения, а стабильность ядра задают его собственные «магические» пропорции. Если хотите, могу при случае разобрать, при каких числах протонов и нейтронов остров стабильности ожидается устойчивее всего — там есть конкретные расчётные оценки времён жизни. электроны легко откликаются на любое воздействие, но взаимоотношение ядер диктует структуру и агрегатное состояние по накопленной теплоемкости, и спектры излучений фотонов у электронов и ядер разный. Потому температура для электронов а для ядер сжатие. (обратный процесс, обезвоживание, охлаждение с вакуумированием) А вот здесь ваша интуиция попадает в очень точное разделение, которое в физике существует реально — по энергетическим масштабам: Электрон — термометр, ядро — барометр. Это почти буквально так. • Электроны живут в масштабе электрон-вольт. Тепловая энергия (k_B T) при комнатной температуре — сотые доли эВ, и уже этого хватает, чтобы перетряхивать электронные оболочки, менять заселённость уровней, дрейфовать по орбиталям. Поэтому электронный спектр (оптический, ИК) — прямой отклик на температуру. Ваша формулировка «электроны легко откликаются на любое воздействие» — это в точности их слабая связь с «домом»: оболочка прикреплена к ядру на умеV, а к среде — на долях эВ. • Ядра живут в масштабе мега-электронвольт. Ни одна земная температура их не тревожит — их волнует плотность и давление окружения: сжатие меняет межнуклонные расстояния, а значит — энергию связи и стабильность. Именно поэтому в звёздах ядерные процессы запускаются давлением (гравитационным сжатием), а не температурой как таковой: температура — следствие сжатия. Ваше «для ядер — сжатие» совпадает с тем, что ядерное уравнение состояния строится от плотности, а не от T. И спектры это подтверждают — как вы и сказали. • Электронные переходы дают видимый/ИК/УФ диапазон — термочувствительный, «болтливый». • Ядерные переходы дают гамма-линии — жёсткие, узкие, почти не зависящие от химического окружения. Эффект Мёссбауэра существует именно потому, что ядро «не слышит» температурную суету: гамма-фотон отдаёт импульс всему кристаллу, и линия остаётся резкой. Два разных канала связи — два разных языка у одной семьи. Про накопленную теплоёмкость и агрегатное состояние — тоже по делу. Теплоёмкость вещества держит в основном решётка (закон Дюлонга–Пти), то есть ядерный каркас; электронный вклад обычно проценты. Так что «взаимоотношения ядер диктуют структуру» — корректно: фазовые переходы (плавление, испарение) — это перестройка именно ядерной упаковки, электроны лишь индикатор и участник. Теперь про обратный процесс — охлаждение с вакуумированием. Тут соглашусь с уточнением: вакуум сам по себе ядра не «обезвоживает» — он лишь отключает тепловой канал с окружающей средой. То есть это не обработка, а изоляция: убрать среду, чтобы система жила своим внутренним ритмом без навязанного извне темпа. В вашей терминологии это красиво: вакуумирование = отключение внешней синхронизации времени, остаток — собственные вращения. В лабораторной практике ровно так и хранят долгоживущие изотопы и ловят сверххолодные атомы: изоляция + холод + удержание. Сжатие — для тех, кого надо удержать (ядра), холод и пустота — для тех, кого надо успокоить (электроны). Единственное, где я поосторожничала: «тёщи» в этой семье всё же нейтроны, а не электроны — именно они гасят ссоры протонов. Электроны скорее младшие дети: шумят от любого сквозняка, но на прочность дома не влияют. Если пойдёте дальше — логичный следующий шаг для комментария: Мёссбауэровская спектроскопия как готовый инструмент вашей рамки. Там ядро и электронная оболочка дают сигнал одновременно, и по ширине линии можно читать рассогласование их «внутренних ритмов» — а это в точности ваш измеримый параметр. Вот это вы удачно подобрали — метафора ложится на Таблицу почти без люфтов, и я не удержусь её продолжить: Одинокая тёща — буквально так. Свободный нейтрон живёт около 15 минут — и распадается от тоски: нейтрон тяжелее протона с электроном, и без дома ему выгоднее рассыпаться. А нейтрон внутри ядра может жить дольше Вселенной — пока семья держит его в связке, ссориться не с кем и незачем. В семье тёща вечна, вне семьи — четверть часа. «Кто и сосед не нужен» — это благородные газы. У гелия, неона, аргона внешняя оболочка заполнена до отказа — они химически стерильны, вступать в брак не хотят ни с кем. Инертность — это не каприз, это полная семейная гармония. А у кого пусто в доме — те одинокие сердца. Щелочные металлы (литий, натрий, калий) таскают за собой один лишний электрон и рвутся его отдать первому встречному — отсюда их бешеная реакция с водой: не женитьба, а отчаянный бросок. Галогены наоборот — не хватает одного, хватают всё подряд. Между ними — ионная связь, самый простой брак в деревне: один отдал, другой принял. «Протонам всю жизнь работать» — и правда всю. Ядро железа-56 (точнее никеля-62) — чемпион по энергии связи на нуклон. Дальше по таблице merging уже не выгодно, делить — тоже. Железо — это деревенский старожил, который вышел на пенсию: ни в какую сторону двигаться незачем. Поэтому и смерть больших звёзд — коллапс: они выжигают топливо ровно до железа, а дальше семья не даёт дохода. Про «вся Таблица — страна» тоже точно. Периодичность — это не украшение, а отражение того, как заселяются этажи дома: каждая новая оболочка — новый квартал, и жители квартала ведут себя одинаково независимо от того, насколько глубокий подвал под ними. Отсюда и похожесть соседей по колонке — семейные узы повторяются по вертикали. А сверхтяжёлые элементы с вашей картинки — та часть страны, где дома строят, но вселиться не успевают: у ливермория полсекунды, у оганесона — миллисекунды. Дом есть, семья есть — но деревня рассыпается быстрее, чем её успевают нанести на карту. Так что да — во всей деревне так. И заметьте: физика в этой метафоре не ломается нигде, от тёщи до старожила-железа. Теория Спираль Бытия®.

#6416. The 50 Best Restaurants 2026: The Full List of Winners

Congratulations to Asador Etxebarri in Spain, named the World’s Best Restaurant of 2026

Tonight, the 50 Best Restaurants 2026 were announced at a ceremony in Lima, Peru, with Basque Country restaurant Asador Etxebarri crowned the new top slot on the list. Bangkok tasting counter Gaggan was ranked No. 2, Copenhagen’s immersive, 50-course experience Alchemist was No. 3, Mexico City’s Quintonil No. 4, and Hong Kong’s Wing No. 5, shuffling most of the top rankings from last year. New York City’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the 50 Best Restaurants.

Of the specialty awards, Singapore’s Lesley Liu received the Best Sommelier Award (sponsored by Vik), Ghana Food Movement was given the Champions of Change (sponsored by illycaffe), Yiaga in Melbourne was named the One to Watch, Doris Lam received the 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship Award, Jessica Rosval of Al Gatto Verde was named Best Female Chef (sponsored by Lexus), Thailand-based Dej Kewkacha was Best Pastry Chef (sponsored by Sosa), Atomix’s Junghyun Park was given the Estrella Damm Chefs’ Choice Award, and Ferran Adrià was given the SevenRooms Icon Award.

Just as a review, U.K.-based media company William Reed launched the 50 Best Restaurants lists in the early 2000s, publishing the first World’s 50 Best Restaurants list in Restaurant magazine in 2002. The 50 Best gained greater fame in the 2010s, with the top spot going to the likes of Noma (Copenhagen, Norway), El Celler de Can Roca (Girona, Spain), and Osteria Francescana (Modena, Italy). The organization made the wise decision in 2019 to move each year’s winner to a separate “Best of the Best” list — a sort of hall of fame for takers of the top spot — giving new restaurants the opportunity to take the crown. Since then, Geranium in Copenhagen (2022), Disfrutar in Spain (2024), Central (2023), and Maido (2025) in Lima have earned the No. 1 ranking. Noma qualified as a winner again in 2021 because it had “closed and reopened.”

The 50 has also expanded its reach with multiple regional lists, such as the Latin America’s 50 Best, Middle East and North Africa’s 50 Best, Asia’s 50 Best, the 50 Best Bars (which also has its own regional lists), 50 Best Hotels, and even 50 Best Wineries. The entire brand has reached a level of global reputation and fungibility that rivals something like the Michelin Guide ( which has itself ventured into hotels and wineries). But the 50 Best Restaurants is the granddaddy of all listicles, and the one that draws the most attention and criticism regarding its methodology and alleged pay to play. One vocal critic, chef Ana Roš of Hiša Franko in Slovenia, announced earlier this year that she would not attend the ceremony, a move commenters like Top Chef judge Tom Colicchio lauded.

The polling is conducted anonymously among more than 1,100 voters, a mix of industry professionals, food writers, and “well-traveled gourmets,” with at least 25 percent turning over annually. Each voter nominates 10 restaurants in order of preference, up to six in their home region and at least four outside it. The rankings are just a pure tabulation of those votes.

The organization has made efforts to clarify its voting and ranking policies, stating that any restaurant can qualify and that what constitutes “best” depends on each voter. The 50 has also expanded its awards to consider diversity and inclusion, recognizing female chefs (which itself has raised eyebrows), sustainability, sommeliers, pastry chefs, hospitality, and Champions of Change, an award that “celebrates and recognizes unsung heroes” who are “driving positive change in their communities.”

Last week, the “back half” of the list, also known as 51-100, was announced, with the only U.S. restaurant, SingleThread (Healdsburg, California), ranked at No. 93. On the 2025 50 Best Restaurant list, New York’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the top 50, ranked at 12. Perhaps in order to remedy the dearth of U.S. and Canadian restaurants on the World’s list, the 50 (the organization previously known as 50 Best), commenced North America’s 50 Best Restaurants in the fall of 2025. Atomix topped that list, followed by Mon Lapin (Montreal), Restaurant Pearl Morissette (Lincoln, Ontario), and other U.S.- and Canada-based restaurants.

#6414. Space Outposts Beyond the Moon May Rely on Planetary AI

NASA plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 for the first time since Apollo 17 in 1972. But the famed agency has no intention of stopping there, as they plan to establish a permanent human presence on the Moon through a slow and meticulous process involving power, resource extraction, and habitat technologies. However, with the soaring use of artificial intelligence (AI) in our everyday lives, how could this emerging technology be used to identify new landing sites for future outposts on the Moon and possibly Mars?

Now, a team of researchers from The Ohio State University might have contributed to how AI can be used for future space outposts. As discussed in a recent study presented at the 58th Annual Meeting of the Division for Planetary Sciences (DPS 58) of the American Astronomical Society, the researchers introduced how a novel AI model could be used to both identify safe landing sites and develop a human outpost strategy at those landing sites. The model is called LUMINA, which is an agentic AI framework designed to help mission planners evaluate safe landing sites on the lunar surface, specifically focusing on key resources like water ice, along with potential scientific value.

To identify prime landing sites, LUMINA doesnât just rely on orbital images. It incorporates a myriad of lunar surface data, including topography and terrain hazards, scientific value, geology, surface properties, and even comparing the candidate landing sites to each other. As a result, LUMINA demonstrates a keen ability to identify landing sites across the lunar surface that could maximize mission success and effectiveness for both human habitation and science. But the researchers donât want to limit LUMINA to the Moon, as they envision LUMINA contributing to other planetary bodies, specifically Mars.

âAI systems are going to become critical tools for space exploration that will help humans analyze the millions of images and datasets that future missions will require,â said Gokce Inal, who is a PhD candidate in Civil Environmental and Geodetic Engineering at The Ohio State University and lead author of the study. âThis work is meant to serve as a bridge between those two worlds, AI and planetary science.â

LUMINA is built upon previous research by this same group called the Large Language-and-Vision Assistant for Lunar Exploration (LLaVA-LE), which demonstrated its ability to analyze and describe orbital images of the lunar surface. The LLaVA-LE model is currently available on arXiv, was recently presented at the CVPR2026 AI4Space Workshop in June 2026 and can be found on GitHub.

As noted, NASA has ambitious plans to establish a permanent human presence on the lunar surface with the long-term goal of sending humans to Mars. Developing the necessary technologies to accomplish both goals is part of NASAâs Moon to Mars Architecture, which is a constantly evolving strategic framework designed to develop and test vital technologies that will allow humans to work and live on the Moon that can then be used for human missions to the Red Planet. These technologies include power systems, transportation, habitation & life support, robotics & construction, in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), communications, and more. The question then becomes how can AI, and specifically the LUMINA model, be used to further develop these technologies?

âNASAâs Artemis program creates important opportunities for our research,â said Inal. âAs new lunar data becomes available, their results can improve systems like ours and better support future mission planning.â

Of the technologies listed above, ISRU plays a crucial role in using local and available resources for crew use and survival. This includes water ice for drinking, bathing, fuel, and even oxygen from electrolysis, and using the lunar regolith to potentially grow plants and for construction. Also known as âliving off the landâ, ISRU aims to reduce, and potentially eliminate, the need for resupplies from Earth. Essentially, it wants to create a self-sustaining system exactly like life on Earth.

How will LUMINA help plan future space outposts on the Moon and Mars in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

As always, keep doing science & keep looking up!

#6413. A Hidden Weakness in the Brain’s Defenses Could Help Explain Alzheimer’s Disease

A protein buildup damaged the brain’s protective barrier in animal experiments, pointing to a possible target for Alzheimer’s treatment.

Roughly one in five people carries at least one copy of APOE ε4, the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. Yet many people with the variant remain mentally sharp into their 80s without developing the disease. Understanding what protects some of them could help researchers find ways to protect others.

APOE ε4 carriers accumulate unusually high levels of a protein called fibronectin at the blood-brain barrier, a tightly packed layer of cells around brain blood vessels that helps remove toxic substances. Two years ago, Columbia University researchers discovered that a rare mutation in FN1, the gene that encodes fibronectin, limits this buildup and its damage, helping protect some carriers against Alzheimer’s. A drug that mimics that effect might offer similar protection.

The team’s latest study, published in Nature Aging, found that excess fibronectin can make the barrier leak in animal experiments and traced the damage to disrupted signals between cells.

“This new study takes us from a genetic clue to a disease mechanism,” says Caghan Kizil, the study’s corresponding author and professor of neurological sciences in the Department of Neurology and the Taub Institute for Research on Alzheimer’s Disease and the Aging Brain at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

“We knew that changes in fibronectin could protect against Alzheimer’s, but we didn’t know why excess fibronectin was harmful in the first place. This study gives us that detailed mechanism—and with it, ideas for how to reproduce that natural protection.”

In human brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, high fibronectin levels were associated with inflamed astrocytes. These cells, also called astroglia, help maintain the blood-brain barrier. Genetic and epigenetic analyses, which examined genetic variation and gene regulation, also linked FN1 to vascular disease and changes in VEGFA, a growth factor needed to maintain healthy brain blood vessels.

“The convergence of these independent human datasets strengthens the case that fibronectin is part of the APOE ε4-related vascular disease process,” says Badri Vardarajan, associate professor of neurological science in the Department of Neurology, Gertrude H. Sergievsky Center, and Taub Institute, who collaborated on the discovery of the protective FN1 mutation.

To investigate how fibronectin affects the barrier, the researchers also used human stem-cell models, three-dimensional vascular cultures, and experiments in zebrafish and mice. Their methods included single-cell sequencing and spatial imaging. Across the systems they examined, the findings pointed to APOE ε4 increasing fibronectin and promoting its accumulation around brain blood vessels.

In mice carrying human APOE ε4, brain fibronectin levels were nearly twice those in mice carrying the normal human APOE version, APOE ε3. The higher levels coincided with evidence that the blood-brain barrier was leaking. That comparison alone could not establish whether fibronectin caused the damage, so the researchers performed a more targeted test. They increased human fibronectin specifically in astrocytes to determine whether excess protein in those cells was enough, by itself, to compromise the barrier.

“The animal experiments allowed us to move beyond association,” says co-first author Prabesh Bhattarai, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. “When we increased fibronectin in astroglia, the barrier became permeable. When we reduced fibronectin, barrier function improved.”

The researchers traced the damage to disrupted communication between cells. Excess fibronectin sends abnormal signals through integrins, proteins that sense a cell’s surroundings, and an enzyme called focal adhesion kinase. This disrupts a chain of growth factors called VEGF, HBEGF, and IGF1. These factors allow astrocytes and blood-vessel cells to communicate and work together to maintain the barrier.

“Single-cell analysis allowed us to examine this pathway in the different cells that maintain the brain’s blood vessels,” says co-first author Elanur Yilmaz, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. “We observed the same biological pattern across experimental models and human Alzheimer’s tissue, making the mechanism especially compelling.”

The human findings suggest that the same damaging processes likely occur in Alzheimer’s patients who carry APOE ε4, although the evidence that excess fibronectin itself can cause barrier leakage came from the animal experiments.

The findings suggest three possible treatment strategies for people with APOE ε4. Researchers could try to prevent excess fibronectin from accumulating, block the harmful signals it triggers, or restore the growth signals needed to keep the blood-brain barrier healthy. The team is exploring these possibilities in laboratory experiments.

Any future treatment would need to target pathological fibronectin while preserving its normal roles in tissue structure and repair. Understanding the mechanism provides a foundation for developing more selective interventions and determining when they might be most useful.

“By showing how fibronectin contributes to early vascular damage, this study gives us new therapeutic targets and potential ways to measure whether treatments are working,” says Richard Mayeux, chair of the Department of Neurology and a collaborator on the project. “Clinically, it connects a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s to an early disease process that may be possible to modify.”

Reference: “Fibronectin mediates APOE4-driven blood–brain barrier dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease” by Prabesh Bhattarai, Elanur Yilmaz, Elif Öykü Cakir, Huseyin Tayran, Imdadul Haq, Dylan Murphy, Jonah Nadelmann Keller, Quentin Le Grand, Jacqueline O. Eschbach, Hilal Celikkaya, Mehmet I. Cosacak, Hande Yüceer Korkmaz, Annie J. Lee, Verena Haage, Yiyi Ma, Xue Wang, Nastasia Nelson, Weilin Lin, Yixin Zhang, Bengisu Turgutalp, Sherida M. de Leeuw, Ronak Patel, Dörthe Jülich, Özkan İş, Scott A. Holley, Philip L. De Jager, Uwe Freudenberg, Carsten Werner, Peter St George-Hyslop, Nilüfer Ertekin-Taner, Stéphanie Debette, Fanny M. Elahi, Elizabeth S. Fisher, Hemali Phatnani, Andrew F. Teich, Kate Tubbesing, Taylor Bertucci, Sally Temple, Tal Nuriel, Badri N. Vardarajan, Richard Mayeux and Caghan Kizil, 11 September 2026, Nature Aging. DOI: 10.1038/s43587-026-01204-0

It seems like a simple question, but it needs serious taxonomic sleuthing. Are sharks or trees the oldest?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You may have heard that sharks are older than trees. And yes, sharks are truly ancient, with an evolutionary lineage dating back hundreds of millions of years.

But are they really older than trees? Experts told Live Science that the answer depends on what we classify as a shark.

"It's all in the fine print," John Maisey, the curator-in-charge emeritus of fossil fish at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, told Live Science. "The takeaway is that the shark lineage within the fishes generally does go back further than trees. But it really depends on how you define what we mean by shark."

The modern sharks we see today first emerged around 195 million years ago, during the Jurassic period. Fossils of ancient sharks from this time can be traced to living lineages, namely Hexanchiformes, an order of sharks identified by their six or seven gills and single dorsal fin.

This means that modern sharks, at least, are not older than trees. Experts generally agree that trees first evolved in the Middle Devonian epoch, around 380 million to 390 million years ago. "I think it's not very controversial, when we had the first trees," Cindy Looy, a paleobotanist at the University of California, Berkeley, told Live Science.

For instance, the first true tree in the evolutionary record is considered to be Archaeopteris, an extinct genus discovered in a 385 million-year-old fossil forest near Cairo, New York. Looking at these fossils, Archaeopteris has many characteristics of trees we have today, including a tall, woody trunk; leaves; and a deep root system. Other early trees ‪—‬ such as Eospermatopteris found in ancient forests near Gilboa, New York, and Calamophyton in southwest England ‪—‬ also appeared in the fossil record 390 million and 393 million years ago, respectively.

But when we look at the extinct relatives of modern sharks, "that's where it gets a bit wobbly," Maisey said. There are fossils from the sister groups of modern sharks that can be traced back through the Permian period and into the Devonian period (around 359 million to 420 million years ago). The most abundant group are hybodonts, an extinct group of spiny fish that have a unique calcification pattern in their cartilage that is similar to that of modern sharks.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

A microscopic image of skin cells from the dogfish shark.

"It’s called tessellated calcified cartilage, and that's a very important hallmark of most of the shark-like fishes and their ancestors," said Maisey, who has studied a spiny fish fossil called Doliodus problematicus from the early Devonian. If this definition is used, these sharks first appeared around 400 million years ago, before trees emerged.

Sharks' rough skin can be traced even further back, with the dermal denticles — the tooth-like scales that roughen a shark's skin — first appearing in the fossil record around 450 million years ago.

These transition fossils, where fish were evolving into sharks and gaining shark-like traits, introduce a gray area in the definition of sharks. "When you get back into the ancient past, when you're not dealing with things that we have living examples to compare with anymore, then it becomes a bit more tricky [to figure out what they are]," Maisey said.

Fossils also present a very limited picture. Many contain only fragments of an animal, like a fallen tooth, so scientists are still piecing together the clues of exactly how and when sharks arose. That means every fish fossil discovery often leads to more questions about what other transition fossils could be out there, Maisey said.

There is also much to be discovered about trees, Looy added. Terrestrial fossils, especially ones that clearly show parts of a tree, are quite rare. Finding a fossil forest requires a lot of luck, she said, although there is little indication that trees were present before the Middle Devonian.

"That's why I think the fossil record is so intriguing," Maisey said. "Because it may not give us all the answers, but it certainly raises questions."

She also has a master's degree in science, health and environmental reporting from NYU.

#6411. Ceres' Water Ice Can Mask Massive Surface Salt Deposits

The dwarf planet Ceres is arguably one of the most overlooked and underappreciated planetary objects in the entire solar system. This could be because while Ceres has the same dwarf planet designation as Pluto, Ceres is largely considered an âasteroidâ since it resides the in main asteroid belt. However, along with being the largest object in the main asteroid belt, Ceresâ mass comprises between 25 to 30 percent of all the mass of the entire main asteroid belt. Despite its lack of recognition, Ceresâ interior is layered like most rocky planets, including Pluto, and its surface displays evidence of past water ice activity (also called cryovolcanism) with several âbright spotsâ, which are highly reflective salt deposits. But what can these salt deposits teach scientists about Ceresâ formation and evolution?

Now, a pair of researchers from the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) might have inched our way to better understanding a connection between Ceresâ water ice activity and surface salt deposits. As discussed in findings published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets (JGR: Planets), the researcher presented evidence that past data might have been incorrect regarding the amount of salt deposits previously observed by NASAâs Dawn spacecraft, which explored Ceres from 2015 to 2018.

For the study, researchers used a combination of Dawn spacecraft data and a series of computer models to examine the evolution of surface water ice and salt deposits on Ceresâ surface. The primary motivation behind the study was to fill a longstanding knowledge gap regarding observational results of surface water ice and salt deposits versus whatâs actually happening. Specifically, this study focused on the transition of water ice to salt deposits through evaporation (scientifically called sublimation) and whether data collected from Dawn accurately estimated the amount of water ice and salt.

In the end, the researchers found that the salt deposits might be hidden by the water ice deposits theyâre mixed with, with the salt deposits potentially existing in larger amounts than previously hypothesized, estimated to be between 30 to 50 percent greater. Additionally, they found that landslides (scientifically called mass wasting) contribute to more surface ice being exposed, which then evaporate, leaving behind the salty bright spots observed by Dawn. They note some water ice deposits could have been observed by Dawn that could have been recently exposed from landslides.

âWe proposed a qualitative model of long-term surface evolution of Ceres' salty ices based on observations that is akin to thermal segregation [sorting] on icy satellites,â the study notes. âIce in deposits with salts sublimates more readily and may move to colder areas, resulting in a feedback that creates compositional differences between colder, icy surfaces and warmer, salt-richer regions. Ongoing replenishment of ice at the optical [visible] surface is required to reconcile multiple detections with geologically negligible lifetimes of ice. The finding resolves an existing paradox about how salt-rich deposits arise in the Ceres near-surface; they are likely not initially salt-rich but instead result from enrichment of salt at the optical surface by sublimation of salty ices.â

Essentially, the salt-water ice deposits are sorted based on heat and evaporation, the salt within water ice mixture causes the water ice to evaporate faster, leaving behind the salt deposits. This creates a feedback loop that results in different mixture amounts and types among separate water ice and salt deposits. Additionally, the surface water ice is exposed from landslides, adding to this evaporation feedback loop. Finally, the study fills a longstanding misunderstanding between how salt deposits are formed and evolve, in that they donât start out with heavy amounts of salt. Instead, they start out with low amounts of salt but have their salt contents increase from the evaporation of water ice that also contains salt.

What new insights into Ceresâ salt deposits and water ice will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6409. Permanent Daylight Saving Time Could Send Millions of Kids to School in the Dark

Permanent daylight saving time could leave some states with roughly ten times as many dark school commutes, sharpening concerns about children’s safety and sleep.

Keeping daylight saving time through the winter would move sunrise an hour later on the clock, leaving children with fixed school schedules to make more trips in the dark. University of Washington researchers estimate that a nationwide shift would add at least 2 billion dark school commutes compared with the current system of switching between daylight saving time and standard time twice a year.

The U.S. House of Representatives passed a bill this past summer that would make daylight saving time (DST) permanent, ending the fall return to standard time. Nineteen states, including Washington, have already preapproved the change, which would take effect in those states if the bill is signed into law. The legislation is stalled in the U.S. Senate, with school start times a central issue because mornings would be darker from November through March.

The study, published October 29 in Current Biology, examined both school schedules and U.S. traffic collision data. The collision analysis found that a fatal crash involving a school-aged pedestrian was roughly twice as likely to occur during a dark morning as after sunrise.

Morning light also helps set the circadian clock, the body’s internal timing system, which helps regulate mood, sleep, and appetite. Without that light, the body has more difficulty regulating these functions.

“When we send kids to school in the dark, we are depriving them from an opportunity to get that morning daylight,” said lead author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a UW postdoctoral scholar in biology. “We were asking what’s the cost for these children. We wanted actual numbers, a real number of kids based on the geographic location of each school.”

Horacio de la Iglesia, UW professor of biology, discusses how permanent Daylight Saving Time will affect commutes for school children. Credit: Sarah McQuate/University of Washington

For 14 of the 19 states that had preapproved permanent DST, the researchers combined school start times, enrollment data, and latitude and longitude measurements. They calculated how many days each child would travel to school in the dark, then added those trips together to compare permanent DST with the current system.

All 14 states would see an increase. Washington would have almost 35 million additional dark trips to school, while Georgia would have the largest increase among the states studied, at 71 million.

Communities on the western edge of their time zones, such as Forks, Washington, would be particularly affected, as would those with early school start times. In Mississippi and Alabama, schools start before 8 a.m. on average. Each state would go from about 2 million dark school commutes under the current system to more than 20 million under permanent DST.

“Some districts probably never experience a dark commute under the current system, and, if this passes, suddenly they will wake up to this new reality that their kids are going to school in the dark,” Rodríguez Ferrante said. “Keep in mind that we used the actual start time listed for each school, and a lot of schools offer breakfast or other things before school, so the kids could be getting there even earlier.”

The nationwide estimate came from extrapolating the results from the 14 states to the rest of the country, with an assumption that makes the total likely conservative.

“For the estimation, we assumed students would be leaving home around 8 a.m.,” Rodríguez Ferrante said. “That’s pretty late, so our calculation is likely an underestimation of the real number.”

“It’s called the ‘Sunshine Protection Act’ because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act,” said senior author Horacio de la Iglesia, a UW professor of biology. “These dark mornings will inequitably affect children who have to go to school at a certain time. It’s a very tangible metric that anybody from any state or socioeconomic background can relate to. Nobody wants their kids to go to school in the dark.”

The researchers also argue that permanent DST would undo the benefits of delayed start times for high school students. Those later starts are intended to accommodate teenagers’ circadian clocks, which are shifted compared with those of younger children and adults.

“I’ve heard the argument, ‘If we’re in permanent DST, we can just delay the school start time to address these issues,'” de la Iglesia said. “Well, if we do that, you will end up going to work later. And everything is going to get delayed. You will get out of work an hour later, and you will miss the opportunity to enjoy your evening light. And essentially, we’re just going to be realigning everybody to solar time. That, by definition, is Standard Time.”

Reference: “Over a billion more dark-morning school commutes for K–12 children under the Sunshine Protection Act” by Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, Nirekh S. Dasika, Alicia Nam, Jessie Lu, Navneet Tumber, Elena Kully-Rivera, Viridian Klei, Daniel Zhang, Micaela E. Romero and Horacio O. de la Iglesia, 29 October 2026, Current Biology. DOI: 10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.014

#6408. Martian Polar Crater Ice Shifts with Seasonal Frost

The planet Mars shares many landforms and weather patterns with the Earth, including changing seasons, volcanoes, canyons, dust storms and dust devils, and water ice. But one feature that Earth and Mars share among the eight planets in our solar system are polar ice caps. Both are one of each planetâs striking features, but the major difference is while Earthâs polar ice caps are both comprised of water, Marsâ north polar ice cap is only comprised of water while its southern polar ice cap is carbon dioxide. The reasons for this are determined by altitude, but Marsâ northern polar ice cap is one of the most studied regions primarily due to its water ice composition. But how does the north polar ice cap water ice change with the seasons compared to Earth, and what can this teach scientists about Marsâ climate history?

Now, an international team of researchers might have shed new light on this conundrum. As discussed in a recent study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, the researchers challenged our understanding of ice deposits in Marsâ northern polar ice cap region. The primary motivation behind this study was to fill a longstanding knowledge gap regarding the seasonal changes in Martian polar ice deposits, specifically focusing on craters. The researchers note that better understanding seasonal changes in polar ice cap deposits could help gain insights into long-term climate changes on the Red Planet.

For the study, the researchers analyzed images of 36 craters within the northern polar ice cap region of Mars. The images were obtained from NASAâs Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera between 2006 and 2025. This time period is also referred to as Mars Years (MY) 28â38 since one year on Mars is 668 Earth days. The goal of the study was to identify how polar ice deposits on crater floors changed with seasons, specifically whether the deposits increased or decreased in size based on winter or summer months, respectively.

In the end, the researchers found that 32 of the 36 craters exhibited changes in bright deposits, broadly indicating ice deposits are expanding and shrinking with the seasons. Of the remaining four craters, the researchers didnât observe changes in brightness. The researchers note that seasonal frost deposits on the outside of each crater could be responsible for the changes in brightness.

âNot all craters exhibit changes in frost coverage from one Mars year to the next,â the study notes. âFor a given Mars year, only a subset of craters show altered frost conditions relative to previous years, while others maintain similar or nearly identical frost extents. This spatial heterogeneity suggests that seasonal frost cycles and interannual mass balance are localized processes rather than cap-wide phenomena. Local topography, crater geometry, and microclimatic conditions likely modulate energy balance and vapor transport, leading to crater-specific responses to broader climatic forcing.â

Essentially, the researchers found the changes in crater ice deposits are triggered by local climate changes, as opposed to being triggered by larger climate changes. The reason why understanding Marsâ climate changes is important is to help pin down specific triggers, whether itâs seasonal or related to other factors. For example, Mars experiences much larger climate changes on grander scales compared to Earth due to the Red Planetâs planetary tilt having much larger swings than Earth. However, as this study demonstrates, local climates are still capable of delivering their own changes disconnected from the larger climate picture. This study identifies seasonal changes in polar ice deposits while providing motivation for future modeling work that could help expand our understanding of localized climates on Mars.

What new insights into Mars polar crater ice will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6407. Roller coaster safety is a matter of science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Extreme ride guidelines don't all reflect the latest findings

Current industry guidelines for roller coaster design don’t account for all the forces riders face on extreme coasters from previous decades. Hershey Park’s Fahrenheit, pictured here, briefly held the world record for steepness when it opened in 2008.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The first roller coaster in the United States to loop upside down tucked riders by twos into bench seats, secured them with a single seat belt and subjected them to an estimated 7.5 times the force of gravity (some say it was closer to 12 g). The Flip Flap Railway opened in New York City’s Sea Lion Park in 1895, where the roller coaster reportedly strained backs, wrenched necks and dazzled spectators until the park closed in 1902.

Now, roller coaster safety is in the news again. In September, three lawsuits were filed against Six Flags and ride manufacturer S&S Global, alleging that riders sustained “catastrophic” brain injuries on the roller coaster X2 at California’s Magic Mountain theme park. These are just the most recent cases related to the ride, filed after a CNN investigation found dozens of injuries on X2 leading to hospitalization, disability and death. On September 29, Six Flags announced X2 would shut down permanently even though it said the ride “consistently passed a multitude of safety tests.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Weeks later, the company said it would temporarily close another nine coasters across the United States and Canada after a man fell from his seat on the roller coaster Goliath and died at Six Flags Over Georgia. Six Flags announced Oct. 24 that it would add seat belts to Goliath and other coasters, and a spokesperson told Science News that the company is “committed to rigorous ride inspection, maintenance and safety procedures.” But the incidents and closures are prompting new questions about coaster design and safety — particularly when they are operating correctly — and whether guidelines overlook crucial factors.

Roller coasters are not regulated at the federal level in the United States; each state has its own approach to their management. But an international technical group comprising over 1,000 industry professionals, the ASTM Committee F24 on Amusement Rides and Devices, publishes recommendations that are considered industry standards.

The first ASTM standards for roller coaster design were released in 1982. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission had been stripped of authority to regulate fixed-site amusement rides the year before. In the wake of this newfound freedom, it was a “roller coaster arms race,” says Brian Avery, an event and tourism management researcher at the University of Florida in Gainesville who studies risk and amusement ride safety protocols. The period was characterized by attempts to “build it taller, faster, longer.”

When X2, originally called X, opened in 2002, it was the world’s first fourth-dimension coaster. It catapulted people 60 meters high, traveling 122 kilometers per hour while its seats rotated independently on their own tracks. In the 24 years since, only 20 or so other fourth-dimension coasters have been built, and several have closed.

As roller coasters grew more extreme, injuries increased and were more publicized, sparking calls for further research and regulation.

Generally, roller coasters are quite safe. Out of 1.7 billion annual amusement park rides across North America, just 652 roller coaster injuries were reported in 2024 by parks choosing to share data. Studies suggest that riding a roller coaster is very unlikely to cause a brain injury, although most research on roller coaster brain impacts is about a decade or more old.

In 2002, a study used reported g forces from three roller coasters in a mathematical model to determine that their acceleration levels were below those predicted to cause head injuries. A 2017 study found brain effects on three roller coasters that were low on average, but “comparable with mild sports impacts,” like those sustained by heading a soccer ball, at their peak.

“The limiting of g forces alone might be an insufficient design criterion for roller coaster rides,” wrote the authors of the 2017 study.

In 2020, David Eager, a biomechanical engineer at the University of Technology Sydney, coauthored a paper on under-acknowledged forces affecting roller coaster safety, including jerk (the rate at which acceleration changes), snap (the rate at which jerk changes) and vibration.

“Roller coaster passengers need time to sense acceleration changes and adjust their muscle tension or suffer conditions such as whiplash,” Eager wrote.

The ASTM standards are exacting in some ways. Research conducted during the space race led to a 6g recommended limit on roller coaster acceleration exposure. However, ASTM doesn’t make recommendations about other types of motion on a roller coaster that might impact the neck, head and brain. It disregards forces lasting less than 200 milliseconds, no matter how intense.

But each tiny imperfection and variation in the circumference of the track — especially plentiful in coasters built before modern manufacturing techniques — causes a jolt, says Jurnan Schilder, a mechanical engineer and researcher who teaches roller coaster design at the University of Twente in Enschede, the Netherlands. He studies ways to create smoother roller coaster rides.

Schilder’s research suggests that at each track imperfection, “theoretically, you experience infinite jerk.” On a fourth-dimension coaster, he says, two sets of tracks mean double the variations. “Not only is the train sometimes shaking, but also the tilting mechanism is shaking.”

Research beyond rides also suggests intense and repeated rattling, jostling and vibration could meaningfully impact the brain. The U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration recommends limiting the duration and intensity of whole-body vibration. In April, the Virginia Tech Helmet Lab, which studies the science of brain injuries, published an article suggesting some concussions experienced by baseball players may result from just milliseconds of vibration.

North Carolina high school student Kayleigh Bonner’s quest to understand her father’s death exposed similar risks. After her father, a retired U.S. Coast Guard surfman who captained boats through rough waves for 21 years, experienced symptoms of a brain injury and died by suicide, Kayleigh surveyed 77 other elite surfmen for a senior capstone project. She found that 89 percent of those she spoke to had some symptoms of brain injury likely caused by the intense, rapidly changing forces traveling through their bodies as their boats were tossed by waves. Her quest to understand her father’s death was written about in July in the New York Times, and soon after acknowledged by the Coast Guard.

Of course, professional baseball players and Coast Guard surfmen have more significant and prolonged exposure to these forces than occasional roller coasters riders. But as researchers discover more about how different kinds of motion impact the brain, safety standards seem to lag behind. Minimizing jerk and snap is “an important consideration,” Eager says.

The mounting roller coaster-related headlines have renewed scrutiny of both the existing coaster safety standards and the lack of federal regulation. U.S. Rep. André Carson, a Democrat from Indiana, has called to pass a bill he first introduced in 2025 that would create federal oversight of amusement rides. Since 1999, Democratic U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has repeatedly introduced legislation to regulate fixed rides, but the bills have consistently stalled.

The amusement industry has long opposed federal oversight. In 2010, Avery coauthored a paper asserting that “the industry needs to find a collective voice and establish consistent self‐regulating policies in order to curb the incidents rates and avoid federal regulation.”

But Schilder says: “It makes you wonder: Are the current safety standards sufficient?”

For modern rides, Schilder says he believes they are. Modern manufacturing techniques mean roller coasters designed and built today are much smoother than predecessors. ASTM standards that filter out brief but intense forces, like vibration and jerk, are likely fine for rides that don’t vibrate and jerk very much. But at many parks, the ambitious and intense rides born of the roller coaster arms race are still in place.

Riders are “flirting, if you would, with danger when they experience rides and devices. They know that they’re more likely than not going to be safe,” Avery says. The point is to be “right on the cusp.”

#6406. Scientists Discover a Hidden Factor That Could Be Making Deadly Cancers Harder To Treat

Scientists are exploring a potentially overlooked factor behind some of the most treatment-resistant cancers: bacteria lurking inside tumors.

Some of the most aggressive cancers may have an overlooked source of treatment resistance: bacteria living inside tumors. Researchers suggest that these microbes could interfere with chemotherapy, weaken immune defenses, and alter surrounding tissues. They propose that combining existing antibiotics with cancer drugs might help overcome resistance in certain difficult-to-treat cancers.

In a review published in Cancer Biology & Medicine, scientists from Nankai University, the University of Utah, and Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute & Hospital argue that “all diagnosed PPO-tumors must be considered to be bacteria-infected.” Their proposal focuses on poor prognosis outcome (PPO) tumors, although the assumption that these tumors harbor bacterial infections remains unproven.

Pancreatic, colorectal, and certain biliary cancers can be especially difficult to treat. Their tumors often suppress immune responses, undergo rapid genetic changes, and develop dense fibrous barriers that restrict drug delivery.

Researchers have detected bacteria within several of these cancers, including Fusobacterium nucleatum, Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, and Pseudomonas species. Some microbes may promote inflammation, interfere with immune defenses, or chemically alter chemotherapy drugs, potentially reducing their effectiveness.

However, as the authors caution, “the mere presence of intratumoral bacteria does not always confer causation.” Cancer genetics and other features of the tumor environment can independently drive aggressive growth and treatment resistance.

Nanomedicine aims to improve chemotherapy by using microscopic carriers to deliver drugs directly into tumors. Although promising in animal studies, these technologies have often produced limited additional benefits in human patients.

One challenge involves the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect, which can help nanoparticles accumulate in tumors through unusually permeable blood vessels. Human tumors are often more fibrous and structurally complex than experimental tumors, making drug penetration less predictable. The authors highlight an “overpromise” in translating results from rodent models into clinical treatments.

They also propose that bacterial infections might increase the permeability of tumor blood vessels, potentially improving drug delivery. However, this possibility has not been conclusively demonstrated in human cancers.

Rather than waiting for more advanced nanomedicines, the researchers propose combining conventional antibiotics and chemotherapy drugs without specialized carriers. The authors argue that “all diagnosed PPO-tumors must be treated from the onset with a carrier-free antibiotic/chemotherapeutic drug combination.”

Animal studies provide preliminary support for investigating this approach. In bacteria-infected tumor models, combining the antibiotic ciprofloxacin with the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine has helped restore treatment sensitivity and suppress tumor growth. Whether similar benefits occur in patients remains uncertain.

A major challenge is the lack of reliable clinical tests for detecting bacterial infections inside living tumors. Treating patients without confirming infection could also disrupt beneficial microbes and contribute to antibiotic resistance.

The researchers recommend examining existing patient records for evidence that antibiotic and chemotherapy combinations improve outcomes. They argue that “retrospective clinical verification can sometimes be the only pathway to clinical progress.”

Such research could help identify patients most likely to benefit, but additional clinical evidence is needed before routinely combining antibiotics with chemotherapy for aggressive cancers.

Reference: “Poor prognosis outcome tumors, bacteria-infected tumors and nanodrugs: current evidence and hypotheses towards a paradigm change for treatment” by Henk J. Busscher, David W. Grainger, JinPu Yu and Da-Yuan Wang, April 2026, Cancer Biology & Medicine. DOI: 10.20892/j.issn.2095-3941.2025.0748

Writer Olivia Maule spoke with biologist James O'Hanlon about his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats." In it, he explores deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it amounts to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most deception in nature happens without much awareness from the creature involved. From a moth that has evolved to look like a hornet to orchid mantises that mimic flowers to lure in pollinators, deception is part of these animals' nature. But in his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), biologist James O'Hanlon turns to tactical deception aimed at manipulating what another animal believes — and whether we can consider this as lying.

Live Science spoke with O'Hanlon about his book, and why so many scientists are reluctant to say "yes, animals can lie."

Read an excerpt: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

Olivia Maule: The chapter opens with a moment from a talk you gave, where a woman at a senior citizens' club asked you a question about orchid mantises that left you stumped: "How does the mantis know to look like a flower?" Why did that moment stick with you enough to open the chapter with it?

James O'Hanlon: Because it was such a simple, straightforward question that I couldn't give a simple, straightforward answer to. At the time, I was thinking about what's going on in the brains of the animals I was looking at — does a camouflaged animal actually know it's camouflaged? Does an insect that looks like a leaf know what a leaf even is?

And it got me thinking: they don't need to. This stuff just sort of works because it works. That's a completely different type of deception to the other things dealt with in this chapter, which is: Do animals actually know that they can lie? Can they intentionally deceive, like we can?

OM: So would you say you have an answer to that question now? And if so, what would it be?

JO: If I had to answer, it would be yes. It looks like it. But scientists are paid to be pedantic, so it's always going to be a "yes, but" or a "possibly." There's a ton of behaviors that look like animals can lie, and they're really good at it, but with any type of science, we're never going to know for certain what's going on in their brains. It's a best-guess situation.

The Pink Orchid Mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) is an insect that uses camouflage as a form of protection in the wild.

OM: How would you help readers hold those two ideas at once — that this is genuine deception in an evolutionary sense, but not necessarily lying in the way we mean it as humans?

JO: When we talk about lying in humans, there's a value judgment attached. We're judging each other on whether we're good or bad people, doing right or wrong things. We kind of have to relax that judgment a bit when we're talking about other animals.

I guess it becomes an ethical question — we look at deception as being right or wrong, morally good or bad, and that's a very human-centric way of thinking. Ethics and morals are things we've developed to help us get along in our own societies. Who knows what's going on in animal societies?

There's an example in the book of golden snub-nosed monkeys that use deceptive alarm calls to scare off other members of their group and steal their food. After a while, those monkeys start to get ignored, and the group stops responding to their calls. So maybe there is some sort of animal-society rules and regulations keeping lying in check. Maybe. We'll see.

OM: I do want to ask about the chimpanzee study, in which chimpanzees intentionally misled competitive handlers to boxes without food, and compare it to the 2017 dog study, where dogs learned to mislead handlers much faster than the chimps did. What did that result do to the assumption that big brains equal better lying?

JO: There's always been this idea that lying is a really cognitively complex task — you need the brains not just to realize what's going on in the real world but to imagine a false possibility, and then to describe that false possibility as if it were real. We talked that up as something you need big brains to do, and there was also a bit of patting ourselves on the back for being such smart animals — maybe we lie a lot because we're such smart animals. But the more we learn about animals and what they're capable of, the more we realize they can do so much more than we thought was possible with the brains they've got.

OM: Does that suggest lying is less about raw intelligence and more a byproduct of needing to survive in a group?

JO: As far as all the examples of tactical deception in the book that look like they're intentional, they all, or mostly all, come from social animals. We don't seem to see it in solitary animals. That's a big sign that maybe it's something that's evolved because individuals can exploit it in a social setting. But it's still such early days, so it's hard to say for definite how different levels of sociality, and how bonded individuals are within groups, correlate with more deception.

OM: Could you elaborate on the distinction between deception and something like the camouflage you introduce in the book with the tiger's stripes?

JO: Compared to the intentional deception we've been talking about, things like camouflage still work regardless of whether the animal doing it is aware of it or not. The idea behind lying and tactical deception is that it only works because it's intentional — there's some sort of choice to do it.

Whether the animals are aware of that choice is another question. Think about the way we do it as humans — are we always aware of it? Whenever your friend asks whether you like their new haircut and you just go, "Yeah, it's great," you don't really think about the fact that you're probably lying. It's just part of our social norms. So it becomes a very blurry gray area very quickly.

OM: It sort of boils down to the choice of it all — whether they can choose to do it or not, which raises the question of whether it's conscious or unconscious.

JO: It's tricky, because as soon as you start talking about it being a conscious decision these animals make, you start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches, giggling at how evil they are for pretending to hide nuts. And you start to think, maybe this isn't the right exact way to think about lying and deception.

OM: The drongo — a bird renowned for its ability to deceive meerkats — doesn't just have one trick, it cycles through different alarm calls and borrows calls from other bird species. Does that put it in a different category of liar than squirrels or monkeys, or is it the same trick with a different toolbox?

JO: It could just be the same trick with a different toolbox. It's essentially doing the same thing as the golden snub-nosed monkeys we were talking about before. But birds are incredible singers and have very flexible call structures, and there are tons of birds that can mimic other birds. Maybe you just pair that ability with this deception adaptation, and it looks a bit different, but it's the same kind of trick.

OM: Do you think these behaviors are inherited, or just innate characteristics of the drongos themselves?

JO: I don't know — I'd be interested to find out. The evolutionary aspect would be that the ones who can do it get more food and are better able to survive and reproduce. Whether they learn it from their parents, it's entirely possible. We know from birds in general that they learn calls from their parents and their social groups, and there are even studies showing birds will start learning calls while they're still in the egg, listening to their parents' calls. So it's entirely possible they learn this trick socially, as far as I know.

Male cuttlefish can change their body pattern to trick competing suitors.

OM: In writing this book, what did you find is the best way to approach understanding animal behavior as it relates to human traits like lying or deception?

JO: I think there's still a little bit of baggage from old-school thinking, that you need bigger brains to be deceptive and tricky in this way, and there are still people who think it must be things like the higher apes and great apes that are capable of this stuff.

As soon as you start studying that in something like an invertebrate, it's really hard to get the idea out there — other scientists will come back and say, "No, that couldn't be possible, this must be some other type of behavior, or it just looks like tactical deception, but it's not." This happened with the researchers who did the work on cuttlefish that change one side of their body to look like a male and the other to look like a female — there was a lot of resistance to that idea, seemingly just because it was a cuttlefish, this little invertebrate, so it couldn't possibly be capable of such cleverness. But as far as the actual evidence goes, and what we can see, it's really no different from what we see in these big-brained mammals, so why not assume the same thing is going on?

A lot of it comes down to the culture and practice of science, and the people doing the science. We're supposed to be as objective as possible, but we're still humans, we're still animals. It takes a while for ideas to change.

OM: Is there a risk that this caution has become its own kind of bias, where we assume human specialness by default until proven otherwise?

JO: Yeah, definitely. It's important, as part of scientific practice, to be as objective as possible, and as a general rule, to not anthropomorphize. But at the same time, we're just animals too — we're just another one of the great apes. We share characteristics with lots of different animals, so it's not a huge stretch to think that what's going on in our brains is also going to be similar to what's going on in other animal brains.

It's just a question of when we apply that kind of thinking, and when it's useful or not. Something similar happened in the field of understanding pain in animals — scientists studying this were always trying not to anthropomorphize, not to assume animals experienced pain the way we did. Then, the more we understood it, it became quite clear that they probably did, and it almost became an ethical question to stop with the anti-anthropomorphizing and instead go, no, we know what pain feels like, we can say that.

We're never going to be able to see what's going on in their brains, but that doesn't excuse us from recognizing what's going on. So I think it became okay not to anthropomorphize but to recognize the similarities between humans and other animals, as opposed to always hinging on the differences between us.

OM: At the end of the chapter, you say that if you buy a scientist a few drinks, they'll eventually admit that animals can lie. I obviously can't buy you a drink over email, so I'll just ask you directly — do you think animals can lie?

JO: Yeah. I'll give a straightforward yes, because I can.

You need to get scientists out of their professional mindset, where they're trained to give the most correct answer that they can. And yes is a bit of a broad-stroke answer for a scientist when they're in professional mode, which is why you need to get them out of the lab and out to a bar or a cafe, and get them talking in human terms again.

OM: What would you say is your favorite example in the book — what are you most excited for readers to walk away with?

JO: I'll go with the cuttlefish example — the one where a male cuttlefish will put male color patterns on one side of its body and female patterns on the other, to trick other male cuttlefish. It might be my favorite because, as a young student, I worked on this particular species of cuttlefish. We were studying them, watching all of their crazy color-changing abilities, and just wondering what on earth they must be talking about, what was going on there. Then, years later, seeing the aforementioned research come out was this sort of lightbulb moment — that's what I was watching them do all along. I think that has a personal connection for me. I spent so much time looking at these creatures, being mesmerized by what they were doing, with no idea what was going on. So it was great to see scientists come in and figure it out, and answer those questions.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6403. New Research Resolves the Mystery Behind Van Gogh's The Starry Night

Starry Night, the iconic painting by legendary Impressionist Vincent Van Gogh, has inspired debate among art historians and astronomers for decades. Was the painting something that Van Gogh was spontaneously inspired to create in the early morning hours in July 1889, or did it present a realistic depiction of the night sky over Saint-RÃ©my (where he painted it)? According to a recent study conducted jointly by South Korean telescope manufacturer SLLAB and the School of Space Research at Kyung Hee University, it's the latter.

For over a century and a half, scholars focused primarily on religious and symbolic interpretations of the painting. It was not until the mid-1980s that studies were presented that analyzed its astronomical aspects. These were conducted by UCLA art historian Albert Boime (1984) and Harvard astronomer Charles Whitney (1986), who examined celestial correspondences and proposed constellation identifications based on a mid-June date. However, the two reached conflicting conclusions, and no studies since have examined the painting using observational geometry.

The study, presented in Scientific Reports (a Nature journal), instead narrows the dates on which a crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades star cluster (which appear closely together in the painting) fell within Van Gogh's field of view. The study's first author, Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, CEO of SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University's School of Space Research, has spent years building telescopes and observing the night sky and was inspired to weigh in on the debate.

(a)The stars in The Starry Night (1889) overlaid by the real stars after matching for size, orientation, and position; red dashed lines show the residual differences. (b) The stars in CafÃ© Terrace at Night (1888), left, and the stars around the Summer Triangle. Credit: Kim et al., Scientific Reports

"To an observational astronomer, the cluster of stars in The Starry Night is the Hyades in Taurus," he said. "But the moment I read the earlier studies explaining it as Aries, I heard the painting calling to me." The research builds on Kim's previous book (released in 2025) and began with two field trips to France in 2019 to gather additional evidence and add quantitative data. Traditionally, the painting was dated to June 18th, 1889, based on a letter Van Gogh wrote to his brother, Leo.

However, on that date, the Moon was in its waning gibbous phase, which does not match the slender crescent in the painting. On July 22nd, the Moon was a crescent, and the Hyades cluster would have been seen rising in the east alongside Venus (placing it in the Taurus constellation). In the past, that date was thought to be one when Van Gogh experienced one of his seizures, but cross-analysis of the original French and Dutch letters and the details mentioned in both suggests his seizure began in late July.

Using on-site photographs taken in Arles, the team verified Van Gogh's field of view overlooking the RhÃ´ne River. Afterward, they traveled to Saint-RÃ©my, where they located the spot where Van Gogh drew the landscape in preparation for his painting. They then conducted a statistical shape analysis to confirm that the five central stars in the painting corresponded to the Hyades cluster, which matched even more closely in the pen drawing Van Gogh made after he finished the painting.

These results suggest that the sky in the painting was based on actual observation rather than pure impressionist feeling. The methods employed could also be extended to other historical night paintings, leading to collaborative efforts between astronomers and art historians. The team has already used the same method on another of Van Gogh's famous creations that features stars in the sky - CafÃ© Terrace at Night (painted in 1888) - and found a possible match to the Summer Triangle asterism.

"I hope this work prompts a renewed, multidisciplinary look at the sequence and working methods of the Saint-RÃ©my paintings, and at Van Gogh's movements that summer," Kim said. "Our conversation with Van Gogh's other skies is still ongoing. We plan to tell those stories one by one."

#6402. Mosquitoes Are Picky Eaters – and Scientists Just Figured Out Why They Prefer Certain People

A person who attracts one mosquito species may be far less appealing to another. In a study involving 119 volunteers, researchers at Florida International University (FIU) found that three major disease-carrying mosquito species consistently preferred different people. Not a single participant was attractive to all three.

The findings, published in iScience, challenge the idea that some people are universally irresistible to mosquitoes. Instead, attraction appears to depend on how individual species detect the chemicals and microorganisms associated with human skin.

The researchers examined three species responsible for spreading diseases such as dengue, Zika, yellow fever, and West Nile virus. Each responded to a different combination of biological signals.

Aedes aegypti, a mosquito that typically bites during the day, preferred people who wore no added fragrance and whose skin lacked certain volatile compounds. It also showed a slight preference for men. Another daytime feeder, Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger mosquito), was more attracted to people with elevated levels of ketones and plant-like chemicals naturally released by the skin.

Culex quinquefasciatus (southern house mosquito), which feeds after dark, responded more strongly to differences in the skin microbiome. This community of bacteria, fungi, and other microorganisms varies from person to person. Certain bacterial families were associated with increased mosquito attraction, while others appeared to discourage feeding.

Human scent contains more than 1,000 volatile organic compounds, many of which remain poorly understood. To investigate which biological characteristics influence mosquito attraction, the scientists collected odor and skin microbiome samples alongside their preference tests.

Led by Ph.D. student Kaylee Marrero, the study was the first to directly compare how multiple mosquito species respond to the same individuals. The researchers had not anticipated such clear differences between species.

“We didn’t expect the species to prefer different people when we started the study,” Marrero said. “Each species having a distinct microbial signature that they use as a cue was so surprising to me.”

The results suggest that mosquitoes have evolved different ways of detecting and interpreting the complex chemical signals produced by human skin.

“This connected so well with the differences in skin bacteria and odors,” said Matthew DeGennaro, a neurogeneticist who leads the research team and directs the Biomolecular Sciences Institute at FIU. “It is clear to me now that our skin microbiomes define our human odor signature. Each species found its own way to decode that signature.”

Understanding which chemicals attract or discourage individual mosquito species could help researchers develop repellents designed to interfere with specific scent signals rather than relying on a universal approach.

“Isolating the components of human odor that attract or repel mosquitoes could lead to novel strategies to combat vector-borne diseases,” DeGennaro said.

By identifying the chemical compounds and microbial signatures associated with each species, the researchers are establishing a foundation for more targeted mosquito control. Future repellents could potentially be tailored to the species responsible for transmitting diseases in particular regions, although further research will be needed to translate these findings into effective protection.

Reference: “Individual humans are more attractive to certain mosquito species” by Kaylee M. Marrero, John S. Castillo, Dani Lucas-Barbosa, Anthony J. Bellantuono, Matthew A. Marrero, Dariel Cid, Andre L. Costa-da-Silva, Niels O. Verhulst and Matthew DeGennaro, 31 July 2026, iScience. DOI: 10.1016/j.isci.2026.117006

Funding: Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
