#6401. Researchers May Have Solved a Puzzling Contradiction in the Ryugu Sample

The Solar System's asteroids are sometimes referred to as fossils because they preserve evidence of the conditions when the Solar System formed. Asteroids are critically different than their planetary counterparts. On the rocky planets, the rock itself has been subjected to billions of years of change. On Earth, tectonic plates have melted rocks, exposure to water has altered its mineral content, and pressure deep inside the Earth has transformed its crystalline structure. Cosmic and solar radiation has also driven fundamental changes on some worlds, and across Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, a mixture of these factors have altered the rock.

But asteroids and the parent bodies they came from haven't been subjected to all of these forces. In many ways, they remain unchanged from the early days of the Solar System, 4.5 billion years ago. They haven't remained completely unchanged; that would be next to impossible. But their ancient state and what it can teach us about the Solar System's history is why we've sent missions to collect samples and return them to Earth.

In 2020, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA)Hayabusa 2 successfully completed its sampling mission to asteroid Ryugu and returned its precious sample to Earth. Almost six years after its arrival on Earth, the Ryugu sample is still generating valuable scientific results, as researchers examine its mineralogical and chemical composition.

The newest results are in research titled "Pervasive poorly crystalline Mg-rich hydrous silicate material in C-type asteroid matrices." It's published in Nature Communications Earth and Environment, and the lead author is Reon Okumura from the Division of Geosciences and Civil Engineering at Kanazawa University, Japan.

Ryugu and other carbonaceous chondrites present an apparent contradiction. It involves aqueous alteration, where contact with water creates mineralogical and chemical changes in rocks and minerals. Aqueous alteration isn't a rare action that happens only in space environments; it's common on Earth. The best-known example is how clay forms from common silicate rocks in Earth's crust, from exposure to water. It's basically how soil is created.

A JAXA official successfully retrieving the 16 kg capsule that it contained a sample from the asteroid Ryugu. (Courtesy: JAXA)

There's obviously no soil on Ryugu, but there is aqueous alteration. "C-type asteroid-derived samples, including Ryugu and carbonaceous chondrites, consist primarily of fine-grained matrices of magnesium-rich hydrous silicates formed by aqueous alteration," the paper states.

The contradiction stems from the matrix of minerals in the asteroid. There seems to be two components, each altered under a different set of aqueous conditions. That implies that Ryugu's interior matrix is patchy, which is highly improbable. An asteroid can be clumpy on a macroscale, but how can it have two components in the same mineral matrix? That's been a nagging question in cosmochemistry: how can aqueous alteration happen to some of the matrix while leaving some of it more intact?

The authors write that Ryugu's matrix is "commonly interpreted as mixtures of serpentine- and saponite-like phyllosilicates..." Serpentine and saponite are both found on Earth, where they're created when rock is aqueously altered. But despite the fact that they're generally interpreted to be these substances, "their mineralogical characteristics do not fully correspond to these well-crystalline terrestrial layered silicates."

To dig into this apparent contradiction, the researchers used the SPring-8 synchrotron radiation facility and the Photon Factory High Energy Accelerator, both in Japan. Both of these research facilities use powerful x-rays to look deeply into the Ryugu sample.

They found the expected serpentine and saponite, but they also identified something else: poorly crystalline magnesium silicate hydrate (M-S-H).

âWhat makes M-S-H particularly interesting is that it can accommodate a wide range of magnesium-to-silicon ratios,â said study corresponding author Keisuke Fukushi of Kanazawa University. âThis flexibility may be key to understanding how water-rock interactions proceeded without erasing pre-existing chemical differences within their parent asteroids.â

The composition of most materials remains stable when subjected to the same aqueous conditions. But previous research and lab work shows that M-S-H is a bit of an oddball: it can exist in the same aqueous conditions and have different magnesium to silicon ratios. So this work suggests that M-S-H is the initial starting point, and that if it formed into serpentine and saponite phases, the presence of M-S-H can explain the two different outcomes without necessarily requiring a different aqueous alteration for each one.

This illustration helps explain the findings. The previous interpretation on the left shows tighly packed grains of serpentine and saponite, with the parallel lines representing their orderly crystal structure. The alternating blue and green lines in some grains represent interleaves of serpentine and saponite layers in the same crystal. There's almost no empty space between grains. The image on the right shows the new model, with a background of poorly crystalline M-S-H, making up the bulk of the matrix. In this model, serpentine and saponite are a minor part of the matrix, and are poorly-formed intrusions. Image Credit: Keisuke FUKUSHI, Kanazawa University (2026)

The study says something not only about Ryugu, but about carbonaceous chondrites. Much of their matrices could be poorly crystalline M-S-H. If this material precipitated first and then was transformed later, the different compositions of clay-like minerals found in the matrix could have arisen without a separate, distinct water environment for different regions of the parent asteroid.

"Assuming its initial precipitation and subsequent mineralogical transformations, a wide range of compositional variation can be produced without requiring separate aqueous conditions for each local composition," the authors write. "This framework provides a physicochemical basis for explaining the compositional variability and associated phyllosilicate diversity of C-type chondritic matrices within a parent-body alteration scenario."

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) is developing a reputation for successful sampling missions, one of the most difficult type of missions to complete. The original Hayabusa mission, though plagued with difficulties, still managed to return a small sample from asteroid Itokawa in 2010. Hayabusa 2 was a complete success, as this research shows. And at this moment, JAXA's Martian Moons eXplorer mission is on its way to collect a sample from Phobos, the largest of Mars' two moons.

That sample should be on Earth five years from now. What questions will it answer?

#6399. Human-Elephant Conflict Could Explode Across Southern Africa As Scientists Warn of a Growing Crisis

Human-elephant conflict could intensify across Southern Africa as expanding farmland and increasingly dry conditions reshape the landscape.

By 2085, the area of Southern Africa facing a high risk of elephant crop raids could expand by 33% to 100%, according to a new study. Researchers predict that growing human populations, expanding farmland, and increasingly dry conditions will intensify encounters between elephants and farmers, with human land use playing the largest role.

Southern Africa is home to more than 290,000 African savanna elephants (Loxodonta africana), representing roughly 70% of the continent’s savanna elephant population. As agricultural communities expand into elephant habitat, crop raids can destroy valuable harvests, threaten household incomes, and undermine local support for wildlife conservation.

To understand what causes these encounters, Evan Patrick and colleagues analyzed reported elephant crop raids from 2004 to 2020 across 38 communal conservancies in Namibia. They combined statistical methods designed to identify causal relationships with machine learning models that predict where conflicts are most likely to occur. Their analysis extended across a larger landscape encompassing northern Botswana and parts of Angola and Zambia.

“We find that human population growth, cropland expansion, and climate-driven aridity in core elephant-protected areas drive conflict risk,” the authors write.

Population growth was linked to higher crop-raiding rates during both wet and dry seasons, while expanding cropland and developed areas were associated with increased incidents during the wet season. Drier conditions within protected elephant habitats also predicted more wet-season raids in neighboring communities, suggesting that shortages of natural resources may push elephants toward agricultural land.

The researchers mapped potential conflict hotspots by examining vegetation cover, proximity to rivers, roads and wildlife fences, population density, and vegetation productivity. Tree cover and vegetation greenness were particularly influential predictors, while roads and fences appeared to shape where elephants encounter human settlements.

High-risk areas included regions north of Namibia’s Etosha National Park, the northeastern Zambezi Region, and parts of northern Botswana surrounding the Okavango Delta and Moremi Wildlife Reserve. Many of these landscapes connect important elephant habitats with areas used for farming.

Crop raids also showed pronounced seasonal differences. Historical records revealed that average incidents per mapped grid cell were more than ten times higher during the wet season than during the dry season, when agricultural activity and vegetation conditions differ.

Using projections of climate, population growth, and land use, the team modeled potential changes through 2085. All four scenarios predicted increasing crop-raiding activity and a wider distribution of high-risk areas, although the magnitude depended on future development patterns.

The greatest increases occurred under a scenario involving substantial population growth and land conversion, known as “regional rivalry.” Under this pathway, projected wet-season crop raiding was approximately twice as high as under the more sustainable development scenario. Even the scenario with the most severe climate impacts did not produce the highest conflict levels.

“Aggressive human land-use expansion leads to the most dramatic increases in conflict, with climate impacts playing a significant but smaller role,” the researchers explain.

Reference: “An expanding human footprint drives escalating human–elephant conflict across a transboundary African landscape through 2085” by Evan Patrick, Maxwell Pepperdine, Christy Yu, Sophie Pesek, Olivia Somhegyi, Joana M Krieger, Nickolas McManus, Ezequiel Fabiano, Colgar Sikopo, Patrick R Roehrdanz and Ashley Larsen, 7 July 2026, PNAS Nexus. DOI: 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag205

#6398. The JWST May Have Found Where Heavy Black Hole Seeds Formed

Astrophysicists think that the supermassive black holes (SMBH) we see in the modern Universe are the result of a long drawn-out process. That process is referred to as the hierarchical black hole mergers framework. It explains how some SMBH can reach such staggering masses. Some of the most massive appear to have billions of solar masses.

The idea is that these SMBH start out as seeds, and those seeds are stellar-mass black holes. Two processes create them. One is when massive stars between about 8 and 50 solar masses reach the end of their lives of fusion. They either explode as supernovae, and their cores collapse, forming black holes, or they collapse directly into black holes. The other is when two neutron stars merge.

In between stellar mass black holes and SMBH are intermediate mass black holes (IMBH.) These black holes range in mass from about 100 solar masses to 100,000 solar masses. The observational evidence for IMBHs is still thin, but it's persistent.

A 2024 paper focused on Omega Centauri, a globular cluster on the outskirts of the Milky Way, as the site of an IMBH. A group of fast-moving stars in the center of Omega Centauri can only be explained by the presence of an IMBH with about 8,200 solar masses, according to that work.

Gravitational waves from a black hole merger are also evidence of an IMBH. A 2020 paper presented the only direct evidence of an IMBH when the waves showed that two black holes, with 85 and 66 solar masses, merged to create an IMBH with about 142 solar masses.

But what are the birthplaces of these IMBH? Some must have formed in the early Universe to act as seeds for the SMBH we see today.

Research titled "Massive star clusters detected by JWST as natural birth places to form intermediate-mass black holes" may have the answer. It's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics, and the lead author is Viola Bocchi. Bocchi is from the Sapienza University of Rome.

"The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a population of dense stellar systems at high redshifts, including the âCosmic Gemsâ arc (zââ¼â10.2) and the âFirefly Sparkleâ (zââ¼â8.3). With masses in the range 105 Mââ107 Mâ and half-mass radii in the range â¼0.4â15 pc, these systems are ideally suited to form intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via collision-based models," the authors write.

The Cosmic Gems arc is a gravitationally lensed galaxy, and the JWST observed its light when the Universe was only about 460 million years old. The JWST found five dense star clusters there.

The Cosmic Gems was first discovered by the Hubble during its Reionization Lensing Cluster Survey (RELICS) and was identified as a powerful source of radiation during the Epoch of Reionization. In 2024, the JWST took another look and found the five Young Massive Clusters (YMC), the first discovery of such ancient clusters.

The Firefly Sparkle is another gravitationally lensed early galaxies, imaged only about 600 million years after the Big Bang. The JWST found 10 YMCs in the Firefly Sparkle.

This image shows the Firefly Sparkle galaxy, where the JWST found 10 YMCs. It also shows a pair of companion galaxies. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Chris Willott (National Research Council Canada), Lamiya Mowla (Wellesley College), Kartheik Iyer (Columbia University)

This research shows that not only were all these YMCs sources of ionizing radiation, they may have been the birthplaces of IMBH.

Due to the density in these YMCs, n-body simulations weren't viable. Instead, the researchers used a model based on runaway collisions and mass-loss by stellar winds to estimate the resulting IMBH masses. They then validated these results against direct N-body simulations of compact star clusters.

"With masses in the range 105 Mââ107 Mâ and half-mass radii in the range â¼0.4â15 pc, these systems are ideally suited to form intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via collision-based models," the authors write. "Our estimates yield typical IMBH masses in the range â¼102 Mâ to â¼4âÃâ103 Mâ, implying typical formation efficiencies on the few percent level."

The clusters in the Cosmic Gems yieled the heaviest IMBH, with masses ranging from 1600â2700 Mâ. "The extreme compactness of the Cosmic Gems clusters (Rhââ¼â1 pc) facilitates the formation of black hole seeds with high masses of 1600â2700 Mâ," the authors write. Rh â¼â1 pc is the radius of the sphere that contains half of the clusterâs total mass and measures how compact a cluster is.

"The low metallicity (Zââ²â0.02âZâ) is a critical factor for retaining the seed mass despite stellar winds," the authors write.

These young clusters also have low metallicities because not enough stars have lived and died in them to generate higher metallicity. Their low metallicity played a critical role in forming IMBH. Low metallicity limits mass-loss due to stellar winds, and that let the objects keep growing.

The results from the Firefly Sparkle are different. "In contrast to the Cosmic Gems, these clusters exhibit significantly larger radii (Rhââ¼â4âââ6 pc) for typically lower total masses (105âââ106âMâ)," the authors write. That creates cores that are less massive, limiting the potential for the runaway collision process to create IMBH. The black hole masses in Firefly Sparkle range 1.8âÃâ102âââ8.1âÃâ102âMâ. That's about 180 to 810 Mâ, which represents the lower boundary for IMBH masses.

This artist's illustration shows what the Firefly Sparkle galaxy looked like about 600 million years after the big bang if it wasnât stretched and distorted by gravitational lensing. This illustration is based on images and data from NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Ralf Crawford (STScI). Science: Lamiya Mowla (Wellesley College), Guillaume Desprez (Saint Mary's University)

Overall, the lower range for IMBH masses in this work (~100 solar mases) is comparable to black holes formed by massive Population III stars, the Universe's hypothetical first stars, which were likely extremely massive. But, "the upper bound extends significantly higher, allowing the most massive clusters to produce objects firmly in the âheavy seedâ regime," the authors write. "Forming such heavy seeds is highly beneficial to form SMBHs at high redshift."

These results aren't observational in the sense that the JWST didn't observe any IMBH. But they do show a plausible environment where IMBH could form and potentially lead to the SMBH we see in the centers of galaxies like ours.

These results could also explain the JWST's Little Red Dots. Their spectra are often interpreted as being powered by SMBH. "Our results suggest that dense massive star clusters could provide possible massive seeds from which the SMBHs in the LRDs may have grown," the researchers write.

The researchers state some caveats, based on some acknowledged weaknesses in their work. Many properties of these clusters are unknown, including their rotation and their internal structure, which could change the outcomes and lower the IMBH masses.

The initial mass function also isn't known, but it could be top-heavy. "This possibility, along with a possible primordial mass segregation, would favor the formation of massive IMBHs, though we did not explore it here in detail," the authors explain.

Researchers will no doubt dig deeper into these young massive clusters and try to fill in some of the blanks that remain. But this research shows that they could be the source of the heavy seed IMBH that eventually form SMBH.

"Our results suggest that these dense, metal-poor clusters are viable factories for heavy seeds that are capable of growing into the supermassive black holes observed in the early Universe," the authors conlude. .

#6397. How brain implants turn thoughts into speech

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Casey Harrell, here at home in the summer of 2026, uses a brain-computer interface to communicate with his family.

Regents of the University of California, Davis

Casey Harrell lost his voice to ALS or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. As a volunteer in a clinical trial, he’s helping scientists test a brain-computer interface. Electrode arrays that are implanted in Casey’s brain send signals to nearby computers, where those signals are translated into words he intended to say.

Casey uses this system every day to talk with his wife, daughter, friends and work colleagues. The moment he realized that it worked was “pure joy,” Casey says. Even though the researchers scripted his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”

This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me follows Casey and the fast-moving neuroscience that enables him to speak.

Patients paralyzed from the neck down can manipulate robotic arms with their thoughts. The woman in this video is controlling a robot with her mind. The so-called BrainGate system relies on a sensor of electrodes implanted in the motor cortex of the brain. Researchers hope by implanting electrodes in the brain it can read the brain signals meant to move the muscles involved in speaking, and translate the person’s intention to speak into comprehensive speech produced by a computer.

Laura Sanders: Controlling things with your mind. It sounds like science fiction, but it’s definitely real. Today, we’re going to explore what it’s like to communicate with a brain implant that decodes your thoughts and turns them into words.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? The voice is absolutely an integral part of your identity. Hello? That added layer of it being you. Do you want to talk? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: From Science News, I’m Laura Sanders, and this is The Deep End, Talk to Me. Okay, so what is BrainGate? It’s an experimental system that connects electrodes that are implanted in a person’s brain to a nearby computer. It’s called a brain-computer interface, or BCI. The goal here is big: to help people with paralysis or brain injuries or missing limbs regain control over their world.

Leigh Hochberg: BrainGate clinical trials have now been going on for nearly 22 years. It’s 21 point something at the moment.

Sanders: Leigh Hochberg is the director of the BrainGate Consortium and Clinical Trials. He also has a job at Massachusetts General Hospital, Brown University and the VA.

Hochberg: People who may have had a brainstem stroke and suddenly lost the ability both to move and to speak, or for somebody with ALS who is progressively losing the ability to move or to speak, there’s long been a hope that particularly implantable brain-computer interfaces could restore communication and could restore mobility.

Sanders: In 2004, a BrainGate device was implanted into a person’s brain for the very first time. That person was a man named Matthew Nagle, and he had been paralyzed in an accident. With BrainGate, he could control a computer cursor with his thoughts. Here’s a 2008 report from IT World.

Technology gave him hope. He was one of four testing BrainGate, a new technology where a chip is implanted in the brain that picks up electrical impulses. A computer then interprets those impulses as actions.

Hochberg: Those early studies have been really encouraging, and I think speaks to the potential for the field.

Sanders: Over the years, there’s been amazing examples of people using BrainGate. People have used it to click around on the internet, play video games, one woman who was paralyzed was even able to drink a cinnamon latte with a robotic arm.

Casey: I am using a decoder for about ten to 14 hours a day, seven days a week, for the past almost two years, making me the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.

Hello.Sanders: Next up, those algorithms assembles these phonemes into words by making its best guess about what Casey wants to say.

Sanders: Jules hates when people read his screen before he’s ready to say what he wants. This particular hate inspired a joke in his stand-up routine.

[Jules audio]: People read off my screen while I’m typing and try to finish what I am saying. It’s like having to constantly deal with an over-competitive charades partner.

Sanders: Jules and Casey encounter other people’s impatience constantly. Not that it isn’t well-intentioned but still, it does not help. Even worse, they face other people’s misconceptions about what they’re capable of. Casey is an interesting, funny and compelling conversationalist. That might not be apparent to everyone who doesn’t slow down to hear him. And that’s an assumption that really bothers him.

Casey: It is incredibly undignified and a terrible consequence of the health care system to treat me like this very quickly.

Sanders: Brandman has seen this dismissal, this mistreatment too. It happens with some of the volunteers he works with on the BrainGate 2 project I mentioned earlier. That’s the same trial Casey’s in.

Brandman: I think as healthcare professionals, we conflate the inability to communicate with the lack of understanding. And I’ve witnessed this firsthand as I’ve watched doctors and nurses interact with my BrainGate participants and then treat them as if they are invalid. Or they’re not there because they’re unable to express themselves. And in fact, I go out of my way in the intensive care unit on the wards and dealing with anyone who’s dealing with my participants to say, look, you know, they’re inside. They’re there. They can understand everything that’s happening. They just happen to not be able to speak. And so please treat them with the respect and dignity that they deserve. And it’s a constant challenge for the participants that I work with. And it’s the reality of which we face and it’s the bias that we have against people that can’t speak for themselves.

Sanders: Casey and the other people with ALS are not alone. Many people who have trouble talking or who just need more time can be judged this way. Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.

Nagin: It’s how people see you. And so when you have ALS and you cannot move and you don’t even have facial expressions and you’re hooked up to machines, people assume you’re not there. And we see this every day where people either don’t talk to the person with ALS, assuming that they can’t respond. They speak really loudly and slow. Their mind is completely working.

Sanders: For now, Casey’s words may be slow. But despite all the drawbacks, they are still an absolute marvel. Remember Hochberg from the start of this episode? He’s one of the neuroscientists who works with Casey, and he told me a story from the first few days of testing after Casey’s BCI was implanted.

Hochberg: We gave him a 50-word vocabulary on day one. And even on day one, he was able to say some key sentences from those 50 high-value words.

Sanders: At this point in the testing, Casey was asked to say some pre-specified sentences so researchers could test their system out.

Casey: Most of the sentences were what we called closed loops.

Sanders: That means that the researchers already knew what brain activity patterns should go with the words Casey thought about saying. It was a test to see if the system was working.

Casey: The decoder would be able to verify whether I was right or wrong, giving me short preloaded sentences to say. I was asked to say, “What good is that?”

Sanders: “What good is that?” is not the most poignant sentence ever uttered, but it had a big effect both in the room and for researchers joining remotely by video.Casey: “What good is that?” Everyone is crying after I am successful.

Sanders: Later on, there was time for Casey to actually express himself.

Sanders: Things only got better from there. To set the scene here, during this session, Hochberg was in his office and Casey was at his home, sitting in his living room. Hochberg was watching Casey on a screen.

Hochberg: On the second session, came back and gave him the full 125,000 plus word English dictionary to be able to select from. That is, the decoders and the AI and the machine learning language models would be able to select from basically a full dictionary. And the first thing that he said was something along the lines of, “Is this thing on?” Kind of a funny statement.

The next thing that he said on the second day of using brain-computer interface, or the second thing that we decoded was, “I’m looking for a cheetah.” And it’s the second day. We know there’s all kinds of opportunities for decoding errors. And when I saw that, I said, you know, there’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using an implanted brain-computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah. You know, that’s obviously a decoding error and that’s fine.

Sanders: Hochberg could see Casey on the screen, but he couldn’t see something really important that had just happened in the room.

Hochberg: His four-year-old daughter had just walked into the room dressed as a cheetah.

Sanders: Here’s Casey remembering the same moment.

Casey: Yes, I remember this time very well. It was the second session of talking that I experienced early in August 2024. My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit. This was one of her favorite animals. They were going through a phase where everything they did was super fast, running from thing to thing. Everyone was thinking that it must have been a mistake that I could not use this language. It was so random. This was only from the people like Leigh who were not in the room with us. The researchers who were there could validate that, yes, I said this. I meant it because of the unique context.

Sanders: It’s one of those moments that many parents have. A kid does something cute, a parent plays along. But in this moment for Casey and his child, it was anything but ordinary.

Hochberg: And she was born around the time that he was diagnosed with ALS. And one could imagine that because the voice that was coming out of the computer was a version of his own voice, and then the rest of the interaction was between dad and daughter. And it was between parent and child.

Sanders: The BCI had given Casey something priceless, a minute to play with his sweet little cheetah.

Casey: I was quietly confident that it would work the way it ended up working for me. I had done a lot of research and the thing was that the technology was on the cusp of a breakthrough. And why not me? I asked myself.

Sanders: Early on in the research project, Casey and his wife had been told not to expect it to work. This was an experiment and the outcome was far from certain. Casey, however, was optimistic.

Hochberg: So to me, seeing it work that quickly and that powerfully really, really emphasized that these are technologies that are going to be able to restore not only activities of daily living, not only key kind of instrumental activities of daily living, but they’re going to restore communication between parent and child. They’re going to restore communication between friends and family and care partners and health care providers.

Sanders: Because this is a podcast about the human voice, I’ve been asking people I interview what their voice means to them. Here’s Casey’s answer.

Casey: It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: Getting it back, even in a limited form, is everything.Casey: It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond, respond to my daughter, especially because that was lacking completely from my life up to that point.Sanders: Casey’s restored voice changed his life.

Casey: It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends. Timing is everything, and that is why having nothing, this is completely revolutionary. And to look back on my previous answer, it is something that really can still improve.

Sanders: At the beginning of the experiment, the research team had told Casey and his wife that they’d be able to try using the BCI for casual chats just a few hours a week. Those hours felt like a huge gift at the time, considering that they hadn’t been able to talk meaningfully for a long time. Here’s Brandman.

Brandman: As we kept coming to his house two or three times a week, things kept getting better and better. And it got to a point where Casey wanted to use the system to say all the things that he wanted to say.Sanders: Early on, only the researchers could set Casey up with the system, plugging him into the Matrix, as he puts it.Brandman: And so our research technologist would start coming to his house three, four, five times a week to don and doff the system to enable him to communicate so that he could go about his day. And so at a certain point, we saw, well, he really wants to use the system. Can we streamline this for him? And so we petitioned the FDA to actually allow us to change the clinical trial protocol slightly so that we could train his care partners to don and doff the system without us being there. And so since then, he’s been a near daily user of the system.

Sanders: That’s a far cry from a few hours a week. I’m going to read you some numbers from a research paper Brandman and his colleagues published about Casey’s BCI in Nature Neuroscience in June of 2026.“Over nearly two years, the participant, that’s Casey, used the BCI for more than 3,800 hours at home with no researchers present to maintain rich, interpersonal communication with his family and friends, independently control his personal computer, and sustain full-time employment, despite being paralyzed. He communicated 183,060 sentences, totaling 1,960,163 words, at an average rate of 56 words per minute. He labeled 92 percent of sentences as being decoded at least mostly correctly.”

Those numbers in this very bare-bones science kind of way are dry, if we’re being honest. But when you stop to think about it, each sentence, each of those nearly two million words, is a tether that connects Casey to his life. They’re messages to his daughter, jokes with his partner, texts to his friends. They’re games of Wordle with his wife and kid. Here’s Casey and his family in a video shot by UC Davis Health.

Okay, so no A, but we got an E. M-I. O. M-I. Good job, team. We are almost there.

Sanders: We’ve talked a lot about words here and the fundamental ways that Casey’s BCI has restored his ability to say them. But Casey’s BCI goes a little bit farther than that. It gives him the ability to add some extras. He’s got some bells and whistles up his sleeve.Casey: It is really a communication device, first and foremost, and less of a tool that I use to make funny remarks. But I do have that as well in my repertoire. For example, I have the ability to add sound effects to what I am saying.

Sanders: For instance, Casey has a sad trombone sound.

Casey: So if I find something funny and want to say, LOL, the theme from the TV show, Seinfeld, will play.

[theme song]Sanders: This is what he means. These jokes make me think of Jules, which made me wonder if Casey, like Jules, could also swear with his system.

Casey: To answer your question of whether I can curse with this device, I most certainly [beep] can.

Sanders: So for all your inquiring minds, there you have it. Looking ahead a bit, there’s a lot happening on the horizon. The science here is moving fast and many companies are working on similar systems. We’re going to cover that in a few episodes. But for now, Casey is alone. He is an N of 1, as the scientists say – the only person using a brain-computer interface for communication this heavily.

Casey: I hope to have this changed very soon because I feel like everyone who wants this should have the opportunity to have it, especially those who are with my disease.

Sanders: Hochberg tells me that this drive to help others is common among people who volunteer for these sorts of clinical trials.

Hochberg: Each participant in the trial has been just so generous and so clear that they recognize that it’s early days in the research, but they’ve told us that they want to help other people with paralysis. They want to be able to allow people with brainstem stroke or cervical spinal cord injury or ALS or other paralyzing illnesses or injuries to have improved function, to be able to regain control over that computer or regain the fluent speech and communication that they had previously. So it’s that generosity of spirit that has really defined the participants in our BrainGate studies.

Sanders: Casey’s generosity, his drive to help other people, really shines through as we talk. But I want to get back to him. I ask Casey what it’s been like to have this technology in his home, in his brain. He tells me how precious our voices are, and how easy it is for many of us to forget that.Casey: We take them for granted. The ability to scream when you are running and want to get out some stress. The ability to say sweet nothings into your partner’s ear. These are the things that life is all about. And when you are robbed of those times, you want them back at all costs. And this is why this is good enough for now, and we should have accelerated approval for devices like this.

Sanders: Casey’s BCI is slow compared to the pace of a normal conversation. And it gets things wrong occasionally.Casey: Sorry, I am trying to answer you. And it is changing what I want to say. And I am being stubborn instead of trying to say it another way, which I will do now.[Sanders audio] I’m not in any rush. You take as much stubborn time as you want.

Sanders: And it needs an internet connection and power. And let’s not forget that Casey has an adapter coming out of the top of his head. But these are solvable problems, one that scientists are actively working on. So not perfect, but as Casey puts it, good enough for now.

Scientific efforts to restore voices have been transformative for Jules, Casey, and others. But the ability to separate a voice from a body also raises new possibilities for our societies and for our lives.

MA: His voice will live on in whatever videos or things we’ve captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally, and that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: On the next episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into a strange new digital world where voices might not be what they seem.

Hany Farid: And so we are living in, I think, in equal parts an exciting time and a terrifying time. And somehow those are coexisting.

Sanders: What changes are coming in a world where voices can be so easily cloned?Farid: Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

#6396. The Mystery of Hair Growth Patterns May Finally Have a Simple Explanation

A new study reveals how subtle interactions between cells and chemical signals may shape the intricate patterns of mammalian hair.

The precise arrangement of hair follicles across an animal’s skin may arise from a surprisingly simple process. Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have developed a mathematical model showing how cells responding to chemical signals can generate distinct hair patterns in two mammalian species, without requiring a complex system to determine where each follicle forms.

Published in PNAS, the research challenges a long-standing explanation for hair follicle development and suggests that variations in the same underlying cellular process could produce different patterns across species.

Hair follicles begin forming before birth in specialized embryonic structures called placodes. These structures also give rise to feathers and most types of scales. Their arrangement varies between species, but scientists have long debated how developing tissues establish such organized patterns.

For laboratory mice (Mus musculus), the prevailing explanation has been the expansion-induction model. According to this theory, each newly formed placode releases an inhibitory molecule that temporarily prevents others from developing nearby. As the skin expands, new areas move beyond the molecule’s influence, allowing additional placodes to form in the spaces between existing ones.

Although this model can account for the developmental patterns observed in laboratory mice, researchers have not experimentally established that it explains hair follicle organization more broadly across mammals.

A research team co-led by Athanasia Tzika, Senior Lecturer, and Michel Milinkovitch, Professor in UNIGE’s Department of Genetics and Evolution, investigated a different mechanism called chemotaxis. This process allows cells to move in response to chemical gradients. It also helps white blood cells navigate toward areas of inflammation.

The researchers created a mathematical model in which mobile cells in the dermis respond to an attractive chemical signal produced by the epidermis, the skin’s outer layer. As the simulated embryonic skin grows, these interactions spontaneously produce placodes in patterns that closely match the developmental sequence observed in laboratory mice.

“Our findings show that the observed patterns do not require a complex system telling each placode where to form,” explain Muhamet Ibrahimi and Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, researchers in the Department of Genetics and Evolution. “Instead, placodes emerge spontaneously from local interactions between cells and chemical signals.”

The researchers next examined the spiny mouse (Acomys dimidiatus), a rodent whose hair follicles form a highly regular, directionally organized pattern. Unlike the arrangement found in laboratory mice, this distinctive configuration cannot be explained by the traditional expansion-induction model.

Using experimental data obtained through three-dimensional imaging of embryonic skin, the team adapted its mathematical model to reflect the spiny mouse’s particular biochemical characteristics and skin growth patterns. The same chemotactic mechanism successfully reproduced the species’ characteristic follicle arrangement.

These simulations suggest that different mammalian hair patterns could emerge from a shared process governed by cell movement and chemical signaling, with species-specific differences in how those interactions unfold. The results provide a potential alternative to the conventional model, although mathematical agreement with observed patterns does not establish that chemotaxis is the mechanism operating in living skin.

“Our work suggests that simple cellular interactions can generate the remarkable diversity of tissue architectures observed throughout evolution,” concludes Athanasia Tzika. “The differences observed between species therefore result from the same self-organization process, but with variations in the interactions between cells and chemical signals.”

Reference: “Chemotactic self-organization captures the dynamics of mammalian hair follicle patterning” by Muhamet Ibrahimi, Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, Athanasia C. Tzika and Michel C. Milinkovitch, 2 July 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2530407123

In his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats," biologist James O'Hanlon surveys deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it adds up to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most trickery in nature happens without a shred of awareness behind it. An orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) doesn't know it looks like a flower, and a moth with eyespots on its wings has no concept of the predator it's startling. These are adaptations shaped by natural selection over countless generations, not conscious choices. But a smaller set of animal behaviors look like something else entirely — deliberate tactical, and aimed at manipulating another individual's beliefs, the same way human lies do.

Figuring out which is which turns out to be one of the trickiest questions in animal behavior research, James O'Hanlon, zoologist and science communicator, told Live Science.

In this excerpt from his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), O'Hanlon explores camouflage, mimicry and misdirection throughout the natural world, building toward the book's central question: Can animals tell lies?

In it, O'Hanlon examines one of the strongest candidates for an animal that deliberately lies: the fork-tailed drongo (Dicrurus adsimilis), a small African bird whose ever-changing repertoire of false alarm calls has made it a favorite subject for scientists studying tactical deception.

James O'Hanlon interview: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're publishing for free to all our readers. If you'd like more exclusive book excerpts, as well as news analysis, scientist interviews and in-depth features, please consider subscribing.

Fork-tailed drongos are remarkable vocal mimics and can do an uncanny impression of a meerkat alarm call. The meerkats respond to it just as they would one of their own and scamper to safety. Meanwhile the drongo flies in once more to steal the meerkats' abandoned food.

They don't stop there; drongos mimic a whole range of other animals' signals, mimicking various avian neighbors like the caped glossy starling or the pied babbler. Those ever-watchful meerkats fall for the ruse once more, leaving their meals behind. Researchers have identified over fifty unique deceptive vocalizations in the drongo's arsenal.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By constantly rotating their "cry-wolf" tactics, these birds ensure their victims don't grow wise to the deception, allowing the theft to continue unabated. Yet, their cleverness isn't reserved solely for exploited meerkats.

This remarkable talent for mimicry extends to other creatures as well. Pied babblers and sociable weavers, who both forage in groups upon the earth, frequently find themselves bamboozled into fleeing their food by these false warnings. Had the legendary boy who cried wolf possessed such adaptive ingenuity, he might have successfully maintained his trickery.

It would, however, have resulted in a peculiar fable with an entirely different, perhaps darker, moral lesson.

It's early days in our understanding of whether animals can tell lies. Social group-living animals are likely candidates for finding animal tricksters in the wild, and we have only scratched the surface of what kinds of trickery goes on in these societies. Time will tell whether similar forms of deception are happening in the subsonic songs of whales and dolphins, the chemical mists of ants and termites, or the barks and howls of wild dogs.

Meerkats are tricked by fork-tailed drongos mimicking the alarm calls, so the birds can swoop in and steal their food.

Despite the growing list of evidence, scientists are still hesitant to conclude definitively that animals can intentionally deceive another, in a similar way to humans. This might have more to do with the professional conduct of scientists than it has to do with the reality of what goes on in animal societies.

Firstly, one of the most important rules in studying animal behaviour is to not anthropomorphise animals. In other words, don't project human-like qualities or emotions onto other species. Scientists must be completely objective and not assume that other animals think, behave or make decisions for the same reasons we do.

Since lying has always been perceived as a human behaviour, scientists are incredibly hesitant to conclude that it could be happening in other animals.

The second reason is that scientists are trained to never definitively conclude anything. There is an idea in science that you can disprove things, but never really prove things. This is why you will find scientific writing littered with phrases like "the evidence suggests," "it's probable that," or — my personal favourite — "the most parsimonious explanation is," and so on and so forth.

A professional scientist will often give a direct "No" answer but rarely a direct "Yes." It's like squeezing blood from a stone. But this is a good thing. What often sounds like indecisiveness or a lack of certainty is actually just good professional practice. It's part of a scientist's job description — to consider all possible explanations for the observations they have made and examine every possibility on its own merits.

Then the conclusions that are drawn come down to which of these possibilities is most likely. In a universe of infinite possibilities and scales of enquiry, it would take an impossible amount of overwhelming data for scientists to exclude all possibilities but one.

To understand how these creatures swindle their way to survival, Liars, Cheats, and Copycats reveals the science behind camouflage, mimicry, and masquerade. Taking readers on a journey from tropical rainforests to the darkness of deep ocean trenches, James O’Hanlon explores how animals and plants use deception to avoid predators, lure in prey, and even reproduce.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

#6394. The Vera Rubin Has Found Two More of the Milky Way's Dim Satellites

Massive galaxies like the Milky Way have a retinue of smaller, dim satellites on their outskirts. They're hard to detect, and while astronomers have found about 65 of the Milky Way's dwarf satellite galaxies, and about 40 globular clusters in its halo, they suspect there are many dwarf satellites and globular clusters yet to be found. Now the Vera Rubin Observatory has found two more.

The Milky Way's satellites are either small dim galaxies or globular clusters, and both are part of the assembly history of the Milky Way through mergers. These two detections by the Rubin, found in its Early Data Preview 2 (EDP2) released in July 2026, are almost certainly the beginning of many more discoveries of Milky Way satellites by the powerful observatory. One is a most likely a dim dwarf galaxy named Aquarius IV, and one is a globular cluster named Rubin-GC1.

This figure shows the locations of both Rubin-GC1 and Aquarius IV. Rubin-GC1's detection was particularly impressive, since it's in the direction of the Milky Way's bulge, a region with a dense stellar population and thick dust. Image Credit: NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA, ESA/Gaia/DPAC, W. Cerny

The discoveries are presented in two new papers.

One is titled "Discovery of the Distant, Ultra-faint Milky Way Satellite Aquarius IV with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Early Data Preview 2." It's published in Research Notes of the American Astronomical Society, and the lead author is William Cerny, an astronomy student in Yaleâs Graduate School of Arts and Sciences.

"We present the discovery of Aquarius IV (RubinâJ2201â0234)âthe first ultra-faint Milky Way (MW) satellite to be identified using data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory," the authors write. It was confirmed in images from the Dark Energy Camera. The authors say it's a low-luminosity, compact stellar system in the outer Galactic halo.

It's stellar population is ancient and low-metallicity. "These properties closely resemble those of the smallest and faintest confirmed ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs), though a globular cluster classification is not ruled out," the researchers write.

Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies can have as little as a few hundred stars, which makes them smaller than some globular clusters (GCs). But there's one critical difference between UFDs and GCs: UFDs have dark matter while GCs don't (except for a few possible outliers).

Only a small number of the stars in Aquarius IV have been detected so far, so whether or not it is a UFD for sure will depend on deeper imaging and spectroscopy.

âWhat I find especially exciting is that these discoveries are just the beginning for Rubin,â said first author Cerny. (He is also the second author of the Rubin-GC1 study, which has been accepted by The Astrophysical Journal Letters.)

âIf the observatory can find systems this faint and difficult with only its preview data, its full 10-year survey will undoubtedly provide us with many more Milky Way satellite discoveries,â Cerny said. âThese new satellites will give us new opportunities to test models of galaxy formation, trace the assembly history of the Milky Way, and investigate the nature of dark matter.â

These panels are images centered on Aquarius IV. The star in the lower panel marks a Blue Horizontal Branch star used to determine the distance to Aquarius IV. The stars in the bottom panel are also coloured according to their probability of being members of Aquarius IV. The grey stars are almost certainly not members, while colours ranging from purple through red, orange, and yellow represent increasing probability. Image Credit: William Cerny et al 2026 Res. Notes AAS 10 239

The second paper is "Rubin Observatory Reveals a Dust-Shrouded Halo Globular Cluster in Ophiuchus," and it will be published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. It's currently available at arxiv.org and the lead author is Aashay Pai. Pai is a graduate student in the Department of Physics at the University of Chicago.

"We present the discovery of the Milky Way satellite Rubin-GC1 (Rubin J1628â1735) using data from the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatoryâs Early Data Preview 2," the authors write. The stars in Rubin-GC1 have an intermediate age of about 9.2 billion years, and are moderately rich in metals, meaning it's most likely a very faint GC. "Together, these properties suggest Rubin-GC1 is most likely a star cluster in the faint tail of the luminosity function of globular clusters surrounding the Milky Way," the authors write.

Based on comparisons to the Sagittarius dwarf spheroidal galaxy, Rubin-GC1 is most likely a cluster accreted to the Milky Way, associated with the Sagittarius leading arm. The Sagittarius leading arm is a massive tidal stream of stars from the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy, torn away as that galaxy merges with the Milky Way.

The panel on the left shows the Sagittarius trailing and leading arms. (The DES images are not part of this work.) The image on the right shows roughly where Rubin-GC1 is located, shown with the gold star. The Milky Way's center is shown with the black cross, and the circle with the dot inside is the Sun. Image Credit: Left: By NOIRLab, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=139367207. Right: Aashay Pai et al. 2026.

âFinding new Milky Way satellites in Rubin Observatory data has been an exciting future prospect for most of my career,â said Marla Geha, a professor of astronomy and physics in Yaleâs Faculty of Arts and Sciences, and co-author on both studies. âIt is remarkable this is now a reality.â

Rubin-GC1 was detected in the direction of the galactic bulge, where stellar density is very high and the dust is thick. Finding it in those conditions makes the detection even more impressive. "The discovery of Rubin-GC1 highlights the potential of Rubin to uncover faint, resolved satellites in dust-shrouded regions of the Milky Way, including remnants of the accretion events that have shaped the Galaxyâs hierarchical assembly," the authors write.

The panel on the left is what's called a 'smoothed isochrone filtered stellar density map.' It's a visualization tool in astronomy used to detect and map faint structures like ultra-faint dwarf galaxies by masking out field stars based on a color-magnitude curve. The panel on the right is a more familiar type of image used to show the region itself. Image Credit: Aashay Pai et al. 2026.

âThese discoveries are incredibly promising,â Geha said. âContinued discoveries will allow us to complete the census of satellite galaxies around the Milky Way, which is a key to understanding how the faintest galaxies form.â

The Vera Rubin Observatory is mostly known as a transient-detecting observatory, and as the maker of a ten-year long movie of the sky in its Legacy Survey of Space and Time. But it's more than that. As it images the sky repeatedly, dim objects will become clearer. "The sensitivity of Rubin LSST will steadily increase, and systems similar to Aquarius IV are ultimately expected to be detectable with >85% efficiency using the same search algorithm applied here," the authors of the first paper write.

Not only that, but its observations will work with observations from other observatories, like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, to detect even more objects. "The identification of Rubin-GC1 heralds an exciting era of discovery as Rubin, Euclid, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope pierce the shroud of Galactic dust to reveal faint satellites that were hitherto hidden by our Galaxy," the authors of the second paper write.

Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies and globular clusters are puzzle pieces in the history of the Milky Way's growth through mergers. The mergers are ongoing, as interactions between the Magellanic Clouds and the Milky Way show.

By finding more of the Milky Way satellites, a picture of all of these mergers, and the role dark matter plays, will become clearer. By mapping out these objects and the streams they're sometimes a part of, astronomers can detect where dark matter also concentrates in clumps. These dark matter sub-halos will show how our galaxy grew larger by consuming smaller galaxies with their own dark matter halos.

#6392. Comets Probably Didn’t Bring Life’s Ingredients to Earth After All, New Study Reveals

New research suggests Mars may have been better suited than Earth to receive life’s chemical ingredients from comets, although the chances remain surprisingly slim.

Comets have long been considered possible sources of the chemical ingredients that helped life emerge on Earth. But new research suggests these icy visitors were extremely unlikely to deliver those molecules in sufficient quantities, challenging a theory that has shaped scientific thinking for nearly a century.

Using advanced computer simulations, researchers led by the University of Cambridge found that comet impacts would almost always destroy fragile organic compounds before they could contribute to the chemistry of early life. Even under favorable conditions, successful delivery would have been extraordinarily rare. The findings, published in Scientific Reports, also suggest that Mars may have offered slightly better conditions for receiving these molecules.

Comets contain carbon and nitrogen-bearing compounds, including hydrogen cyanide (HCN), a molecule involved in chemical reactions that can produce some of life’s essential building blocks. Their ability to transport these substances across the Solar System has made them central to theories about how prebiotic chemistry began on Earth.

“Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a ‘get out of jail free card’ that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life,” said lead author Dr. Richard Anslow from Cambridge’s Institute of Astronomy. “It’s kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it’s highly unlikely.”

The problem lies in the violence of comet impacts. According to the simulations, comets generally approach Earth at speeds and angles that make the survival of their organic cargo extremely unlikely. Most of these molecules would vaporize during impact rather than reach the surface intact. The researchers reached this conclusion by combining models of comet trajectories, atmospheric interactions, impact physics, and the formation and evolution of comet populations.

To investigate the likelihood of successful delivery, the team concentrated on HCN, which is regularly detected in Solar System comets. Their calculations showed that impacts capable of preserving the molecule and depositing it at useful concentrations would have been exceptionally uncommon.

The number of comets striking Earth also fell sharply during the planet’s first 500 million years, leaving at most a handful of opportunities for meaningful HCN delivery. Even if some molecules survived, they would likely disperse before the chemical reactions needed for life’s emergence could advance far enough.

“It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going,” said Anslow. “We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way. But it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke.”

The investigation builds on earlier research published in 2023, when Anslow and several colleagues proposed that closely spaced planets could help comets deliver organic molecules. In such systems, gravitational encounters might allow comets to move between planets while gradually slowing down, increasing the chances that their chemical cargo could survive an eventual impact.

The new study examined whether similar conditions could have existed in our Solar System, using recent advances in simulations of comet impacts and planetary dynamics.

“We’re learning more and more all the time about how our Solar System and the Earth formed, and pulling this together with lots of different advances in modeling, which allowed us to investigate this idea that has been around for close to a century,” Anslow said.

If comets were not a major source of Earth’s prebiotic molecules, other explanations remain possible. Asteroids struck the early Earth much more frequently, and their impacts could have triggered chemical reactions that produced organic compounds. Alternatively, the necessary ingredients may have formed through chemical processes occurring on Earth itself, without requiring delivery from space.

Although the results cast doubt on cometary delivery to Earth, the researchers identified Mars as a somewhat more favorable destination. Mars is smaller than Earth and currently has a much thinner atmosphere, conditions that could allow more cometary material to reach its surface. This may have increased the chances of organic molecules surviving impacts during the Solar System’s early history, when comet collisions were more common.

However, the simulations do not establish that comets successfully delivered prebiotic molecules to Mars. They indicate only that the process may have been more feasible there than on Earth.

“This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars,” said Anslow. “Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative, is that it didn’t happen on either planet.”

The findings could also help astronomers assess the chemical environments of planets orbiting other stars. In planetary systems where several worlds orbit close together, gravitational interactions might slow incoming comets enough to improve the prospects for delivering organic molecules.

Future observatories, including proposed successors to the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory, could help investigate these planetary systems. Identifying environments where “bouncing” comets might survive long enough to deliver their chemical cargo could provide one way to narrow the search for potentially habitable worlds.

Reference: “Cometary impacts an unlikely pathway towards the origins of life on Earth” by Richard J. Anslow, Catriona H. McDonald, Amy Bonsor, Paul B. Rimmer and Auriol S. P. Rae, 28 October 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-74214-y

The research was supported in part by the Royal Society, the Leverhulme Centre for Life in the Universe, and the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI).

#6391. Stubborn Asteroids Around White Dwarfs Resist Becoming Dust

White dwarfs are the remnants of a stars like our Sun. For their sizeâthey're roughly the size of Earthâthey're extremely dense, and have about as much mass as the Sun. That means they have enormous gravitational power, enough power to tear apart objects that get too close.

For a long time, white dwarfs appeared to be alone in space, not including any stellar companions. Then observations showed that some of their surfaces were polluted with metals. Astronomers surmised that these metals were raining down onto their surfaces from rocky debris. Then came observations that some white dwarfs were surrounded by debris disks. After that, even more piercing observations found evidence of rocky bodies in the disks: small planets, moons, or asteroids.

An example of these is WD 1145+017, which seems to be orbited by several small rocky bodies, being torn apart and raining debris down onto the white dwarf's surface.

Scientists are curious about this process and how effectively white dwarfs can shred smaller bodies and form debris disks. As they find white dwarfs with disks, asteroids, and even planetary systems, explanations need to keep pace.

In new research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, researchers examined how efficiently white dwarf tidal forces can break asteroids apart. The research is titled "Size Limits on Tidal Debris around White Dwarfs: The Kilometer-size Barrier." The lead author is Jordan K. Steckloff, senior scientist at the Planetary Science Institute.

"Compact disks of planetary debris orbiting white dwarfs provide a crucial window into our understanding of evolved planetary systems," the authors write. "The formation of these disks has been widely modeled with tidal fragmentation of minor planets that are rubble piles with no internal strength."

This artist's illustration shows a white dwarf surrounded by a debris disk, with asteroidal fragments in the foreground. The more astronomers find white dwarfs with debris disks, the more they want to understand how they're created. Image Credit: NASAâs Goddard Space Flight Center/Scott Wiessinger

That's a problem because real rubble piles have some cohesive strength. Also, all three of the asteroids we've sampledâItokawa, Ryugu, and Bennuâare rubble piles. The force that holds these types of asteroids together is called the Van der Waals force. It's a weak, short-range force that attracts and repulses atoms and molecules. But as gecko feet show, it can be very effective.

In their work, Steckloff and his co-authors show what happens when this strength is included in modelling: "breakup of these rubble piles sets a maximum fragment size, and we calculate this size for water ice, iron, and material densities corresponding to the lunar highlands, Vesta, and the Earth," they write.

âNothing is truly strengthless,â Steckloff said. âTiny attractions between grains called Van der Waals forces give comets and asteroids a minimum strength 10 to 100 times weaker than pulling apart freshly fallen snow.â

According to this research, the typical internal strength of a rubble pile is â¼10â1000 Pa, which is about one million times weaker than solid rock. In that range, the maximum size for fragments is about the same as small asteroids, between about 0.1 and 1 km in diameter. "This limitâthe kilometer-size barrierâalso represents the characteristic sizes of tidal fragments," the authors explain. "Most of the debris mass is contained in fragments of this size."

These panels show characteristic debris size by distance from a white dwarf with about 0.6 solar masses and cohesive strength. The panel on the left is for a strength of 10 pascals, and the panel on the right is for a strength of 1 kilopascal. The results show characteristic fragment sizes of about 100 meters and 1,000 meters respectively. Image Credit: Jordan K. Steckloff et al 2026 ApJL 1004 L27

The authors say that as a consquence, models of disk formation around white dwarfs need to include another dust-generating factor in order to explain the dusty disks in observations. That likely means collisions rather than tidal forces.

The force that shapes the end-state of the disk is called PoyntingâRobertson drag. It explains how solar radiation affects dust grains around stars, including white dwarfs, making the dust spiral inward. This only works if the dust grains are small enough to be subjected to the drag but not so large that radiation pressure drives them away. This work shows that fragmentation itself isn't enough to create dust this small.

Observations in our Solar System agree with these results. When the comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 approached Jupiter in 1992, the gas giant's powerful tidal force pulled the comet apart. But not into dust; instead, the comet was torn into fragments 100m to 1,000m in diameter, which then plunged into the planet.

This Hubble Space Telescope image shows comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 broken into fragments after it approached Jupiter in 1992. Two years later the fragments approached Jupiter again and plunged into its atmosphere. Image Credit: NASA.

The research extends beyond asteroid fragment sizes in disks. It also shows that fragments maintain their orbits. They experience only tiny, fractional changes in their velocities "on the order of one part per million to one part per 100 million," the authors explain. "Such tiny changes in speed result in negligible changes to the orbits of the fragments, which remain in practically the same orbit as prior to disruption."

There are a lot of factors involved in the creation of a white dwarf's dust disk, and this work places an important constraint on one of them. "Understanding the progression from an intact minor planet to a sea of dust that is accreted onto a white dwarf is an outstanding challenge," the authors write. "In this Letter, we demonstrate a sharp constraint on the first step of this process." The work shows that some type of grinding process like collisions is required to generate white dwarf dust disks.

âUnderstanding the details of how debris around white dwarfs is produced and evolves is important for putting the observations into context,â said study co-author Kat Volk from the Planetary Science Institute. âThis will help us understand what happens to the small bodies in orbit around a star as it undergoes the end stages of its life.â

#6390. Comets probably didn’t deliver life’s building blocks to Earth

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The speed and angle of impact would have destroyed most organic compounds from comets

Comet McNaught shines over Australia a safe distance from Earth in this photo taken in 2007. Most comets that collided with the early Earth would have been moving too fast and at too steep an angle for prebiotic molecules to survive the collision and kick off chemical processes that gave rise to life, a new study suggests.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The chemical building blocks that gave rise to life on Earth probably didn’t come from comets.

Most comets would have been traveling too fast and at too steep an angle to Earth for prebiotic compounds to survive impact with the planet, researchers contend October 28 in Scientific Reports. While the study doesn’t completely rule out the possibility that comets brought these molecules to Earth, it contradicts the long-standing idea that comets seeded Earth with the chemicals necessary for life to arise.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Even though we see that comets contain all of these molecules in really high concentrations, it’s not straightforward to go from there to saying we’re going to have all of these available for prebiotic chemistry on the surface of the Earth,” says Richard Anslow, a planetary scientist at the Met Office, the national meteorological service for the United Kingdom in Exeter.

Comets carry carbon- and nitrogen-containing molecules left over from early in the solar system’s formation. These molecules can react to form biologically important compounds like sugars and DNA. Scientists have long thought that comets could have delivered these building blocks to Earth when they collided with the planet during its first billion years.

But it’s important to revisit these ideas as our understanding of both comets and the early solar system improves, says Nicolle Zellner, a physicist at Albion College in Michigan who was not involved in the study.

In the new work, Anslow and colleagues used computer simulations to predict the likelihood that a chemical called hydrogen cyanide would survive a comet’s journey through Earth’s present atmosphere and its impact with the planet’s surface. The early Earth’s atmosphere was probably much denser, so would have been even more destructive.

The strong chemical bond between the carbon and nitrogen atoms in hydrogen cyanide can release energy that drives later chemical reactions necessary for life. It also makes the molecule particularly stable compared to other carbon-based chemicals.

“It’s probably one of the more robust molecules to surviving impacts,” Anslow says. “So if things look bad for hydrogen cyanide, then we think it’s going to be much harder for other, more complicated molecules that are more likely to be broken down during these impacts.”

Based on the simulations, a comet impact that kept hydrogen cyanide intact would be extremely unlikely, the team found. On average, the simulations suggest that only one impact would have been able to deliver a meaningful amount of hydrogen cyanide to the planet’s surface over more than a billion years. For hydrogen cyanide to survive the crash, the comet would have to be larger than 100 meters across, slow moving and traveling at an oblique angle to Earth.

A comet that met those narrow criteria would also have had to crash into land, rather than an ocean, to kick off any biologically useful chemistry. If the comet landed in the ocean, any hydrogen cyanide that survived would be diluted too quickly to trigger those reactions.

While still improbable, comets may have been more likely to deliver carbon-based molecules to Mars than to Earth, the simulations showed. Mars’ thinner atmosphere and smaller size meant that comets would impact at lower speeds. That could mean that more compounds could survive the collision.

If Earth’s carbon-based chemicals didn’t come from comets, they may have come from carbon-rich asteroids called carbonaceous chondrites, says Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist at Western University in London, Canada, who was not involved in the study. Other sources might have included volcanoes and hydrothermal vents.

The study “definitely will make people think twice about comets being the originator for the delivery of organics,” Osinski says. “I hope other people will try to reproduce these results [and] then potentially try something similar with carbonaceous chondrites as well.”

R. Anslow et al. Cometary impacts an unlikely pathway towards the origins of life on Earth. Scientific Reports. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41598-026-74214-y

#6389. 120 Million Years Ago, Something Extraordinary Was Happening in Earth’s Oceans

Colombia’s ancient seas supported an extraordinary diversity of top predators, offering clues to how life may undergo major evolutionary changes without a mass extinction.

Mass extinctions have reshaped life on Earth, but they may not be the only way ecosystems undergo dramatic evolutionary change.

Roughly 120 million years ago, the seas covering what is now central Colombia were home to an extraordinary mix of ancient Jurassic survivors and emerging Cretaceous predators. Fossils from this remarkably complex ecosystem suggest that some of evolution’s biggest turning points may unfold without a catastrophic mass extinction.

The evidence comes from the Early Cretaceous Paja Formation near Villa de Leyva, Colombia, where the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) houses most of the formation’s fossils. The research at McGill University and CIP was conducted by PhD graduate Dirley Cortés and Professor Hans Larsson of McGill’s Department of Biology.

“This geological formation has produced an exceptionally rich fossil record that includes giant marine reptiles like long-necked plesiosaurs and marine crocodile relatives, as well as turtles, sharks, crustaceans and others,” Cortés explained. “Together, these animals formed the Paja Biota, one of the most ecologically complex marine communities found to date.”

In a previous study, the researchers estimated the Paja Biota’s food web, the network of feeding relationships among its animals. They found it was among the most complex ever to have evolved, with a high diversity of apex predators, animals at the top of the food chain.

“The Paja Formation records an extraordinary process in the history of life, when a ‘perfect storm’ of environmental factors we know to promote ecological complexity coincided with ancient lineages that were about to disappear. At the same time, new groups were beginning to flourish,” Larsson said.

The researchers suspect that greenhouse temperatures, high sea levels, and nutrient-rich coastal waters helped support this exceptional biodiversity and biological transition. New marine connections between the eastern Pacific and early Atlantic oceans through what is now Colombia were probably also part of that rare convergence. Many of these same factors help drive biodiversity today, they noted.

Cortés and Larsson propose calling the pattern a “Biotic Inflection,” a period when many evolutionary lineages nearing extinction coexist with newly emerging groups that later diversify.

“I think we’ve discovered a new model of global biodiversity change. Now we’ll need to see just how widespread this could be in Earth’s history and how we can quantify its impacts,” Larsson said.

Testing the proposal will require additional fossil sampling, more precise dating, and comparisons with deposits elsewhere in the world. Those investigations would help establish how widespread the Biotic Inflection pattern was and when similar events may have occurred in Earth’s history.

Reference: “The Paja Formation of Colombia records uniquely high biodiversity during a biotic inflection in an Early Cretaceous Gondwanan marine ecosystem” by Dirley Cortés and Hans C. E. Larsson, 15 May 2026, Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution. DOI: 10.3389/fevo.2026.1848892

Funding to DC was provided by BESS-NEO program, NSERC CREATE 46283-2015, the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, the Anders Foundation, the 1923 Fund, and Gregory D. and Jennifer Walston Johnson, the Fonds de recherche Nature et technologies Québec (FRQNT no. 30251), and the McGill Biology Department Writing-Year Award 2024-2025. Funding for HL was supported by NSERC RGPIN-2016-06725 and RGPIN-2022-04370.
